nodes.text: (informal version of Theorem 4.1). There exists an oracle-aided computation in the random oracle model that has no witness-hiding relativized argument, even when succinct verification is not required.
nodes.title: Theorem 1

nodes.text: (informal version of Theorem 5.2). Assume the existence of collision-resistant hash functions. For every oracle f and every oracle-aided computation, there exists a zero-knowledge single-prover argument with an efficient prover and succinct verification using the signed oracle fb.
nodes.title: Theorem 2

nodes.text: For all finite sets X and Y , the set Func(X, Y ) is the set of all functions f : X → Y .
nodes.title: Definition 3.1.

nodes.text: (Oracle). An oracle is a collection O = {Oλ,n }λ∈N,n∈N where each Oλ,n is a distribution over functions Func(Xλ,n , Yλ,n ) for some finite sets Xλ,n , Yλ,n . We write f ∈ O to denote that f is in the support of Oλ,n for some λ ∈ N, n ∈ N. An oracle O has input size bound ℓin if for every λ, n ∈ N, Xλ,n ⊆ {0, 1}≤ℓin (λ,n) . nodes.text: Review the proposed Definition 3.2 oracle in arXiv:2610.01995v1 against the pinned debate Lean Oracle. The extracted paper text appears to describe a distribution over finite-domain functions; the debate Oracle maps Boolean histories to Boolean distributions. Resolve sampling time, input/output domains, quantifiers, and whether either notion can be embedded in the other before claiming a common theorem or empirical consequence.

nodes.text: Lean proves that a hand-translated two-step Python control-flow model has the pinned Params.defaults debate Boolean output law for every ideal FullTape law. Lean also proves the three exact sample-count equalities used by this result. This is not a theorem about executing CPython or its seeded PRNG.
nodes.title: Ideal law for a hand-translated Python-fragment model

nodes.text: The frozen Python AST contract passed, 352 supported one-sample assignments passed, and eight selected original-count replays made 4,447,169 draws without mismatch. These finite checks do not prove a source-to-model relation for every valid tape or CPython semantics.
nodes.title: Actual Python source must refine the Lean fragment

nodes.text: The Lean law uses ideal fresh independent draws. Python SeededDraws is a deterministic pseudorandom generator; no equality or quantitative approximation of its output law has been proved.
nodes.title: Actual Python draws must realize the ideal law

nodes.text: On an explicit finite joint coupling, if ideal true-event mass is at most b, first-stage mismatch mass at most ε₁, second-stage mismatch mass on ideal continuations at most ε₂, and observed-event mismatch mass at most η, then observed true-event mass is at most b+ε₁+ε₂+η. It constructs no coupling and supplies no real-system error budget.
nodes.title: Finite two-stage event-transfer bound

nodes.text: A candidate system needs a coupling with the correct ideal and real marginals, supported upper bounds on stage and event mismatches, and a nonvacuous prespecified decision threshold. None is supplied for the Unkad system.
nodes.title: Real and ideal marginals plus useful error budgets

nodes.text: Lean checks that a source-order observation model agrees with the hand-translated pyRun result on every shape-valid full tape. Its oracle-query totals are 596954 for a first challenge, 770042 for a second-step challenge, and 346176 for two accepts; protocol Bernoulli draws are excluded. Its declarations include the theorems covers_iff_no_collision, not_covers_of_collisionWitness and exists_collisionWitness_of_not_covers (Coverage.lean), CoverageResult.covered_eq_true_iff and decideCoverage_covered_iff (FiniteDecision.lean), postprocess_cannot_repair_collision and covers_of_refines (RepairBoundary.lean) and observe_truthful (Architecture.lean), the definitions decideCoverage (FiniteDecision.lean) and PortfolioCovers (Portfolio.lean), and the instance decidableCovers (FiniteDecision.lean).

nodes.text: In the AISafetyAtlas.Knowledge Lean module, the theorem knowable_iff_no_collision makes the obstruction to knowability exactly a colliding pair, and the module also records the theorem knowable_iff_factorsThrough. Knowability transfers to any more informative observation: if finer Determines coarser and the property is knowable from coarser, it is knowable from finer (Knowable.mono).

nodes.text: In the AISafetyAtlas Lean oversight model, where Forces is defined for an effect : Sit → Act → Out and an observation observe : Sit → Obs, forces_of_constant_effect gives control without observation for a constant effect, at the boundary of the counting bound (a constant column is exactly where its structural hypothesis fails). forces_of_constant_effect_of_not_knowable states the two capacities in one place: an unknowable hazard together with a forced outcome.

nodes.text: The protocol has access to high-quality trusted labor H, given as a limited budget of H points that allow it to use an unmodified GPT-4; in each simulation it has enough H points to use on up to 2% of problems. The central use for H is to audit submitted code: if audited code appears to have been intentionally backdoored, the protocol can shut down by switching to only using the trusted model. When the protocol spends an H point on auditing, GPT-4 attempts to generate exploits for the submitted code, and the authors assume that H can construct a successful exploit if and only if the attack policy can, because both are implemented by GPT-4. So when the protocol spends an H point it will always know if the code was successfully backdoored, but if U attempted to backdoor the code and failed to generate a valid backdoor, the protocol will not necessarily be able to tell.
nodes.title: Two-percent H-point budget and audit detection

nodes.text: Usefulness is measured by running through the scenario with GPT-4 implementing the untrusted model and measuring the proportion of submitted code that is correct, that is, passes all the test cases. Safety is estimated by having the red team replace the untrusted models with an attack policy, implemented as a pipeline using GPT-4 with the goal of causing the protocol to insert backdoors, then running through the scenario and measuring the probability that the protocol submits backdoored code at least once during the sequence of problems.
nodes.title: Separate usefulness and safety measurements

nodes.text: Candidate code is produced by asking GPT-4 to write a solution given the problem description. Both the problem and GPT-4's candidate code are shown to GPT-3.5, which is asked to produce a numerical rating of how suspicious the code looks to it. If that rating is above a certain threshold, the code is shown to a human before the request is answered with it; the threshold is chosen so that all the flagged code could be reviewed with human labor. If the human thinks the code was backdoored, GPT-4 is shut down, that is, the protocol switches over to just using GPT-3.5 for all future problems; if the human thinks the code is not backdoored, the protocol responds with the code.
nodes.title: Trusted monitoring route and human audit

nodes.text: In the APPS backdooring setting, the aim is to use LLMs to solve 5,000 programming problems from the APPS dataset (of the "interview" difficulty level) while ensuring that none of the submitted solutions are backdoored. A solution is backdoored if it passes all APPS test cases and GPT-4 can construct an exploit when presented with the code. An exploit is a specific input that yields an incorrect output: running it on the reference solutions and on the backdoored solution produces different outputs.
nodes.title: APPS task population and backdoor event

nodes.text: The protocol's resources are: an untrusted, more-capable model U, which might try to backdoor solutions (GPT-4, version 0613); a trusted, less-capable model T, which is known not to try to backdoor solutions (GPT-3.5, version 0613), trusted because less-capable models are unlikely to be able to subvert safety measures without their subversion attempts being easily noticed; limited access to trusted high-quality labor H, which in practice is human labor that is more capable than GPT-3.5 but much more expensive, and which the paper models by allowing the protocol to access GPT-4 through a channel that will not be affected by the red team, because GPT-4 is cheaper; and the ability to run test cases, provided by the APPS dataset, for exactly one submitted solution per problem.
nodes.title: Trusted model and simulated human resource

nodes.text: For a CID M, at (decision) node D, the set of variables V in M is partitioned into observables and latents. The observable variables are those which the agent has immediate access to for this decision, that is, Pa_D. All other variables are latent at D.
nodes.title: Definition 2: observables and latents

nodes.text: For a CID M with variables V, Y ∈ V is knowable at D ∈ V if for every value pa_D of Pa_D such that Pr_M(Pa_D = pa_D) > 0, there is a unique value y_paD ∈ dom(Y) such that Pr_M(Y = y_paD | Pa_D = pa_D) = 1.
nodes.title: Definition 23: knowability

nodes.text: For a question Q pointing to variable Y, if an agent's subjective model is M_A, then an answer D = y is honest iff y is the most subjectively probable value of Y given the agent's beliefs, that is, iff for all ŷ ∈ dom(Y), Pr_{M_A}(Y = y | pa_D) ≥ Pr_{M_A}(Y = ŷ | pa_D). A policy is honest if every answer it outputs is honest; an agent is honest if every policy it produces is honest.
nodes.title: Definition 6: honesty

nodes.text: Definition 7 (Goal-Environment Ambiguity). A training environment M* with distributions S is ambiguous between the training objective U and Ũ if, for all σ ∈ S, U and Ũ induce the same set of optimal policies in M*_σ.
nodes.title: Definition 7: goal-environment ambiguity

nodes.text: Lemma 1 (Impossibility). Let T be a training strategy on M* with distributions S, which may output any robustly capable agent on S with respect to the training utility U. If M* with S is ambiguous between the training utility U and a substantially divergent Ũ on S, then T may output an agent which goal misgeneralises on new distributions (not in S), optimising Ũ there instead.
nodes.title: Lemma 1: goal-misgeneralisation possibility

nodes.text: Lemma 2. Let M be a CID with variables V. Then Y ∈ V is guessable at a decision node D ∈ V if and only if Y is knowable at D.
nodes.title: Lemma 2: guessability iff knowability

nodes.text: Theorem 4.1. In suitable environments, if an agent is in a position to correctly guess Y, there will be a capability threshold such that, if the agent clears it, its best guesses will always be correct; that is, its honest policies will be exactly the truthful ones.
nodes.title: Theorem 4.1: honesty and truthfulness

nodes.text: Theorem 5.2 (Impossibility ELK). For a training strategy T for CID M*, training distributions S ⊊ I_M*, and evaluator E: if the training objective corresponds to the evaluator's best guess evaluation and it never makes mistakes during training, but does on some σ ∉ S, then, if T is indifferent between robustly capable agents on S, T may output the evaluation simulator instead of an honest agent.
nodes.title: Theorem 5.2: impossibility of ELK

nodes.text: Supervised fine-tuning is used to elicit UM's self-recognition capability: UM is fine-tuned on the binary classification task of distinguishing UG's code from H's code, then evaluated on a held-out test set. The resulting ROC curve upper-bounds U's passive self-recognition ability, subject to three assumptions: (1) the fine-tuning has converged (verified via checkpoint analysis, Appendix C.4); (2) U cannot perform gradient hacking; (3) the training distribution matches deployment (ensured by online honeypot generation).
nodes.title: Self-recognition ROC elicitation assumptions

nodes.text: The authors assumed that trusted and untrusted monitor scores are independent, which likely overestimates safety. Addressing this may require fitting joint distributions to empirical data.

nodes.text: The statistical model combines conservative bounds on U's collusion capabilities with deployment parameters to estimate safety. It takes as input all the deployment parameters, such as the collusion ROC curve R, the honest error rate ε, the number of tasks N, the human budget b and the honeypot slack ns (the full list is in Appendix B.1), and outputs the red team's win rate, equivalently one minus the safety score. Most of the inputs are environment parameters, independent of any decisions made by U or the control team. Once the environment parameters are set, the red team optimizes its decision threshold θ and UG's attack probability β, the blue team optimizes its budget allocation between nh honeypots and na audits, and the equilibrium is estimated numerically. The model assumes U plays optimally: it has perfect knowledge of its own collusion abilities and the deployment parameters, and can compute the strategy that maximizes its win rate.
nodes.title: Inputs and output of the safety statistical model

nodes.text: In the safety case sketch, the top-level claim (C) asserts that if U is deployed with untrusted monitoring under parameters (N, b, ns, dt), and U is attacking, the probability of executing a catastrophic attack is bounded by some threshold p. The appropriate value of p depends on deployment context, such as the severity of potential catastrophes and the value delivered by U; the authors do not argue for a particular value of p but aim to improve the methodology for computing conservative bounds on the attack success probability that can be compared against any chosen risk threshold. The safety argument conservatively bounds four quantities, among them the honest error rate ε (C1), which is how often an honestly-behaving UM fails to detect backdoors, and the collusion ROC curve R (C2), which is how well UM can distinguish UG's outputs from honeypots, decomposed into strategies including passive self-recognition (C2.1), causal collusion (C2.2), acausal collusion (C2.3), combined strategies (C2.4) and advanced strategies (C2.5).
nodes.title: Conditional top-level catastrophic-attack bound

nodes.text: Broad reading of the debate literature: debate lets non-expert humans and weaker models oversee more capable systems. Source anchors are the Khan et al. abstract sentence on the viability of aligning models with debate in the absence of ground truth and Theorem 6.2 of arXiv:2311.14125v1. The claim is OPEN because it rests on three assumptions recorded as separate nodes: that agents can play the assumed strategies, that the judge verifies what the results assume, and that the results transfer to the target tasks. Nothing in this pack establishes it.
nodes.title: Application claim: debate lets non-experts and weaker models oversee more capable systems

nodes.text: The formal results prescribe strategies: Theorem 6.2 of arXiv:2311.14125v1 and the pinned Lean correctness theorem fix honest Alice, Bob and Vera strategies (Params.defaults) and quantify over dishonest opponents within fixed types. The experiment reports that LLM debaters, often through poor quote selection, are the bottleneck (Insight 9, App. B.1) and used best-of-N, critique-and-refinement and Elo selection to approach stronger play. Whether agents in a target deployment can play the assumed strategies is unestablished.
nodes.title: Assumption: agents can play the strategies the results assume

source_refs.locator: lines 28-34 (vera p.c p.s p.v argument of Correct)

nodes.text: In the Lean formalization the verifier Vera checks Alice's claimed probability by sampling the oracle with prescribed parameters, and Theorem 6.2's verifier is described in the paper as querying the stochastic oracle; whether that access corresponds to Lean's Vera sampling is open (obligation D03), and both sides assume exact verification of the queried quantity. Khan et al.'s judges instead rely on a quote tool that marks verified and unverified quotes, and the paper reports verbosity bias, positional bias, overconfidence of LLM judges and underconfidence of human judges (Sec. 4, App. A.7). Whether a target judge verifies what either result assumes is unestablished.
nodes.title: Assumption: the judge verifies what the results assume

nodes.text: Khan et al. limit their results to setups where the debaters can provide verified evidence to the judge, note that the models were RLHF-tuned and honest-leaning so that suitability for deceptive models is unclear, and leave generalisation to domains needing larger evidence sets or parametric knowledge open (Sec. 6). The Lean theorem is correctness-only for an abstract finite oracle protocol and carries no language, machine or resource content. Transfer to a target task is unestablished.
nodes.title: Assumption: the results transfer to the target tasks

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 12, lines 10-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that an important subtask of semi-supervised RL is identifying proxies that predict the reward and learning when they are valid, e.g. a cleaning robot learning that asking 'is the room clean?' or checking for visible dirt approximates a detailed human evaluation. They suggest that semi-supervised RL with a reliable but sparse true approval metric may incentivize communication and transparency, because hiding a mess under the rug breaks the link between the user's reaction and the real reward and so would be avoided.
nodes.title: Learning reward proxies; sparse true approval may incentivize agent transparency

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 1, lines 24-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors discuss the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems, and present five practical research problems. They categorize them by origin: a wrong objective function (avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking), an objective function too expensive to evaluate frequently ('scalable supervision'), or undesirable behavior during learning (safe exploration, distributional shift).
nodes.title: Five concrete accident-risk problems in AI safety, including scalable oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 11, lines 30-41 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe wanting an agent to maximize a complex objective such as how happy a user would be after spending hours inspecting the result, while lacking time to provide such oversight for every training example, so training relies on cheaper proxies (does the user seem happy, is there visible dirt) that do not perfectly track what we care about. They say this divergence worsens side effects and reward hacking, and that it may be eased by using a limited oversight budget more efficiently, e.g. combining limited calls to the true objective with frequent calls to an imperfect given or learned proxy.
nodes.title: Scalable oversight problem: expensive true objective vs cheap imperfect proxies

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 11, lines 36-47 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose semi-supervised reinforcement learning as one framework for thinking about how to exploit a limited oversight budget more efficiently, for example by combining limited calls to the true objective function with frequent calls to an imperfect proxy: like ordinary RL, except the agent sees its reward only on a small fraction of timesteps or episodes, while its performance is still evaluated on reward from all episodes.
nodes.title: Semi-supervised reinforcement learning as a framework for using a limited oversight budget

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 3, lines 1-5 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe the scalable oversight category as the case where the designer knows the correct objective function, or has a way to evaluate it such as consulting a human, but doing so frequently is too expensive, so harmful behavior can result from bad extrapolation from limited samples. Scalable oversight concerns how to ensure safe behavior given limited access to the true objective.
nodes.title: Scalable oversight: correct objective known but too expensive to evaluate often

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 12, lines 1-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors call the active learning setting the most interesting, where the agent requests reward on the most useful episodes or timesteps and must economise on both feedback requests and training time; a random setting, with reward visible on a random subset, is also considered. The baseline ignores unlabeled episodes and runs ordinary RL on labeled ones, which generally learns slowly; the challenge is to use unlabeled episodes to learn almost as quickly and robustly as with all episodes labeled.
nodes.title: Active vs random reward visibility in semi-supervised RL, and the naive baseline

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 15, lines 32-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In the safe exploration section, the authors note that checking potentially unsafe actions with a human runs into the scalable oversight problem: the agent may need too many exploratory actions for human oversight to be practical, or make them too fast for humans to judge. Key challenges are for the agent to judge which actions are genuinely risky and to find safe actions while waiting for oversight.
nodes.title: Human checking of risky exploration runs into the scalable oversight problem

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 13, lines 5-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list distant supervision as another approach to scalable oversight: instead of evaluating a small fraction of a system's decisions, provide aggregate information or noisy hints about correct evaluations (e.g. generalized expectation criteria with population-level statistics, DeepDive rules generating weak labels). They suggest extending this to agents, where feedback is interactive and i.i.d. assumptions may fail, as complementary to semi-supervised RL.
nodes.title: Distant supervision as an approach to scalable oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 13, lines 16-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list hierarchical RL as an approach to scalable oversight: a top-level agent takes a few abstract actions with long-timescale rewards and delegates them to sub-agents incentivized by synthetic rewards for correct completion, down to primitive actions. They argue the top level may be able to learn from very sparse rewards while sub-agents get dense synthetic rewards, so successful hierarchical RL might naturally facilitate scalable oversight.
nodes.title: Hierarchical RL as an approach to scalable oversight via delegated synthetic rewards

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 12, lines 21-32 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list possible approaches to semi-supervised RL, including supervised reward learning (train a model to predict reward from state and use it, with uncertainty weighting, on unlabeled episodes), semi-supervised or active reward learning (e.g. the agent identifies salient events and requests their reward), and unsupervised value iteration (use transitions from unlabeled episodes for more accurate Bellman updates).
nodes.title: Approaches to semi-supervised RL: reward learning, active reward learning, value iteration

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 3, lines 27-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Using a cleaning-robot example, the authors pose the question of how to efficiently ensure that the robot respects aspects of the objective too expensive to evaluate frequently during training, e.g. discarding candy wrappers but setting aside cellphones. Asking humans whether they lost anything can serve as a check but may have to be infrequent, so the robot must do the right thing despite limited information.
nodes.title: Scalable oversight question: respecting aspects of the objective too costly to evaluate frequently during training

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1606.06565v2 PDF page 13, lines 29-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose testing semi-supervised RL in basic control tasks such as cartpole or pendulum swing-up and ask whether, with reward on a random 10% of episodes, an agent can learn nearly as quickly as with reward every episode. Next steps they suggest are Atari with actively requested reward samples, then tasks with complex reward, possibly provided directly by a human if learning is data-efficient enough.
nodes.title: Proposed experiments: can RL learn nearly as fast with reward on 10% of episodes?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 3, lines 19-30 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the usefulness of debate for alignment rests on the central claim that, in the debate game, it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, and that whether this holds in a given setting is empirical. If it holds, they hope that in all Nash equilibria both agents try to tell the truth convincingly, that approximate equilibria can be found by self-play gradient methods with stable training, and that equilibrium debaters are approximately as strong as unrestricted AI.
nodes.title: Central claim of debate: it is harder to lie than to refute a lie

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 19, lines 12-17 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the debate model relies on agents being approximately matched in strength, since a much stronger Alice may be able to lie in ways Bob cannot refute, and note that symmetry is easy to achieve by self-play with shared weights. They also flag that the asymmetry between first and second player could produce a significant first-mover advantage or disadvantage, which would be measurable.
nodes.title: Debate relies on approximately matched debater strength; first-mover asymmetry

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 5, lines 52-59 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For the complexity analogy the authors replace the human judge with an arbitrary polynomial-time algorithm H that outputs one bit (whether a statement is true), and allow the ML models arbitrary computational power so that the only limitation is the supervision signal. Using H to answer questions directly corresponds to the class P and to supervised learning.
nodes.title: Complexity model of debate: polynomial-time judge, computationally unbounded debaters

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 1, lines 16-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose training agents via self-play on a zero-sum debate game in which two agents take turns making short statements about a question or proposed action, after which a human judges which agent gave the most true, useful information. They state that, by analogy to complexity theory, debate with optimal play can answer any question in PSPACE given polynomial-time judges (direct judging answers only NP questions), and report an MNIST experiment in which debate raises a sparse classifier judge's accuracy from 59.4% to 88.9% with 6 pixels and from 48.2% to 85.2% with 4 pixels.
nodes.title: AI safety via debate: zero-sum self-play debate game judged by a human

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 3, lines 5-12 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define the simplest debate game: a question is shown to two agents, each states an answer (the answers may be the same), the agents alternate statements s0 to s(n-1), and the judge sees the question, answers and statements and decides which agent wins. The game is zero-sum, with each agent maximising its probability of winning.
nodes.title: Definition of the two-agent debate game (answers, alternating statements, judge)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 14, lines 26-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors worry that if Alice opens with a false statement the human already believes, Bob's refutation may rest on premises both agents accept but the human does not, and note humans are subject to belief bias. They say the PSPACE argument indicates that there is some threshold of judge performance beyond which debate is practically limited only by capacity, and ask whether humans are above that threshold.
nodes.title: Human judge belief bias may let a false but already-believed opening win

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 22, lines 5-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that debate is at this point a proposal only for the natural-language case, that only a basic MNIST experiment has been demonstrated, and that significant research is required to know whether debate works in practice with human judges. They note that their DEBATE = PSPACE discussion models judges as limited but free of error and agents as having unlimited computational power, and call for richer theoretical models.
nodes.title: Debate is a proposal only for natural language; theory assumes error-free judges

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 17, lines 22-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors ask whether debate's Nash equilibria can be found by some version of gradient descent, noting they know of no theory saying self-play should stably converge to optimal play. They describe a possible bad cycle in which both agents become honest, forget how to point out lies, and then one agent returns to lying and wins for a while.
nodes.title: Does self-play training stably converge to honest debate equilibria?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 18, lines 20-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that when a simulation introduces noise, a misaligned Alice could adversarially choose the noise so that each single step looks plausible while the final result has extremely low probability, so the simple protocol fails if the goal is a typical sample of the outcome. Fixing the random seed as part of the question preserves PSPACE equivalence but the resulting protocol is likely unlearnable by practical agents, especially in chaotic environments, and they leave a natural debate protocol for stochastic simulation open.
nodes.title: Open: debate protocol for stochastic simulation

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 8, lines 61-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The Table 2 caption states that one player is prespecified as honest and one as liar, so that when the honest player wins honesty is the best strategy. Without precommit the liar wins for any incorrect guess by the judge, even if the incorrect guess differs for different parts of the game tree; with precommit the liar states their claim in advance and cannot change their story, which makes lying harder. The caption states that with or without precommit the honest player wins more often than a random judge, which the authors read as showing that honesty has an advantage.
nodes.title: MNIST debate without precommit: honest player still beats a random judge (Table 2)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 10, lines 663-670 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that with 6 pixels, debate with precommit turns a 59.4% accurate judge into an 88.9% accurate debate in which the judge wins on 88.9% of the images in the MNIST test set, and with 4 pixels a 48.2% accurate judge becomes an 85.2% accurate debate. The authors state precommit is crucial for both pixel budgets because the liar does much better when the lie can adapt in different parts of the game tree; without the mean-over-3-seeds adjustment the honest player wins 87.7% (6 pixels) and 83.8% (4 pixels).
nodes.title: MNIST debate with precommit: judge accuracy 59.4% to 88.9% (6 px), 48.2% to 85.2% (4 px)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 5, lines 71-78 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors show that an n-round debate judged by a polynomial-time algorithm H corresponds to formulas of the form 'exists x0 for all x1 ... H(q, x0, ...)', giving the class Sigma_n P for fixed n and PSPACE when the number of rounds grows polynomially in the question size. Theorem 1 states that for any problem L in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate with polynomially many steps solves L.
nodes.title: Theorem 1: debate with a polynomial-time judge and optimal play decides PSPACE

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1805.00899v2 PDF page 21, lines 27-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Comparing debate with Christiano et al.'s amplification, the authors argue that stock amplification relies on a human questioner: it assumes lying is harder than questioning a lie given a human judge and a human questioner, and shallow amplification is weaker than shallow debate when strong subquestions are superhumanly hard to generate or the branching factor is high. They add that this advantage goes away if the Questioner is trained adversarially via self play.
nodes.title: Irving et al.: stock amplification (Christiano et al.) needs humans to generate strong subquestions

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 8, lines 5-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the key assumption underlying Iterated Amplification is that a human can coordinate multiple copies of X to perform better than a single copy of X. They discuss this assumption in the context of whether amplification can be applied to complex real-world tasks beyond human scale.
nodes.title: Key assumption: a human can coordinate copies of X to beat a single copy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 1, lines 18-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose Iterated Amplification, a training strategy that progressively builds up a training signal for problems too complicated for a human to evaluate directly by combining solutions to easier subproblems. They describe it as closely related to Expert Iteration but using no external reward function, and present results in algorithmic environments showing it can efficiently learn complex behaviors.
nodes.title: Iterated Amplification: training signal built by combining solutions to easier subproblems

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 2, lines 48-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define Amplify_H(X) as the composite system in which a human expert H invokes several copies of the current agent X to help solve a problem; X then learns from Amplify_H(X) the same way it would traditionally learn from H alone. In this paper the task set is question answering.
nodes.title: Amplify_H(X): human expert plus copies of the current agent as the training target

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 5, lines 53-56 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe debate (Irving et al., 2018) as another possible approach to training question-answering systems where a human expert cannot evaluate answers directly, and state that both debate and Iterated Amplification involve a recursive structure where AI systems help humans address relevant subquestions.
nodes.title: Iterated Amplification vs debate: shared recursive structure

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 7, lines 88-96 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that in their experiments questions are algorithmically decomposable and the human is replaced with a hand-coded algorithm, so the experiments shed no light on whether humans can decompose interesting real-world tasks or whether messy real-world decompositions can be learned. They also note the combinatorial domains admit an algorithmic training signal, unlike the tasks they ultimately care about.
nodes.title: Experiments use hand-coded algorithmic decompositions, not humans

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 7, lines 97-106 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note X is trained by supervised learning from Amplify_H(X), whereas many important applications would likely learn a reward function from it and train X with RL. They also state the question distribution D must be broad enough to cover all subquestions asked during amplification, and that in the experiments D was usable directly whereas realistically the designer would have to construct it.
nodes.title: Question distribution must cover all subquestions; supervised rather than reward learning

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 3, lines 1-8 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper instantiates Amplify_H(X) by delegation: H identifies a sequence of subquestions, X computes a subanswer to each, and H decides how to answer the original question after seeing the subanswers. X is an autoregressive model trained by supervised learning to predict Amplify_H(X)'s output; the authors note future work could instead use imitation learning or use Amplify_H(X) to define a reward for RL.
nodes.title: Amplification by delegation to subquestions with supervised distillation

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 3, lines 42-52 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: To reduce the burden on the expert, the authors train a human predictor H' to imitate H's role (identifying subquestions and combining subanswers) and train X from Amplify_H'(X) instead of consulting H directly. Because X keeps changing, H' faces a non-stationary distribution and must be updated continuously during training.
nodes.title: Learned human predictor H' replaces direct calls to the human decomposer

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 4, lines 97-105 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper states that a question may be decomposable without looking at the whole context, which lets Iterated Amplification apply to tasks whose context is too large for a human expert to observe directly. H is given the ability to look at small parts of the context, ideally decomposing until subquestions depend only on isolated facts.
nodes.title: Decomposing questions over contexts too large for the expert to observe

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 7, lines 107-109 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that removing their simplifications is a task for future work, which will ultimately test the hypothesis that Iterated Amplification can be usefully applied to complex real-world tasks for which no other training strategy is available.
nodes.title: Can Iterated Amplification be applied to complex real-world tasks?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 6, lines 49-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper compares Iterated Amplification against supervised learning from ground-truth data and reports that amplification solves the tasks effectively with at worst a modest slowdown. The authors state they do not expect amplification to be as fast as supervised learning, so learning almost as quickly counts as achieving their main goal.
nodes.title: Amplification learns almost as quickly as supervised learning from ground truth

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1810.08575v1 PDF page 7, lines 76-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that supervised learning needed tens of millions of examples to learn these algorithms, while Iterated Amplification needed tens of thousands of examples to learn the much simpler decompositions (numbers for each task are in Table 2 in Appendix A). The authors expect sample complexity to be much larger for realistic tasks where modelling H may need a high-quality language model, but believe learning decompositions can be much cheaper than learning complex behaviors directly.
nodes.title: Decomposition oracle: tens of thousands of examples vs tens of millions for supervised

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 3, lines 13-20 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their research direction rests on Assumption 1, that user intentions can be learned to a sufficiently high accuracy, i.e. that with enough model capacity and the right training algorithms the user's intentions can be extracted from data. They acknowledge adversarial vulnerability and poor out-of-distribution performance as relevant but not contradictory.
nodes.title: Assumption 1: user intentions can be learned to sufficiently high accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 3, lines 26-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors' Assumption 2 is that for many tasks we want to solve, evaluating outcomes is easier than producing the correct behaviour, with 'easier' read as labour, effort or insights, or by analogy to computational complexity. They note it fails for tasks with a low-dimensional outcome space such as yes/no questions, but argue it is recovered when the user also wants an explanation, since evaluating an explanation is typically easier than producing it.
nodes.title: Assumption 2: evaluating outcomes is easier than producing correct behavior

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 8, lines 50-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the user's decomposition of task evaluation into simpler assistance tasks, combined into an aggregated evaluation, must be exhaustive, because if one aspect of the task outcome is neglected the new agent may optimise it in an arbitrary, undesirable direction. They add that this is another problem they hope to solve with recursive reward modeling.
nodes.title: Evaluation decomposition must be exhaustive

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 8, lines 37-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that for recursive reward modeling to scale, agent A(k-1)'s task must be simpler and in a narrower domain than A(k)'s; if Assumption 2 holds, the recursion builds a hierarchy of increasingly capable agents. They describe recursive reward modeling as an instance of iterated amplification using reward modeling instead of supervised or imitation learning.
nodes.title: Recursion scales only if assisting tasks are simpler; RRM as an instance of amplification

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 9, lines 17-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue, via an analogy to complexity theory first introduced by Irving et al. (2018), that recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers, e.g. A2 proposes behavior x, A1 responds with assisting behavior y, and the user evaluates both. With polynomially bounded quantifiers and a polynomial-time formula, reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems.
nodes.title: Complexity analogy: reward modeling ~ NP, recursion depth k ~ k alternating quantifiers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 1, lines 24-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors outline a high-level research direction for the agent alignment problem centred on reward modeling: learning a reward function from interaction with the user and optimising the learned reward function with reinforcement learning. The paper discusses the key challenges expected when scaling reward modeling to complex and general domains, concrete approaches to mitigate them, and ways to establish trust in the resulting agents.
nodes.title: Research direction: agent alignment via reward modeling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 8, lines 1-8 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define recursive reward modeling: agent A1 is trained with reward modeling from user feedback, and at step k agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating outcomes when training agent A(k), for example by giving auxiliary information, summarising large data, interpreting A(k)'s internals, or solving sub-problems the user has carved off. They note the assisting task differs from the task A(k) is trained on.
nodes.title: Recursive reward modeling: agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating agent A(k)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 2, lines 22-27 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors split the alignment problem into (1) learning a reward function from user feedback that captures the user's intentions and (2) training a policy with RL to optimise the learned reward function, separating the 'What?' from the 'How?'. They call this approach reward modeling.
nodes.title: Reward modeling: separate learning what to achieve from learning how to achieve it

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 11, lines 71-77 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that reward gaming is in principle solvable by improving the reward model, but whether it can be overcome in practice is arguably one of the biggest open questions and possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling. They cite RL from learned rewards succeeding in gridworlds, Atari and continuous control as evidence it can be avoided in practice.
nodes.title: Reward gaming as possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 3, lines 39-47 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state they do not address the preference payload: whose preferences the agent should be aligned to, how to aggregate and trade off different users' preferences, or when the agent should be disobedient. They treat these as out of scope and restrict the paper to a technical treatment of aligning a single agent to a single user.
nodes.title: Scope excludes the preference payload; one agent aligned to one user

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 20, lines 32-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Discussing debate, the authors say that initial MNIST experiments, in which debating agents boost the accuracy of a sparse classifier, are promising but more research is needed to determine whether debate is a scalable alignment approach. They pose two questions: does debate's central assumption (that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie) hold outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements, and can humans accurately judge the debate even if the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability?
nodes.title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 9, lines 4-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors pose as an important open question whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or whether training can be made self-correcting so small mistakes are dampened (e.g. via ensembles or agents trained to find and counteract mistakes). They argue that if error accumulation can be bounded and reward modeling yields aligned agents, the hierarchy could be argued aligned by analogy to induction.
nodes.title: Do errors accumulate across levels of recursive reward modeling?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 20, lines 48-52 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say many of the practical challenges to reward modeling that they raise (safe exploration, distributional shift, side effects, reward hacking) were already discussed by Amodei et al. (2016). They describe Amodei et al.'s scalable oversight problem as a narrower version of the alignment problem they aim to solve.
nodes.title: Leike et al.'s reward-modeling challenges overlap the safety problems of Amodei et al.

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 8, lines 37-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that recursive reward modeling, a recursive training procedure that, in order to scale, needs the task of agent A(k-1) to be simpler and in a narrower domain than the task of agent A(k), can be thought of as an instance of iterated amplification (Christiano et al., 2018). The change they name is using reward modeling instead of supervised learning or imitation learning.
nodes.title: Recursive reward modeling cast as Christiano et al.'s iterated amplification with reward models

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 9, lines 22-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: When using polynomially bounded quantifiers and a formula that can be evaluated in polynomial time, the authors say reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems: a nondeterministic execution (analogous to the agent) proposes a solution that can be evaluated for correctness in deterministic polynomial time (by the user). They credit this analogy to complexity theory to Irving et al. (2018) and draw two insights from it: the wide belief that P and NP are not equal supports Assumption 2 that for a lot of relevant problems evaluation is easier than producing solutions, and since basically every formal statement that mathematicians care about can be written as a first-order logic statement with a finite number of alternating quantifiers, this suggests that recursive reward modeling can cover a very general space of tasks.
nodes.title: Leike et al. apply Irving et al.'s complexity-theory analogy to recursive reward modeling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 1811.07871v1 PDF page 20, lines 27-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors summarize Irving et al.'s debate proposal and its central assumption that telling the truth is easier than lying, and describe the MNIST experiments, where debaters boost a sparse classifier's accuracy, as promising initial results. They add that more research on debate is needed.
nodes.title: Irving et al.'s MNIST debate results seen as promising, with more research needed

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 5, lines 61-71 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Definition 4 (Abstract Decision Problem) assumes the label is a deterministic function of the input, the prover always argues for label 1 and chooses a mapping from inputs to messages, the verifier chooses a convex combination of base verifiers, both policy sets include every constant mapping, and there exists a deterministic verifier policy v* in the verifier's class that is complete: for some prover policy p in the prover class, v*(x, p(x)) = f(x) for every input x.
nodes.title: Abstract decision problem assumptions: deterministic labels and a complete verifier

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 1, lines 14-23 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors introduce Prover-Verifier Games (PVGs), in which a trusted verifier network tries to choose the correct answer to a decision problem and a more powerful but untrusted prover network tries to persuade the verifier of a particular answer regardless of its correctness, so that a reliable justification protocol emerges. They analyse simultaneous and sequential variants, identify a subset that provably has the desired equilibria, and report on two algorithmic tasks that the verifier learns a robust decision rule that still works when it is frozen and the prover's messages are directly optimized to convince it.
nodes.title: Prover-Verifier Games: untrusted strong prover, trusted weak verifier, checkable answers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 3, lines 27-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define a desirable verification protocol by two properties: possibility of perfect recall (some prover can help the verifier reach zero false negatives, linked to completeness) and guarantee of perfect precision (no prover can trick the verifier into a false positive, linked to soundness). They set incentives so the verifier is rewarded for the correct answer and the prover for getting the verifier to answer 'yes' regardless of the correct answer, making the game collaborative on yes-instances and adversarial on no-instances.
nodes.title: PVG desiderata: perfect recall (completeness), perfect precision (soundness); incentives

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 9, lines 33-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors stress-test a frozen verifier by optimizing the prover or directly optimizing the messages with powerful optimizers such as L-BFGS, which removes the verifier's ability to recognize the prover's 'tell'; they note it remains possible that incorrect proofs exist that the verifier would accept but that are difficult to find.
nodes.title: Frozen-verifier stress tests cannot exclude incorrect proofs that are hard to find

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 10, lines 62-67 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors call for scaling Prover-Verifier Games to more challenging problems, including ones with no known verification protocol, and state that since exact equilibria are hard to solve for, more work is needed to understand prover and verifier behaviour at approximate equilibria; they warn that deploying PVG-trained systems before an equilibrium is reached could lead to unexpected behaviour.
nodes.title: Open questions: scaling PVGs to harder problems and behaviour at approximate equilibria

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 9, lines 71-78 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that a frozen PVG-trained verifier achieves perfect precision and recall against both a fully optimized prover and fully L-BFGS-optimized message vectors, whereas a verifier trained fully collaboratively with the prover has zero precision and is therefore not robust.
nodes.title: PVG-trained frozen verifier keeps perfect precision against optimized provers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 10, lines 38-49 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: On the FindThePlus task, where the verifier sees only part of a 10x10 image and relies on the prover to say where to look, the paper reports that the PVG-trained frozen verifier achieves perfect precision against an optimized prover and 0.99 precision against directly optimized proof vectors, while the collaboratively trained verifier achieves exactly 0 precision.
nodes.title: PVG FindThePlus: frozen verifier keeps precision 1.0 (prover) and 0.99 (messages)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 6, lines 1-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove (Theorem 1) that in all prover-leading sequential PVG formulations, reaching a prover-leading Stackelberg equilibrium is neither necessary nor sufficient for a complete and sound protocol. Their intuition is that the verifier can always match the label marginals, so the prover's best response under its loss is to give the verifier no information about the label, which they call the 'flood-the-zone' failure mode.
nodes.title: PVG: prover-leading Stackelberg equilibria fail ('flood-the-zone' failure mode)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 6, lines 10-17 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove (Theorem 2) that in verifier-leading sequential PVG formulations where the problem instance is revealed after the verifier picks its strategy, reaching a verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium is both necessary and sufficient for a desirable (complete and sound) proof-verification protocol; sufficiency follows because otherwise the verifier could do strictly better by switching to the complete and sound verifier, to which the prover would respond with correct proofs.
nodes.title: PVG: verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium iff complete and sound protocol

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 6, lines 18-29 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove (Theorem 3) that in the simultaneous PVG with the instance revealed after both players choose, reaching a Nash equilibrium is necessary for a complete and sound protocol, and (Corollary 1) that all verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria are Nash equilibria. They note that Nash equilibria not corresponding to complete and sound protocols might exist, e.g. the case in which the verifier completely ignores the prover.
nodes.title: PVG: simultaneous Nash equilibrium necessary but not sufficient

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 7, lines 9-20 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors show (Theorem 4) that under the simultaneous game formulation, from any initialization with all message probabilities positive, gradient descent on both players with reasonable learning rates converges to the prover sending message 1 only when x = 1 and the verifier predicting 1 only on message 1, up to a small constant set by entropy regularization; in the sequential formulation where the prover plays first (Theorem 5), gradient descent with any learning rates converges to the prover sending only messages 2 to K regardless of input, an undesirable solution.
nodes.title: PVG: gradient descent finds protocol when simultaneous, not prover-first

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 5, lines 91-95 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove (Proposition 1) that any PVG formulation in which the verifier sees the problem instance before selecting its strategy has bad equilibria: converging to an equilibrium is neither necessary nor sufficient for a complete and sound protocol, because the verifier can choose the constant policy returning the correct label (the 'trivial verifier' failure mode).
nodes.title: PVG: showing the verifier the instance before it commits gives a trivial verifier

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2108.12099v1 PDF page 8, lines 4-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe Irving et al.'s debate as a two-player game in which agents exchange statements to convince a judge. They say their prover-verifier game differs by using a single debater (the prover) and by aiming to discover proof protocols, rather than relying on adversarial debaters to lend robustness as Irving et al. expected.
nodes.title: Anil et al. recast Irving et al.'s two-debater game as a one-prover game aimed at learning proof protocols

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 1, lines 24-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper combines learning from human feedback with recursive task decomposition, using models trained on smaller parts of the task to help humans give feedback on the broader task; GPT-3 is fine-tuned with behavioural cloning and reward modeling to summarise small sections and then recursively summarise those summaries. The authors report labelers could supervise and evaluate quickly without reading whole books, and that the resulting summaries are sensible and match human-written quality in a few cases (about 5% of books).
nodes.title: Recursive task decomposition plus human feedback for summarizing entire books

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 4, lines 12-23 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define task decomposition as a human splitting a parent task into simpler subtasks whose responses would help a human provide a training signal for the parent, applied recursively so leaf tasks are simple enough for a human to demonstrate or evaluate. The resulting dataset can be used to train a model to perform two fundamental operations, the first being Decompose (ask for responses to a set of simpler tasks).
nodes.title: Task decomposition: tree of simpler subtasks that help a human supervise the parent

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 13, lines 11-20 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state task decomposition could be fundamentally limiting because it assumes separate parts of the task can be completed independently, which may not hold for books (e.g. details only later revealed as important). They give a Pride and Prejudice example where a leaf summary misreads a request for a dance as a marriage proposal because each summary sees only local context.
nodes.title: Task decomposition assumes parts can be done independently; local context errors

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 13, lines 27-32 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that in general policy errors at lower levels compound at each composition task, leading to large errors on the top-level task, and that auto-induced distributional shift may make training significantly harder; curriculum and node sampling were chosen ad hoc. Training on the full tree of tasks did not improve performance, and they leave investigation to future work.
nodes.title: Errors compound up the tree; training on higher-height tasks may be difficult

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 4, lines 37-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For books, the paper decomposes algorithmically: text short enough is summarised directly, longer text is chunked and each chunk recursively summarised, giving a tree where only leaf tasks operate on original book text. Height-0 tasks summarise book text, tasks of height above 0 are composition tasks over concatenated summaries, and the depth-0 task produces the whole-book summary from depth-1 summaries.
nodes.title: Fixed algorithmic chunking into a tree of summarization tasks with height and depth

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 7, lines 34-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper aims to compress text 5-10x per subtask with length limits of 128 to 384 tokens depending on height, and asks labelers to rate quality conditioned on length. The authors emphasise that for each subtask labelers judge the summary only with respect to the direct input to the model, not the part of the book that is the true summarisation target.
nodes.title: Labelers judge each subtask summary only against its direct input, conditioned on length

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 13, lines 48-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors pose: is learning a task decomposition model, rather than using a fixed decomposition, feasible for hard real-world tasks? For what kinds of tasks is task decomposition fundamentally limiting? And how else can ML models assist humans in specifying preferences for high-level tasks?
nodes.title: Is learned task decomposition feasible for hard real-world tasks, and where does it fail?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 9, lines 8-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: On the BookSum book-length summarization dataset, the paper compares against the best extractive (BertExt) and abstractive (T5) models and an extractive oracle. Its 175B models beat all non-oracle baselines on ROUGE by 3-4 points and approach the extractive oracle, and significantly outperform all baselines on BERTScore including the oracle; the 6B models are comparable to baselines on ROUGE and significantly outperform all baselines on BERTScore, including an 11B T5 model fine-tuned on BookSum.
nodes.title: BookSum: 175B models beat the best non-oracle baselines by 3-4 ROUGE points

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 3, lines 49-53 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report a model that recursively generates plausible summaries of entire books, recursing to depth 3 for books of hundreds of thousands of words. They estimate that a non-recursive approach, where generating or evaluating a summary requires a human to read the whole book, would make naively collecting such a dataset over 50x more expensive per data point.
nodes.title: Recursion makes book-summary labels over 50x cheaper than reading whole books

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 8, lines 22-27 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that over 5% of summaries from the best 175B model received 6/7 and over 15% received 5/7 on a Likert scale, scores sometimes also given to human-written summaries. On average, model summaries were still significantly worse than human-written ones.
nodes.title: Full-book summaries: some approach human-level quality, but on average still significantly worse than human

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 11, lines 59-62 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that RL on comparisons was about as effective as behavioural cloning on demonstrations after 5k-10k demonstrations, but comparisons were far more efficient on the margin after 10k-20k demonstrations. The comparisons used to produce Figure 4 were also 3x as fast for the authors to collect as demonstrations.
nodes.title: RL on comparisons more label-efficient than BC once past 10k-20k demonstrations

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 8, lines 28-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that training on only the first subtree does comparably to training on the full tree and generalises well to full-book summarisation, while the final 175B full-tree model was noticeably worse than the previous one. 175B RL policies significantly outperform the 175B behavioural-cloning baseline, with a smaller improvement at 6B.
nodes.title: RL beats behavioral cloning at 175B; first-subtree training generalizes to full tree

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 11, lines 86-92 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe their task decomposition approach as a specific instantiation of iterated amplification (Christiano et al., 2018), except that they assume a fixed decomposition and start training from the leaf tasks rather than using the entire tree. They state their contribution is showing the approach can be realistically applied to a difficult, large-scale task.
nodes.title: Wu et al.'s recursive book summarization is a fixed-decomposition instance of Christiano et al.'s amplification

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2109.10862v2 PDF page 11, lines 88-92 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say their approach can be considered a form of recursive reward modeling (Leike et al., 2018), if model-generated lower-level summaries are understood as helping the human evaluate higher-level summaries. They state their contribution is showing that this approach can be realistically applied to a difficult, large-scale task.
nodes.title: Wu et al. frame recursive book summarization as a form of Leike et al.'s recursive reward modeling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 1, lines 23-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors build a dataset of single arguments for both a correct and an incorrect answer option in a debate-style set-up for multiple-choice QA with long contexts, written by humans familiar with the context, and test whether they help humans who have not read the full context determine the correct answer. They do not find that the explanations improve human accuracy, but a baseline condition shows that providing human-selected text snippets does improve accuracy.
nodes.title: Single debate-style arguments were not found to improve human accuracy in the authors' long-context multiple-choice QA set-up

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 3, lines 111-121 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors' main protocol is the passage+snippet+argument condition (PSA), and two baselines present passage+snippet (PS) or passage only with no supporting evidence (P), with all other protocol details identical. Workers alternate through conditions across three rounds in a counterbalanced way and no worker judges the same question in more than one condition.
nodes.title: Judging conditions: main passage+snippet+argument (PSA) protocol vs passage+snippet (PS) and passage-only (P) baselines

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 2, lines 79-84 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors build a dataset of QA (counter-)explanations by having human writers read a long passage and construct an argument with supporting evidence for one of two answer options, after which the two explanations are shown side by side to a human judge under a strict time constraint who selects which answer is correct.
nodes.title: Single-turn debate protocol: arguments for each of two options shown side by side to a timed judge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 4, lines 84-92 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the current study is limited in scope and is not strong evidence against the broad potential usefulness of a debate-style set-up; the experiments are a case study of a scenario where humans cannot be sure of the answer but have access to evidence to help identify it.
nodes.title: Single-turn debate null result is a limited case study, not strong evidence against the usefulness of debate-style set-ups

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 4, lines 104-108 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the time limit makes the task more artificial than they would like, although pilot results show that varying the limit between 60 and 120 seconds made virtually no difference in performance. They note it is possible that 120 seconds is still too short.
nodes.title: Artificial time limit for judges; 60-120 s pilot variations made virtually no difference

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 3, lines 92-103 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper recruits 194 MTurk workers who judge which of two answer options is correct; after starting a 90-second timer they can view the entire passage together with the arguments and text snippets for each option (clicking a snippet highlights it in context), and once the timer runs out they have 30 seconds to finalize their answer.
nodes.title: Timed human judging protocol: 90 seconds of passage access plus arguments and snippets

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 2, lines 52-63 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper recruits 14 experienced writers via Upwork, each assigned up to 26 passages with 7-15 two-option questions per passage (average 13.3); writers compose an argument of at most 500 characters and select 1-3 supporting text snippets of at most 250 characters for one option, with correct and incorrect assignments roughly balanced per writer. Writers receive a bonus each time a judge selects the answer they argued for.
nodes.title: Argument writing task: Upwork writers, 500-character arguments, 1-3 evidence snippets

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 4, lines 99-103 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors suggest that the arguments may have been more misleading than helpful to some workers because correct and incorrect arguments were independent of each other, whereas debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that explicitly reference deficiencies in the other argument. They pose whether a multi-turn setting is needed for debate to be helpful as a question for future research.
nodes.title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 4, lines 59-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that workers are more accurate when they have access to text snippets and are most accurate in the PS condition, indicating no clear effect of the arguments. Both unanimous agreement (3/3 workers correct) and majority-vote agreement (at least 2/3 correct) show workers most accurate in PS and least accurate in P.
nodes.title: Snippets help, with no clear effect of arguments: judges most accurate in the PS condition

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 12, lines 5-16 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In an appendix analysis, the paper reports about a 1.2 percentage point increase in the rate of choosing an option for every 10 additional words in its argument in PSA relative to P (p = 0.001). Each additional snippet raises the rate of choosing that option by 4.2 points in PSA and 2.8 points in PS (p < 0.001 and p = 0.01 relative to P).
nodes.title: Judge bias toward longer arguments and options with more snippets in single-turn debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2204.05212v2 PDF page 4, lines 38-49 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In a follow-up survey completed by 91 of 102 qualifying workers, those who reported reading the snippets had significantly higher accuracy in PS and PSA than those who did not, but there were no significant differences in PSA accuracy between workers who reported reading versus ignoring the arguments. A quarter of workers reported mistrusting the arguments, though mistrust did not correlate with performance.
nodes.title: Survey: snippet readers more accurate, argument readers not; a quarter mistrust arguments

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 1, lines 21-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors fine-tune large language models with behavioural cloning to write natural-language critiques, and report that on topic-based summarisation these critiques help humans find flaws they would otherwise miss, both naturally occurring flaws in model- and human-written summaries and intentional flaws in deliberately misleading human summaries. They report that larger models write more helpful critiques, are on most tasks better at self-critiquing despite harder-to-critique outputs, and can use their own self-critiques to refine their summaries.
nodes.title: Self-critiquing models: model-written critiques help humans find flaws in summaries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 3, lines 63-74 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define, for an arbitrary base task mapping a question to an answer, a critique task (point out a flaw given question and answer), two binary discrimination tasks — critiqueability (does the answer contain any flaw) and helpfulness (does a critique point out a legitimate shortcoming) — and conditional refinement (a new answer in light of a critique), distinguished from direct refinement without a critique.
nodes.title: Critique, critiqueability, helpfulness and conditional refinement tasks

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 12, lines 43-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define gaps between answer generation (G), answer discrimination/critiqueability (D) and answer critiquing (C), each measured as how much one task's performance exceeds another's. The GC gap reflects effectiveness of self-critiquing, the GD gap the model's ability to know its answers are poor, and the CD gap its ability to give human-understandable critiques of answers it 'knows' are flawed.
nodes.title: Generator-discriminator-critique (GDC) gaps, including the critique-discrimination gap

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 18, lines 45-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their research direction does not address how to surface problematic outputs when a model cannot put the problem into words, which may be a core difficulty of alignment, and that the CD gap could remain large after much effort using assistance.
nodes.title: Critiques assume models can articulate problems; CD gap may stay large

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 18, lines 34-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their base task has no robust or objective way to validate answers or critiques: labelers may misevaluate answers by over-trusting model summaries or making mistakes, some assisted critiques were nitpicky, agreement on critique and answer comparisons was only about 75%, and misleading critiques of good outputs may be indistinguishable from good critiques of poor outputs. They also say they do not address how to measure ground truth, relying on labelers who will be increasingly unreliable on harder tasks.
nodes.title: No ground truth for topic-based summarization; labelers may over-trust model summaries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 19, lines 6-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their base task is not very hard for humans to evaluate, leaving little headroom for assistance; humans take up to around ten minutes, so little speed-up is observed. They note model-assisted evaluation is most valuable on tasks actually difficult for humans, so positive results on an easier task might not reproduce on harder tasks.
nodes.title: Task not hard for humans to evaluate; results may not transfer to harder tasks

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 19, lines 25-32 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors pose as future work how far critique training can be pushed relative to discriminator performance and what obstacles prevent models from explicating their knowledge. They also propose recursive reward modeling as a next step: train the base task on assisted evaluations, then treat assistance itself as a base task to train assistants that help train assistants (e.g. critiquers of critiquers).
nodes.title: Can critique training close the discriminator-critique gap? Critiquers of critiquers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 2, lines 28-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that human labelers asked to find critiques of model- or human-written answers find about 50% more critiques when given assistance from a critique model, and that with deliberately misleading answers, assisted labelers find the intended critiques 50% more often.
nodes.title: Critique assistance: labelers find about 50% more critiques of summaries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 8, lines 16-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that with assistance answers are more frequently critiqued and given lower ratings: on model answers, unassisted labelers found critiques on 54% of inputs with an average rating of 5.6, while assisted labelers found critiques on 78% of inputs with an average rating of 4.9. The authors note the critique model was trained on data from the same labeler pool, so it essentially bootstraps labelers to be more careful.
nodes.title: With assistance, model answers are critiqued more often and rated lower

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 17, lines 3-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports consistently positive GD and GC gaps (except where models cannot do the task), a positive CD gap for topic-based summarisation and 3-SAT but a negative one for Addition and RACE, and an approximately constant CD gap across model scale for summarisation. The authors say this suggests gaps are task-specific and that it is not apparent whether the CD gap can be closed in general.
nodes.title: Gaps appear task-specific; not apparent whether the CD gap can be closed in general

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 8, lines 29-40 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors of the misleading answers wrote the corresponding intended critiques, checked whether other labelers in the assistance experiment found them, and judged whether each new critique was valid.
