The paper reports assisted labelers found the intended critique 45 ± 5% of the time versus 27 ± 5% without assistance; the fraction of critiques judged valid did not appreciably decrease (71% vs 73%), while the number of valid critiques was much higher (0.96 vs 0.62) and valid novel critiques rose (0.24 vs 0.18).
nodes.title: Misleading answers: assisted labelers find intended critiques 45% vs 27% unassisted

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 11, lines 5-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: On topic-based summarisation the paper reports that larger models are better at critiquing their own outputs, even without filtering for critiqueable answers and even though their answers are harder to critique. On synthetic tasks the authors generally observe similar trends in the critiqueable case, though the story is less clear, and they state they have no strong reason to believe positive critique scaling is a fundamental trend, nor know whether it would survive RL training of both answer and critique models.
nodes.title: On topic-based summarisation, larger models are better at self-critiquing despite harder-to-critique answers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 18, lines 24-29 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say feedback in preference learning [CLB+ 17] is very information-sparse, with humans often spending several minutes on a comparison that yields a single bit. They contrast this with their own result that models can condition on natural-language critiques to improve their outputs.
nodes.title: Preference-learning feedback [CLB+ 17] called information-sparse, in contrast with natural-language critiques

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2206.05802v2 PDF page 28, lines 67-78 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In Appendix B the authors argue that critiques are a particularly natural form of assistance from the perspective of proof systems, starting from the analogy motivated by [ICA18] between scalable oversight and interactive proof systems from complexity theory, with humans as analogous to polynomial-time Turing machines and models as computationally unbounded; they ask what classes of decision problems can be solved by humans interacting with models.
nodes.title: Building on the [ICA18] interactive-proof analogy to argue critiques are natural assistance

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 1, lines 27-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors test whether adding a second round of counter-arguments to single-turn debate arguments helps human judges answer reading comprehension questions, and report that humans perform similarly on their task regardless of whether they have access to arguments. They say these findings suggest that, in the case of answering reading comprehension questions, debate is not a helpful format.
nodes.title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments did not help humans on the authors' reading comprehension task

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 29-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Under the 'simple' incentive structure judges are rewarded for abstaining unless at least 60% sure and for choosing the strongest confidence only once at least 70% sure. Because judges reported higher-than-expected confidence in the first two rounds, the authors switch to an 'encourage abstain' structure where abstaining is advantageous unless at least 75% sure and the strongest confidence only at 85% or more.
nodes.title: Abstention incentives: 'simple' (abstain below 60%) vs 'encourage abstain' (below 75%)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 27-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors compare judges who read arguments for both answer options (Passage+Snippet+Argument, PSA) with judges who do not (Passage+Snippet, PS). They omit a no-snippet condition because Parrish et al. (2022) had already shown that snippets increase human accuracy on this task.
nodes.title: PSA vs PS conditions: judging with and without debate arguments, snippets in both

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 2, lines 108-119 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper builds on the passages, questions and arguments from Parrish et al. (2022) and hires professional writers through Upwork (it received 32 proposals, selected the most qualified 15 for a paid qualification task and invited the highest performing 10) to write a counter-argument against one of the two existing arguments per question, in sets of six passages with 10-14 questions each. Writers are explicitly instructed to focus on responding to their assigned argument.
nodes.title: Counter-argument writing: professional writers rebut existing arguments from Parrish et al. (2022)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 14-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Judges make a first judgment based only on the initial arguments and a second judgment additionally based on the counter-arguments. The paper keeps the top half (16 of 32) of pilot judges by post-passage performance and, from their pilot response times, sets a limit of 5 minutes per judgment in the main task.
nodes.title: Judging protocol: first and second judgments, top-half pilot judges, 5-minute limit

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 5, lines 1-3 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors conclude that debate may be helpful in other set-ups, such as highly technical tasks, but that for multiple-choice reading comprehension the debate set-up is potentially harmful to human accuracy, particularly when judges lack a strong incentive to abstain when unsure.
nodes.title: Could debate help human judges in other set-ups such as highly technical tasks?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 42-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Classifying responses as correct, incorrect or abstain, the paper reports judges are most accurate when not shown arguments and not strongly encouraged to abstain, and least likely to be incorrect when shown arguments and strongly encouraged to abstain. A 2x2x2 repeated-measures ANOVA (+/- argument x 1st/2nd judgment x incentive structure) with abstentions removed shows no main effects and no interactions.
nodes.title: No significant effect of arguments, judgment round or incentive on binary judge accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 4, lines 113-121 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In a qualitative analysis of four randomly selected passages rated by two annotators on a 1-10 scale, the paper reports that arguments and counter-arguments supporting the correct answer are rated higher quality than those supporting the incorrect answer, while the average rating for all arguments is above 7/10.
nodes.title: Debate arguments average above 7/10; correct-side arguments and counter-arguments rated higher

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 4, lines 103-112 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that when strongly incentivized to abstain when unsure, judges who read arguments are only slightly less likely to be confidently correct than those who do not, and also slightly less likely to be confidently wrong. A 2x2x2 repeated-measures ANOVA on the full 7-point scale shows a main effect of incentive structure (F(1,12)=13.2, p<0.01) and no other main effects or interactions; the authors take away that arguments are slightly harmful to accuracy when there is only a weak incentive to abstain (not statistically significant), a trend that disappears when judges need to be more sure before moving away from abstaining.
nodes.title: Arguments slightly but not significantly harmful under weak abstention incentives; trend disappears under strong ones

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 12, lines 43-52 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Because writers were rewarded only on judge choices and might have ignored the argument they were assigned to rebut, the authors rate whether each counter-argument directly addresses the first argument and report that 90% of correct and 85% of incorrect counter-arguments clearly respond to it.
nodes.title: Counter-arguments mostly rebut the first-turn argument (90% correct side, 85% incorrect)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 40-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Aggregating responses into correct, incorrect or abstain (Table 2), the authors find judges most accurate when not shown arguments and not strongly encouraged to abstain. After removing abstentions, a 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA (+/- argument × 1st/2nd judgment × incentive structure) finds no main effects and no interactions: none of the three factors significantly affects the rate at which judges are correct or incorrect.
nodes.title: Highest judge accuracy without arguments, though no factor has a significant effect

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 3, lines 40-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Aggregating responses into correct, incorrect or abstain (Table 2), the authors find judges least likely to be incorrect when shown arguments and strongly encouraged to abstain. After removing abstentions, a 2 × 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA (+/- argument × 1st/2nd judgment × incentive structure) finds no main effects and no interactions: none of the three factors significantly affects the rate at which judges are correct or incorrect.
nodes.title: Fewest incorrect judgments with arguments and a strong abstention incentive, though no factor has a significant effect

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 2, lines 108-119 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors build on the existing passages, questions and arguments from the dataset created by Parrish et al. (2022) and have professional writers construct a counter-argument to just one of the two existing arguments for each question.
nodes.title: Professional writers add counter-arguments to Parrish et al.'s existing arguments

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2210.10860v1 PDF page 2, lines 93-98 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that, mirroring the mostly null results of Parrish et al. (2022), adding counter-arguments does not improve human crowdworkers' accuracy on hard multiple-choice reading comprehension questions with time-limited passage access, compared with an argument-free baseline. With weak abstention incentives accuracy gets slightly worse, and with strong incentives there is no effect.
nodes.title: Two-turn counter-arguments also fail to help, mirroring Parrish et al.'s mostly null results

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 3, lines 12-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper proposes sandwiching-style experiments as a way to study scalable oversight with current models, and runs a relaxed proof-of-concept in which human participants answer hard multiple-choice questions (MMLU and time-limited QuALITY) by chatting with a dialog assistant. The authors report that this simple protocol does not fully succeed, but model-assisted humans outperform the model alone by about 10 percentage points and exceed their own unassisted performance by up to 36 points.
nodes.title: Sandwiching paradigm for scalable oversight, with a human-plus-LLM-chat proof of concept

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 3, lines 43-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors call a language-model system capable of a task if a small-to-moderate intervention, such as fine-tuning or few-shot prompting with a moderate amount of high-quality task data, makes it perform well, and call it misaligned if it is capable in this sense but performs poorly under naive zero-shot prompting.
nodes.title: Capability vs alignment as used in sandwiching: capable but misaligned model

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 2, lines 20-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe sandwiching as choosing problem settings where a model is more capable than a typical human but less capable than an expert; non-expert participants then try to train or align the model to do the task reliably without any help or input from experts (including preexisting written materials), and experts take part only at the end of each cycle to evaluate how far the non-experts succeeded.
nodes.title: Sandwiching experimental design (Cotra 2021): non-experts align a model, experts evaluate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 1, lines 36-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define scalable oversight as the ability to provide reliable supervision, in the form of labels, reward signals or critiques, to models in a way that remains effective past the point at which models start to reach broadly human-level performance (citing Amodei et al. 2016).
nodes.title: Definition of scalable oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 11, lines 19-23 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that revealing the correct answer to participants after each question removes a major difficulty that sandwiching is meant to elicit, namely knowing when one has a method reliable enough to deploy, and they plan to let participants practise on a different task in follow-up work.
nodes.title: Revealing correct answers after each question removes a core sandwiching difficulty

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 11, lines 33-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their results are not strong enough to validate the human-model chat protocol for high-stakes use, because participants sometimes give highly confident judgments that are wrong and sometimes accept false but confident, plausible-sounding claims from the model, given their limited domain knowledge and ability to fact-check.
nodes.title: Participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgments and sometimes accept confident-sounding false model claims

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 11, lines 13-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the experiment does not fully implement the sandwiching protocol and that the results do not justify concluding that their dialog-based baseline will suffice for overseeing more capable future systems; one reason given is that the relaxations confine the study to unambiguous multiple-choice questions and exclude any further fine-tuning on the elicited knowledge.
nodes.title: Not a full sandwiching test: multiple-choice only, no further fine-tuning

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 4, lines 11-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe an inner loop in which non-experts iteratively try to align the model until they are convinced it performs satisfactorily, after which experts compare the result with a model aligned under their own careful supervision; the outer loop repeats this while developing the oversight strategy and ends with a verdict on whether any scalable oversight strategy of the type being studied is sufficient to align the model on the task and, if not, how often it fails and how harmful its failures are likely to be.
nodes.title: Sandwiching agenda: inner loop (non-experts align) and outer loop (expert verdict)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 6, lines 14-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors hire two groups of five participants through Surge AI, one group per task, collect answers on 100 randomly sampled validation questions per experiment, and report data from only four participants per task because one participant per task was far more accurate unassisted (84% vs 57% on MMLU, 89% vs 49% on QuALITY) and beat the best model result, which they say would likely violate the sandwiching assumption that participants lack knowledge the model can provide.
nodes.title: Experiment setup: Surge AI participants, 100 questions per condition, outlier exclusion

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 12, lines 15-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say the paper introduces a research paradigm that represents an attempt to make concrete the sandwiching proposal first outlined in Cotra (2021), and that its results establish that scalable oversight techniques can be productively evaluated on existing NLP task datasets. They say it lays out a roadmap and that they are eager to see empirical trials of techniques like debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling.
nodes.title: Do debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling work in sandwiching trials?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 9, lines 74-78 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that, for individual human accuracy, the best model results beat unassisted humans (66% vs 57% on MMLU, 67% vs 49% on QuALITY) and model-assisted humans beat the best model results (75% vs 66% on MMLU, 77% vs 67% on QuALITY), with every participant above 71% individual accuracy in the model-assisted condition on both tasks.
nodes.title: Model-assisted humans beat both best model and unassisted humans (individual accuracy)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 9, lines 79-84 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that with confidence-weighted majority vote over participants, the best model beats unassisted humans substantially only on QuALITY (66% vs 66% on MMLU, 67% vs 50% on QuALITY), model-assisted humans beat the best model (78% vs 66% on MMLU, 86% vs 67% on QuALITY), but model-assisted performance falls short of the best known untimed human team on QuALITY (86% vs 94%) and of Hendrycks et al.'s hypothesised expert-committee score on MMLU (78% vs 90%).
nodes.title: Weighted-majority-vote human teams with model help vs model alone and expert estimates

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 6, lines 3-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: To create a challenging QuALITY task that requires model assistance, the authors give participants a 5-minute time limit, roughly paralleling Pang et al. (2022) and Parrish et al. (2022a,b). This prevents them from reading the roughly 5,000-word story in full and forces them to rely on the model to gather relevant information.
nodes.title: Bowman et al. use time-limited QuALITY, roughly paralleling Parrish et al.

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2211.03540v2 PDF page 3, lines 33-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say their proof-of-concept sandwiching experiment shows, echoing Saunders et al. (2022), that present large language models can help humans achieve difficult tasks in settings relevant to scalable oversight.
nodes.title: Bowman et al.'s human-plus-LLM QA results echo Saunders et al.'s finding that LLMs help humans

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 3, lines 33-41 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue AI supervision may be more efficient than human feedback and that humans and AI may collaborate to supervise better than either alone, and say scaling supervision may be one way to oversee AI systems that can perform some tasks at or beyond human level if the supervisor's capability can scale proportionally with the actor's capabilities and the supervisor remains aligned with intended goals and constraints.
nodes.title: Scaling supervision may be one possibility if supervisor capability scales with the actor's and the supervisor stays aligned

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 1, lines 18-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors train a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement without any human labels identifying harmful outputs; the only human oversight is a list of principles (a 'constitution'). A supervised phase fine-tunes on the model's own critiqued and revised responses, and an RL phase trains a preference model on AI judgments of which of two samples is better and uses it as the reward ('RL from AI Feedback', RLAIF), producing a harmless but non-evasive assistant.
nodes.title: Constitutional AI: harmless assistant trained from AI feedback, no human harm labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 2, lines 116-118 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors use the term 'Scaling Supervision' for techniques that leverage AI to help humans more efficiently supervise AI, making it possible to train systems to behave in desirable ways (e.g. to be helpful, honest, and so on).
nodes.title: Scaling supervision: using AI to help humans supervise AI more efficiently

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 12, lines 98-100 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that RL-CAI models can be over-trained, resulting in Goodharting behaviour where models are overly harsh in responding to harmful prompts or include boilerplate language in responses to most red-teaming prompts (e.g. 'you are valid, valued, and cared for').
nodes.title: RL from AI feedback can be over-trained into Goodharting behaviour

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 3, lines 42-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that scaling supervision could have downsides and dangers because it further automates, and quite possibly obscures, decision making, and say their approach uses chain-of-thought reasoning to make decision making more legible.
nodes.title: Scaling supervision risks automating and obscuring decision making

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 16, lines 16-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that by reducing the need for human feedback, constitutional methods make it easier to train and deploy AI systems that have not been thoroughly tested and observed by humans, which could lead developers to deploy models with unforeseen failure modes.
nodes.title: By reducing the need for human feedback, constitutional methods make it easier to deploy AI systems not thoroughly tested and observed by humans

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 10, lines 81-92 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors keep human feedback labels for helpfulness but replace crowdworker comparison labels for harmlessness with labels from an independent feedback model (typically a pretrained LM), which is shown a prompt, two responses and a constitutional principle as a multiple-choice question; the remainder of the pipeline (preference model training and RL) is exactly the same as RLHF.
nodes.title: RLAIF: AI feedback model replaces crowdworker harmlessness comparison labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 5, lines 10-17 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In the supervised stage, a helpful-only assistant generates responses to harmfulness prompts, is asked to critique its response according to a principle drawn at random from the constitution, and then revises the response in light of the critique, repeatedly; a pretrained model is then fine-tuned on the final revised responses. The authors say this stage mainly shifts the response distribution to reduce exploration and training length in the RL stage.
nodes.title: Constitutional AI supervised stage: self-critique and revision against principles

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 15, lines 21-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that removing human harmlessness labels moves them closer to a self-supervised approach to alignment but that they still relied on human helpfulness labels, and leave open whether helpfulness and instruction-following can be achieved without human feedback, starting from a pretrained LM and extensive prompting.
nodes.title: Open question: helpfulness and instruction-following without any human feedback

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 6, lines 24-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: On 438 binary comparison questions about helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness, the paper compares a preference model trained on human feedback with pretrained language models answering the comparisons as multiple-choice questions, and reports that chain-of-thought reasoning significantly improves performance; the authors state the trends suggest models larger than 52B will be competitive with human-feedback-trained preference models.
nodes.title: LM judges of helpful/honest/harmless comparisons approach human-feedback preference models

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 10, lines 57-63 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Comparing critiqued revisions with direct revisions, the paper reports that critiqued revisions achieve better harmlessness preference-model scores for small models but make no noticeable difference for large models; inspecting 52B samples, the authors found the critiques were sometimes reasonable but often made inaccurate or overstated criticisms, although revisions were generally more harmless than the original response.
nodes.title: Self-critique before revision helps small models; 52B critiques often inaccurate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 12, lines 91-97 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Using Elo scores, the paper reports that RL-CAI models are significantly more harmless than RLHF and SL-CAI models, that RL-CAI with chain-of-thought seems slightly less helpful but slightly more harmless than without, and that the feedback model's log-probabilities are reasonably well calibrated on the HHH evaluation.
nodes.title: RL-CAI models are significantly more harmless than RLHF and SL-CAI models in Elo scores

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2212.08073v1 PDF page 2, lines 96-101 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors present Constitutional AI as a method that trains a non-evasive, relatively harmless assistant without any human feedback labels for harms, and say it therefore improves upon and partially replaces reinforcement learning from human feedback (Christiano et al., 2017). They report that the resulting RL-CAI assistant is preferred by crowdworkers over models trained with previously collected human harmlessness labels.
nodes.title: Bai et al.'s Constitutional AI improves on and partly replaces Christiano et al.'s RLHF

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 5, lines 65-67 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that by 'supervision' they mean checking the outputs or behaviour of individual steps in the composition; they supervise the process to improve the LM program, the supervisor is the human developer, and they always have access to the correct answer.
nodes.title: Supervisor is the human developer with access to the correct answer

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 1, lines 13-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe iterated decomposition, a human-in-the-loop workflow for developing compositional LM programs by zooming in on failing components and refining them via decomposition, added context or chain of thought, supported by ICE, an open-source trace visualiser. Applied to three real-world tasks, they report held-out accuracy gains over less compositional baselines: placebo description 25% to 65%, participant adherence 53% to 70%, and Qasper NLP questions 38% to 69%.
nodes.title: Iterated decomposition: human-in-the-loop workflow for refining compositional LM programs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 2, lines 54-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define process supervision as an alternative to outcome-based training in which language models execute human-understandable task decompositions, either by imitating human steps or by rewarding human-endorsed steps. They state it promises increased interpretability, trust and alignment by reducing reliance on black-box computation and letting users inspect and intervene in the model's reasoning.
nodes.title: Process supervision vs outcome-based training of language models

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 2, lines 58-61 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that process supervision is currently ahead because LM capabilities are weak and complex tasks need multiple calls, but that without scalable infrastructure they expect outcome-based training to eventually crush process supervision performance-wise, leading to the alignment problems they describe.
nodes.title: Without infrastructure, outcome-based training may outcompete process supervision

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 15, lines 60-61 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that their p-value for adherence uses Fisher's exact test treating each adherence answer as independent, whereas answers are clustered by trial and paper, so the true p-value is somewhat higher.
nodes.title: Reported p-values assume independent answers; true p-values somewhat higher

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 5, lines 72-79 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper studies process supervision via iterated decomposition, a human-in-the-loop workflow that incrementally improves a task decomposition through error diagnosis and amendment: start with a minimal decomposition into subtasks a LM can perform (e.g. extracting the placebo used in academic studies by first finding the most relevant section, then generating the placebo given that section), then apply it to multiple test inputs with gold standard answers.
nodes.title: Iterated decomposition loop: start minimal, apply to gold-standard test inputs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 17, lines 3-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors expect similar workflows to eventually run mostly or fully automatically, with LMs creating decompositions, doing error analysis and adapting programs. They list the work needed to get there, including faster human iteration, more complex decompositions (noting essentially all decompositions so far are fairly simple even with hundreds of LM calls), more sophisticated developer tools for tracing errors, and making those tools machine-accessible so LMs can learn the diagnosis and improvement steps.
nodes.title: What is needed to automate decomposition, error analysis and program repair?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 10, lines 42-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that a simple regex keyword algorithm (e.g. 'open-label' implies no placebo, 'placebo' implies placebo) does about as well as their task decomposition on placebo classification. They argue keyword approaches do not generalise to harder, more ambiguous tasks such as adherence, which is described with varied wording.
nodes.title: Simple regex keyword baseline matches decomposition on placebo classification

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 10, lines 55-60 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that iterating on the selection and generation steps of a generalisable long-form QA decomposition improved held-out accuracy at extracting experiments from 40% to 70%, trial arms from 55% to 86%, and participant adherence from 53% to 70%.
nodes.title: Participant-flow extraction: experiments 40 to 70%, arms 55 to 86%, adherence 53 to 70%

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 9, lines 42-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that its approach substantially improves classification over the baseline from 71% to 98% correct (p=0.0004). Reviewing the ICE execution traces showed the gain came almost entirely from answering based on each paragraph, not from answering based on trial arms; whenever the arms-based classification tentatively classified a trial arm as a placebo, it also found that participants might be able to tell which arm they were in, and so ultimately said it was unclear whether there was a placebo.
nodes.title: Placebo classification improves from 71% to 98% via paragraph-wise decomposition

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 10, lines 33-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that ranking the most relevant paragraphs and generating from them (the same Rank and Answer step used for classification) raises placebo description accuracy over the Elicit baseline from 25% to 65% correct (p = 0.025).
nodes.title: Placebo description accuracy improves from 25% to 65% with rank-and-answer

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2301.01751v2 PDF page 16, lines 67-73 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that the best participant-flow approach (perplexity classifier plus few-shot prompt from demonstrations) was also best on a Qasper sample, scoring 69% accuracy versus 38% for the top-1 select-then-generate baseline and 55% for perplexity selection without demonstrations. The authors take this as evidence the decomposition is somewhat robust to domain transfer.
nodes.title: Decomposition transfers to Qasper: 38% to 69% accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 4, lines 10-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their method builds on prior consistency work by assuming that inconsistencies are more likely to occur with incorrect claims, and lets an examiner model search for them by questioning the examinee.
nodes.title: Assumption: incorrect claims are more likely to produce inconsistencies under questioning

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 1, lines 13-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose a factuality evaluation framework inspired by legal cross-examination: an examiner LM holds a multi-turn interaction with the LM that generated a claim, asking questions to expose inconsistencies, on the idea that an incorrect claim is likely to be inconsistent with other claims the model generates. They report that on claims from several recent LMs across four benchmarks the method outperforms existing methods and baselines, often by a large gap.
nodes.title: LM vs LM: an examiner LM cross-examines another LM to detect its factual errors

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 2, lines 36-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define an EXAMINER LM that evaluates claims generated by an EXAMINEE LM by asking questions aimed at revealing inconsistencies with the examinee's initial claim. Such inconsistencies are treated as a signal of the examinee's uncertainty in its claim and used to judge whether the claim is correct.
nodes.title: Examiner and examinee roles in LM cross-examination

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 9, lines 48-59 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the method requires multiple queries to both LMs, which could be costly with external APIs when scaling to many claims. They also state that both LMs, mainly the examiner, must follow instructions and reason over a relatively long context, a skill mostly shown by models above 10B parameters, so the method may not work as well for smaller models.
nodes.title: Limits: many LM queries per claim; needs strong instruction-following examiners

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 9, lines 60-64 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that logical flaws in the examiner's operation are likely to affect the whole examination and can lead to inaccurate decisions, though the method still helps on average. They name developing safety mechanisms that detect and mitigate such logical flaws as future work.
nodes.title: Logical flaws in the examiner can lead to wrong decisions

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 2, lines 45-56 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe a multi-turn interaction in which each LM is prompted with the earlier turns, continuing until the examiner has no further questions and gives its final decision, organised in three stages each guided by a specific prompt. In the first (setup) stage the examiner is given its role and the examinee's claim and asked to generate questions.
nodes.title: Three-stage cross-examination; stage 1 assigns the examiner its role

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 9, lines 37-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list as extensions analysing the interpretable related beliefs that cross-examination surfaces to understand why models make mistakes, using several LM instances in factuality detection instead of a single examiner, and training the examiner to ask questions more effectively.
nodes.title: Future work: multiple examiners, trained examiners, and analysing model beliefs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 7, lines 227-232 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that removing the follow-up iterations in the examination process causes a large decrease in performance for GPT-3, e.g. F1 from 78 to 68.3 on NQ and from 77.2 to 71.1 on TriviaQA.
nodes.title: Removing follow-up iterations lowers GPT-3 F1 (NQ 78 to 68.3)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 6, lines 64-71 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Table 4 reports precision, recall and F1 for LM vs LM with ChatGPT as both examiner and examinee, compared to baselines. The LM vs LM row gives P/R/F1 triples of 85.1/70.7/76.7, 82.8/71.6/76.8, 74.5/74.9/77.7 and 83.6/77.1/80.2, and the LM vs LM (Majority) row gives 86.6/75.8/80.8, 84.5/80.8/82.6, 82.3/76.1/79.1 and 87.0/84.0/85.4. An ablation without the follow-up questions stage gives 83.8/68.1/75.1, 82.3/69.7/75.5, 74.8/72.1/73.4 and 82.0/73.3/77.4.
nodes.title: ChatGPT examining ChatGPT: LM vs LM F1 76.7-80.2, Majority 79.1-85.4 (Table 4)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 9, lines 6-14 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that a pattern noted just before this passage occurs in about 80% of the cases where the examiner accepted a false claim and in 45% where it rejected a correct claim. The authors note that in most cases where LM vs LM fails the examinee provided incorrect information to the examiner, which might indicate that it has encoded a large set of wrong facts that are mutually consistent, making it hard for the examiner to detect inconsistencies.
nodes.title: In most LM vs LM failures the examinee gives incorrect information

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 7, lines 218-222 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that on its Falsehood dataset the method successfully rejects the vast majority of false claims, with 87%-98% accuracy using ChatGPT and 75%-99% using GPT-3 across all datasets.
nodes.title: Cross-examination rejects most false claims on Falsehood dataset (75-99% accuracy)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.13281v1 PDF page 7, lines 211-217 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that across all settings the method outperforms the baselines, often by a large gap, e.g. 85.4 F1 vs. at most 65.2 for baselines with ChatGPT on PopQA and 77.2 F1 vs. at most 60.1 for GPT-3 on TriviaQA. The most substantial gains are in recall, and ChatGPT generally outperforms GPT-3.
nodes.title: Cross-examination beats baselines, mainly in recall

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 1, lines 30-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper proposes that multiple instances of a language model propose answers and then debate their responses and reasoning over several rounds until they reach a common final answer. The authors report that this improves mathematical and strategic reasoning on several tasks and improves factual validity, reducing hallucinated answers, using only black-box access and the same prompts across tasks.
nodes.title: Multiagent debate between LLM instances improves reasoning and factual accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 9, lines 72-75 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the most similar prior work is Irving et al.'s debate procedure for verifying accuracy and safety of powerful AI agents, and distinguish it: there, agents alternately provide proof for an input and humans assess the debates, whereas in this paper the language models combine answers themselves.
nodes.title: Multiagent debate vs. Irving et al.'s debate with human judges

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 4, lines 20-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define the procedure: each agent (a copy of the same LLM) first answers independently; in each debate round the other agents' responses are concatenated into a consensus prompt and each agent is asked to verify them and update its own response. The round is repeated for several rounds using the updated responses.
nodes.title: Multiagent debate procedure: agents read others' answers and update over rounds

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 10, lines 8-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that multiagent debate is more computationally expensive than other prompting techniques because it needs multiple generations and a debate procedure. They also observed that as debates got longer, models sometimes failed to process the whole debate and focused mainly on the most recent generations.
nodes.title: Debate is computationally costly, and current models sometimes struggle to process long debates

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 10, lines 16-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that although debates typically converged to a single final answer, that answer was not necessarily correct, and models would confidently affirm an incorrect answer as correct and consistent with all other agents. They attribute this partly to language models not expressing their uncertainty correctly.
nodes.title: Debates can converge confidently on an incorrect answer

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 7, lines 95-104 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that on arithmetic, with debate length fixed at two rounds, performance increases monotonically with the number of agents (larger groups use ChatGPT summaries of other responses due to context length). With three agents, performance increases monotonically with rounds, but more than four rounds gave performance similar to four rounds.
nodes.title: More agents and more debate rounds raise arithmetic accuracy, saturating near 4 rounds

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 6, lines 97-101 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report qualitative cases in which all agents initially give an incorrect answer but the debate still reaches the correct answer as agents critique each other's reasoning. They conclude that debate does not only amplify an initially present correct answer.
nodes.title: Debate can reach a correct answer when all agents start wrong

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 9, lines 51-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports a debate between ChatGPT and Bard on 20 GSM8K problems in which Bard alone solved 11, ChatGPT alone solved 14, and the joint multi-agent debate solved 17.
nodes.title: Debate between ChatGPT and Bard solves more GSM8K problems than either alone

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 7, lines 44-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The results table lists Biographies, MMLU and Chess Move Validity for Single Agent, Single Agent (Reflection) and Multi-Agent (Debate); on Biographies the scores are 66.0 ± 2.2, 68.3 ± 2.9 and 73.8 ± 2.3 respectively.
nodes.title: Biographies: multi-agent debate 73.8 vs 68.3 reflection and 66.0 single agent

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 5, lines 184-195 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In Table 1 the authors report results on arithmetic, grade school math and chess reasoning tasks, mainly using three ChatGPT-based agents with two rounds of debate. In each task, using multiple agents to generate solutions improves performance over a single agent, reflection generally gives a modest boost, and multiagent debate, which may be seen as a combination of reflection and multiagent generation, gives a substantial boost in reasoning across each of the tasks.
nodes.title: Multiagent debate gives a substantial reasoning boost on arithmetic, grade school math and chess

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 4, lines 48-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that how much an agent trusts its own output over others' can be controlled by the debate prompt, and that prompts encouraging agents to be more stubborn led to longer debates and better final solutions. They observed that agents were relatively agreeable, which they suggest may result from instruction tuning or RLHF.
nodes.title: Prompts making agents more stubborn give longer debates and better answers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.14325v1 PDF page 7, lines 81-88 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that agents tended to give different answers when the model was uncertain, although directly asking each agent for its confidence gave high confidence; when agents communicated they quickly moved to a more accurate consensus. On facts where many instances agreed, it was very hard to convince an agent to change its answer, which they suggest makes ease of persuasion a possible signal of factual confidence.
nodes.title: Agents disagree on uncertain facts; confident facts resist persuasion

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 2, lines 46-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define the Degeneration-of-Thought (DoT) problem of self-reflection and propose the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework to elicit divergent chains of thought. They report that GPT-3.5-Turbo with MAD can surpass GPT-4 on Common MT, that an adaptive break and a modest level of 'tit for tat' disagreement are needed for good performance, and that an LLM judge prefers the side that uses its own backbone model.
nodes.title: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) with a judge counters Degeneration-of-Thought in self-reflection

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 1, lines 96-102 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define Degeneration-of-Thought as the situation where, once an LLM-based agent has established confidence in its answers, it cannot generate novel thoughts through self-reflection even if its initial stance is incorrect. They state this problem is proposed and defined by them for the first time.
nodes.title: Degeneration-of-Thought (DoT): self-reflection cannot escape a confident wrong stance

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 3, lines 76-87 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The judge has two different modes. In (a) discriminative mode, the judge decides whether the correct solution can be obtained after all the debaters finish their arguments in the current iteration; if so, the debate is over, otherwise it continues.
nodes.title: MAD judge: discriminative mode decides whether the debate ends

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 2, lines 23-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose MAD, in which two agents argue their positions in a 'tit for tat' state and a judge monitors and manages the debate to obtain a final solution. They argue that in MAD one agent's distorted thinking can be corrected by others, its resistance to change complemented by others, and each agent receives external feedback, so MAD is less susceptible to the causes of DoT.
nodes.title: MAD framework: two tit-for-tat debaters and a judge that manages the debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 9, lines 21-32 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that MAD costs more time because agents interact over multiple rounds, that LLM agents may lose coherence and context in long debates, and that an LLM judge may prefer outputs generated by itself. To mitigate this bias they recommend that all roles, both the judge and the debaters, use the same LLM, or alternatively another arrangement for the judge and debaters.
nodes.title: MAD limitations: time cost, long-context failures, judge self-preference

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 9, lines 15-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list as future work scheduling more agents in the debate in an appropriate manner, multi-agent intelligence for board games, and AI feedback for model alignment.
nodes.title: Future work: more agents, board games, AI feedback for alignment

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 5, lines 238-247 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In Table 3 the authors report reasoning accuracy on Counter-Intuitive AR: Self-Reflect only marginally improves over the GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline, while CoT and Self-Consistency bring more improvements, and their MAD framework, though not as good as GPT-4, outperforms all the other compared methods based on GPT-3.5-Turbo.
nodes.title: Counter-Intuitive AR: MAD beats the other GPT-3.5-Turbo methods but not GPT-4

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 5, lines 171-180 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports on the Common MT test set that MAPS and Self-Reflect improve over the GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline, and that MAD with GPT-3.5 as the backbone model shows significant advancements over GPT-4 across both automatic and human evaluation metrics.
nodes.title: MAD with GPT-3.5-Turbo beats GPT-4 on commonsense machine translation

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 6, lines 3-14 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: A table comparing Self-Reflect and MAD reports bias (lower is better) of 29.0 vs. 24.8 and diversity (higher is better) of 19.3 vs. 49.7.
nodes.title: MAD lowers bias (29.0 to 24.8) and raises diversity (19.3 to 49.7) vs Self-Reflect

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 7, lines 143-154 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that the negative side is believed to contribute to the performance improvement in MAD: on complex tasks the affirmative side tends to make mistakes that should be corrected by the opposing side to achieve improvements. For debaters of different LLMs, the judge shows a preference for the side with the same LLM as the backbone, which the authors read as indicating that LLMs might not be a fair judge when different LLMs are used.
nodes.title: Judge prefers side sharing its backbone LLM; negative side believed to aid MAD

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 7, lines 196-207 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that instructing debaters to disagree ('tit for tat', higher disagreement) is necessary for good MAD performance, but the instruction 'must disagree with each other on every point' (disagreement 0.988) does not give the best performance. The authors speculate that continuous disagreement without finding common ground can contribute to polarization, where the debate becomes more about winning the argument than seeking truth or understanding.
nodes.title: Appropriate 'tit for tat' helps MAD, but disagreeing on every point does not give the best performance

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.19118v4 PDF page 6, lines 96-107 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that with Vicuna-13B judging GPT-3.5-Turbo debaters and vice versa, the quality of the debaters' responses significantly impacts the performance ceiling of MAD: Turbo debaters give better translations than Vicuna debaters regardless of which judge is used, and the choice of judge plays a secondary role.
nodes.title: Strong debaters with a weaker judge work better than weak debaters with a strong judge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 11, lines 19-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue that in some cases safer methods for AI systems can carry an alignment tax (reduced performance) and that any alignment tax may hinder adoption, and state that their results show process supervision incurs a negative alignment tax, which could lead to increased adoption of process supervision that they believe would have positive alignment side-effects.
nodes.title: Process supervision has a negative alignment tax on math

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 1, lines 26-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that process supervision, which provides feedback for each intermediate reasoning step, significantly outperforms outcome supervision, which provides feedback for a final result, for training models to solve problems from the challenging MATH dataset; their process-supervised model solves 78% of problems from a representative subset of the MATH test set. They also report that active learning significantly improves the efficacy of process supervision and release PRM800K, the complete dataset of 800,000 step-level human feedback labels used to train their best reward model.
nodes.title: Process supervision (step-level feedback) outperforms outcome supervision on MATH

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 2, lines 7-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Following Uesato et al. (2022), the authors define outcome-supervised reward models (ORMs) as trained using only the final result of a chain-of-thought, and process-supervised reward models (PRMs) as receiving feedback for each step. They argue process supervision gives more precise feedback by locating errors, is easier for humans to interpret, and more directly rewards following a human-endorsed chain-of-thought, noting that outcome-supervised models can reach correct answers with incorrect reasoning.
nodes.title: Outcome-supervised (ORM) vs process-supervised (PRM) reward models

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 8, lines 65-71 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the large-scale comparison is incomplete because of two confounders: the PRM training set was built with active learning, is biased towards answer-incorrect solutions and is an order of magnitude smaller than the ORM's, and final-answer grading gives positive labels to spurious solutions that reach the correct answer with incorrect reasoning.
nodes.title: Large-scale outcome vs process comparison is confounded by dataset and grading differences

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 3, lines 25-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors use a single fixed generator at each scale and do not improve it with reinforcement learning; 'outcome' and 'process' supervision refer only to supervision given to the reward model, and fine-tuning the generator with RL is described as a natural next step that is intentionally not studied.
nodes.title: Scope: reward models evaluated by best-of-N only; generator not trained with RL

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 4, lines 21-32 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Human data-labelers are shown step-by-step MATH solutions from the large-scale generator and label each step positive (correct and reasonable), negative (incorrect or unreasonable) or neutral (ambiguous, e.g. subtly misleading); the resulting PRM800K training set contains 800K step-level labels across 75K solutions to 12K problems.
nodes.title: PRM800K: human labelers mark each solution step positive, negative or neutral

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 8, lines 72-77 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Because collecting human feedback is costly, the authors cannot easily ablate these factors with human labelers and instead perform the ablations by using the large-scale PRM (PRMlarge) to supervise smaller models, which simulates a large amount of data collection at modest cost.
nodes.title: Large PRM supervises smaller models in place of costly human feedback

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 11, lines 24-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state it is unknown how broadly their results generalize beyond the domain of math and call for future work exploring the impact of process supervision in other domains.
nodes.title: Open question: does process supervision's advantage generalize beyond math?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 9, lines 32-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: By comparing slopes of best-fit lines with and without active learning, the authors estimate that active learning (training on samples scored by PRMlarge, of which 80% are the most convincing wrong-answer samples according to PRMselector and 20% are the most convincing remaining right- or wrong-answer samples) is approximately 2.6x more data efficient than uniform data labelling; the model trained on the largest active learning dataset (200 samples per problem) appears to slightly underperform the expected trend line.
nodes.title: Active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions gives ~2.6x data efficiency

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 7, lines 54-61 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that the ORM performs slightly better than the majority voting baseline while the PRM strongly outperforms both, reaching higher performance for all values of N with a gap that widens as N increases, which indicates the PRM is more effective than both at searching over a large number of model-generated solutions.
nodes.title: PRM beats ORM and majority voting in best-of-N search

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 10, lines 50-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: On a held-out set of 224 STEM questions from the most recent AP Physics, AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AMC10 and AMC12 exams, released after the pre-training dataset was compiled, the paper reports best-of-100 results in which the PRM outperforms both the ORM and majority voting, which the authors read as showing that the PRM can tolerate a modest amount of distribution shift.
nodes.title: PRM advantage holds on held-out recent AP and AMC STEM questions

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2305.20050v1 PDF page 9, lines 8-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: With three series of reward models that differ only in the choice of supervision and are otherwise trained on identical datasets, the paper reports that process supervision significantly outperforms both forms of outcome supervision at all data collection scales (best-of-500), and that using PRMlarge for outcome supervision is noticeably more effective than final-answer checking, which the authors explain by PRMlarge providing better supervision for solutions that reach the correct final answer using incorrect reasoning.
nodes.title: Controlled test: process supervision beats both forms of outcome supervision at all data scales

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 1, lines 25-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that, on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage, human-written debates between two expert debaters (one arguing for the correct answer, the other for an incorrect one) yield 84% judge accuracy versus 74% for consultancy, where a single expert argues for only one answer which is correct half of the time; debates are also 68% of the length of consultancies. Comparing human to AI debaters, they report evidence that with more skilled (in this case, human) debaters, debate performance goes up while consultancy performance goes down.
nodes.title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert judges: 84% vs 74% on hard reading comprehension questions

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 5, lines 35-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define consultancy as a non-adversarial baseline where the judge interacts with a single expert (the consultant) who is assigned, with 50% probability each, to argue for the correct or the incorrect one of two answers; judge and consultant alternate speeches until the judge ends the session, and the consultant's argument and quote limits are doubled (2 l_c, 2 l_q) to match per-round length with debate.
nodes.title: Consultancy baseline: single expert argues for an answer that is correct 50% of the time

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 4, lines 15-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define debates as turn-based textual exchanges between a judge and debaters A and B randomly assigned to two answers, one correct: the judge states prior credences, both debaters give simultaneous opening statements, then the judge, A and B take turns until the judge ends the debate. Each debater turn has up to l_c characters, of which up to l_q may be certified verbatim quotes from the story, highlighted as ground-truth evidence.
nodes.title: Turn-based debate with certified quotes and judge-ended rounds

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 11, lines 42-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that strong dishonest-debater strategies that break debate at the Nash equilibrium may exist which their human debaters did not find or gave up on too easily, so the high judge accuracy may partly reflect dishonest-debater mistakes. Addressing whether debate works in the limit will require more optimization pressure on debaters, which may only be practical with AI systems capable of debating well.
nodes.title: Undiscovered dishonest strategies could break debate at Nash equilibrium

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 11, lines 23-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that debate might behave differently on harder questions, on questions drawing on much larger bodies of scientific or domain knowledge, or on political, ethical or ideologically charged issues; that their judges start with no strong opinion, so robustness to strong prior views or biases like confirmation bias is untested; and that their expertise gap is only privileged access to a source text, so generalization to larger knowledge gaps or reasoning and persuasion skill gaps is unclear.
nodes.title: Limited setting: no strong judge priors, expertise gap only from source-text access

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 11, lines 35-41 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state they have not shown debate extracts all of the debaters' knowledge: on some questions the best strategies of both debaters may produce arguments too complex for the judge, leading to a stalemate. They hope eliciting judge uncertainty lets debate fail gracefully, but this requires well-calibrated judges, which they find remains difficult in the high-confidence regime.
nodes.title: Debate may not extract all knowledge; too-complex arguments could stalemate the judge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 5, lines 4-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Judges are scored as S_j = log2(p*) - 0.05t, where p* is the final probability on the correct answer and t is the number of times the judge chose to continue; the authors note this strictly proper and consistent scoring function incentivizes reporting true beliefs. The authors also note that with each round the judge gains more information, and that if debates could continue indefinitely the debaters could reveal the entire story, fully eliminating the expertise gap between judges and debaters.
nodes.title: Judge scoring rule: log-probability on correct answer minus 0.05 per extra debate round

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 17, lines 1-12 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that in their debates debaters justify positions with a few claims grounded in textual evidence and need to reveal only about 3.5% of the story on average in their human debates, but certain kinds of knowledge, such as knowledge of very complex patterns, knowledge induced from many examples, expert intuition, linguistic knowledge or task know-how, may not admit such simple explanations, or debaters may not know how to justify it succinctly. They state that testing debate on questions about such knowledge, or designing alternative extraction methods, may be needed to know whether it can be reliably extracted from AI systems.
nodes.title: Can debate extract inductive or tacit knowledge that lacks short, citeable justifications?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 16, lines 44-49 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Among the open problems for trustworthy AI debate, the authors state that human judges should be evaluated and trained on hard questions that exploit cognitive or social biases, where judges have strong inaccurate priors, or where the validity of evidence is hard to evaluate, to make sure debate works in such settings.
nodes.title: Does debate still work when judges hold strong inaccurate priors or cognitive biases?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 14, lines 7-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that they do not observe obfuscated arguments to be a significant problem in their setting, noting differences from other debates (explicit recursive structure scaffolding, no grounding in evidence or judge interaction, small-scale experiments on tricky questions). They state that future work running debates on harder questions can monitor whether obfuscated arguments become an obstacle in practice.
nodes.title: Will obfuscated arguments become an obstacle for debate on harder questions?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 7, lines 118-125 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Across 413 debates and consultancies, the paper reports human debate accuracy of 84% versus 74% for human consultancy (p = 0.04 by proportion test), with AI debate and consultancy between them at 78% and 80%. Judges beat chance in all settings, human debate falls 8.5 points short of an estimated 92.5% upper bound, and human-debate accuracy is 88% for judgments made with at least 95% confidence.
nodes.title: Judge accuracy: human debate 84%, human consultancy 74%, AI debate 78%, AI consultancy 80%

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 8, lines 66-75 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Splitting consultancies by consultant honesty, the paper reports that dishonest human consultants successfully deceive judges 40% of the time, while for AI consultants judges do better when the consultant is dishonest (87% accuracy) than when honest (74%). The authors attribute higher AI-consultancy accuracy at least in part to the AIs being much worse at arguing convincingly for the wrong answer.
nodes.title: Dishonest human consultants deceive judges 40% of the time; judges do better against dishonest AI ones

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 9, lines 112-120 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that 52% of consultancy mistakes involve judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and that consultancies are significantly more likely than debates to omit key deciding evidence because no opponent calls out misrepresented evidence. The authors expect this problem to get worse with questions drawing on larger bodies of evidence or with experts better at obscuring evidence.
nodes.title: Consultancy errors: 52% from failing to extract key evidence from a dishonest consultant

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 3, lines 13-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In the paper's error analysis of incorrectly judged debates, in 33% of mistakes the judge ended the session prematurely (after a single round or immediately after changing their preferred answer), and in 46% the debater arguing for the correct answer missed an important argument or piece of evidence. The authors say the most common sources of error should be possible to mitigate with further judge training or stronger debaters.
nodes.title: Debate errors: 33% from judges ending early, 46% from honest debater missing evidence

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 3, lines 42-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe their setup as a variant of the sandwiching experimental design that Bowman et al. (2022) implement, differing in that human debaters serve as the experts, as a proxy for future powerful AI systems.
nodes.title: Michael et al. adapt Bowman et al.'s sandwiching design, using human debaters as the experts

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 13, lines 33-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say their approach builds on Irving et al.'s (2018) AI safety via debate proposal, with notable differences: debaters are assigned answers rather than choosing them, the judge interacts with debaters between turns, and judges are not required to automatically vote against a debater caught in a lie.
nodes.title: Michael et al. build on Irving et al.'s debate: assigned answers, judge interaction, softer lie rule

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 14, lines 24-35 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that in Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debate experiments on QuALITY, debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy, and they point to differences from their own setting. The first is that their debates have unbounded length, so debaters must keep defending their claims, which the authors suggest may produce more useful and informative arguments.
nodes.title: Parrish et al. found no significant debate gain on QuALITY in one- and two-turn debates

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.08702v1 PDF page 14, lines 24-35 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that in Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debate experiments on QuALITY, debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy, and they point to differences from their own setting. The first is that their debates are unbounded in length rather than limited to a single refutation, which the authors suggest may produce more useful and informative arguments.
nodes.title: Unbounded-length debates differ from Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn QuALITY setting

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 6, lines 43-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that with a stochastic oracle, changes of order 1/T in the oracle's distribution can add up to an O(1) change in output probability over a time-T computation, so they require the machine M to be K-Lipschitz at oracle O. This means that for any other oracle O', the change in M's acceptance probability is less than K times the largest change in the oracle's answer probabilities.
nodes.title: K-Lipschitz assumption for debate with a stochastic human-judgement oracle

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 9, lines 35-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their model assumes the AI systems implementing the provers are powerful enough to very accurately simulate human judgements on any query, which may attribute too much power to these systems. They ask whether this accuracy requirement can be relaxed, for example by giving the provers access to an approximately correct oracle O'.
nodes.title: Assumption: provers can simulate human judgement accurately on any query

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 2, lines 31-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors introduce doubly-efficient debate, in which two polynomial-time provers compete to convince a much more efficient verifier of the correctness of a computation that depends on black-box access to human judgements. They prove that, under appropriate assumptions, any polynomial-time computation can be verified using only a constant number of queries to the black box representing human judgement, in time linear in the size of a single query.
nodes.title: Doubly-efficient debate: poly-time honest prover, constant human-judgement queries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 5, lines 19-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors require a debate protocol to specify honest-prover behaviour for both x in L and x not in L, with the honest prover winning with higher probability while running in time Ptime against any computationally unbounded dishonest strategy, which they present as formalising that debates should make telling the truth easier than lying. Doubly-efficient debate is the setting where Ptime is polynomial in n, verifier time is linear in the query length l and linear (ideally sub-linear) in n, and the verifier makes a sub-linear (ideally constant) number of oracle queries.
nodes.title: Doubly-efficient debate definition: efficient honest prover vs unbounded dishonest prover

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 2, lines 38-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that a key requirement and limitation for real-world use is that the debating models must be able to produce (potentially extensive) natural-language reasoning traces for the problem such that (potentially extensive) careful human analysis could have judged the reasoning correct. Given this, they say even very complex computations could be verified by querying human judgements on only a single step.
nodes.title: Limitation: needs a (possibly long) human-verifiable natural-language reasoning trace

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 5, lines 40-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors map the model to practice: debaters A and B are pretrained models trained by self-play on the zero-sum debate game, prover oracle queries are answered from the models' own knowledge of human judgement, and only verifier queries go to actual human raters, so training cost in human judgements equals the number of verifier queries. At inference time the protocol is still run without human feedback, and A's output is trusted as long as B does not abort or point out a flaw.
nodes.title: Training and inference with debate: human labels needed only for verifier queries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 10, lines 1-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that human judgement is fallible and practical oversight trains reward models to approximate it, so the verifier's oracle is likely flawed; Theorem 6.2 only partly addresses this by allowing stochastic answers with a constant advantage over random guessing. They ask whether the results extend to oracles that give incorrect answers on some subset of queries, such as an arbitrary subset of limited size, or arbitrary errors on a randomly selected subset.
nodes.title: Open: debate with a flawed human-judgement oracle that errs on some queries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 9, lines 40-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that powerful AI systems may run polynomial-time computations with no polynomial-length human-verifiable transcript; the original unbounded-prover debate captures PSPACE, but with both provers unbounded it runs into the obfuscated argument problem, where a dishonest prover can in polynomial time produce an argument the honest prover needs exponential time to refute. They ask whether an intermediate model exists where the honest prover always has an efficient strategy but the computation need not have a polynomial-length human-verifiable transcript.
nodes.title: Open: beyond poly-length human-verifiable transcripts without obfuscated arguments

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 6, lines 1-12 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Theorem 5.1 states that any language decidable by an oracle Turing machine M in time T and space S has an (O(T log T), O(S log T), O(1))-debate protocol that deterministically decides it. In the protocol A outputs a supposed middle configuration of the computation of M(x) and B decides which half to recurse on, bottoming out at a single transition of the machine M. The authors compare this with single-prover doubly-efficient interactive proofs, where Reingold et al. [2021] decide any time-T space-S computation in time O(S^2 polylog T) (whether this can be improved to O(S polylog T) is open) with a complex protocol that relies on prior work including the PCP theorem and so does not apply in the presence of a black-box oracle.
nodes.title: Theorem 5.1: (O(T log T), O(S log T), O(1))-debate protocol for time-T, space-S computations

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 6, lines 27-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: With cross-examination, where parties can query independent copies of the debaters (for LLMs, by rerunning the model with earlier debate messages removed from context), Theorem 5.3 gives an (O(T log T), O(l log T), O(1))-debate protocol deterministically deciding any language decidable by an oracle machine in time T with queries of length l. In the protocol A outputs the whole transcript of M(x), B names the location of a supposed mistake, and V checks only that location.
nodes.title: Theorem 5.3: debate with cross-examination verifies time-T computations with O(1) queries

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 7, lines 32-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Theorem 6.2 states that any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machine in time T with query length l has an (O(K^2 T log T), O(K^2 + l log T), O(K^2))-debate protocol with cross-examination deciding it with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5. A proposes the probability of each next bit, the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, and if B aborts the verifier samples from the oracle O to check A's proposed distribution; the authors say savings in verifier time and query complexity are non-trivial when K = o(sqrt T), most interestingly K = O(1).
nodes.title: Theorem 6.2: stochastic-oracle doubly-efficient debate with cross-examination

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 9, lines 1-7 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 cover the case where a witness w is given: for L in NP^O with a time-T verifier there is an (O(T), O(l log T), O(1))-debate protocol with cross-examination that deterministically decides L given w, and for L in MA^O with a K-Lipschitz verifier there is an (O(K^2 T log T), O(K^2 + l log T), O(K^2)) protocol with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5, given w.
nodes.title: Theorems 7.1-7.2: debate with cross-examination given a witness (NP^O, MA^O)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 3, lines 15-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that Irving et al.'s debate proposal captures PSPACE but models both provers as computationally unbounded, leaving open whether real models can implement the protocols efficiently and whether a bounded dishonest prover gains an advantage.
