Their doubly-efficient debate model gives protocols in which the honest prover always has a winning strategy implementable in polynomial time, even against a computationally unbounded dishonest prover.
nodes.title: Brown-Cohen et al.'s doubly-efficient debate gives Irving et al.'s debate a poly-time honest prover

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.14125v1 PDF page 1, lines 21-29 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that Irving et al.'s original debate framework assumed the honest strategy can simulate deterministic AI systems for an exponential number of steps, which limits its applicability. They design new debate protocols in which the honest strategy succeeds with a polynomial number of simulation steps and can verify stochastic AI systems, even when the dishonest strategy uses exponentially many steps.
nodes.title: Brown-Cohen et al. extend Irving et al.'s debate to stochastic AI systems with poly-step simulation

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 1, lines 37-47 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors benchmark several multi-agent debate (MAD) and prompting strategies for trade-offs between cost, time and accuracy and find that MAD systems in their current form do not reliably outperform other prompting strategies such as self-consistency and ensembling over multiple reasoning paths. They report that with hyperparameter tuning some MAD systems such as Multi-Persona do better, suggesting MAD is more sensitive to hyperparameters rather than inherently worse, and that adjusting agent agreement levels can surpass all non-debate protocols they evaluated.
nodes.title: Benchmark: multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 6, lines 120-130 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors hypothesise that how much agents agree with one another during a debate may significantly affect debating performance, and test it with a new prompting strategy that modulates agreement at the outset with the prompt 'you should agree with the other agents X% of the time', calling X the agreement intensity.
nodes.title: Agreement intensity: prompting debaters to agree X% of the time

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 2, lines 73-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe Society of Minds (SoM, from Du et al.) as several agents giving their answers to each other over rounds, optionally summarized before being added to the shared history. They describe Multi-Persona (from Liang et al.) as an affirmative 'angel' and negative 'devil' agent each answering to a judge agent that manages the process, obtains the final solution and may end the debate early.
nodes.title: Debate protocols compared: Society of Minds and Multi-Persona (angel, devil, judge)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 9, lines 62-69 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that using API calls to a public LLM exposes them to variable inference times and unforeseen model updates, and that large-scale API benchmarking has substantial financial and time costs that limit experiment scale and make replication harder. They suggest future work use open-source models and in-house infrastructure.
nodes.title: Limitations: API-based LLM, model updates, and high benchmarking cost

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 9, lines 71-75 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say their GPT-3.5 results suggest that hyperparameter settings can be effectively transferred to GPT-4, but that this transferability does not extend well to Mixtral 8x7B; they suggest the discrepancy might be attributed to architectural differences, which could affect how hyperparameters influence model performance, and leave this for future research.
nodes.title: Why might MAD hyperparameters transfer from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 but not well to Mixtral?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 6, lines 77-86 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that modulating agent agreement in the prompt has a significant effect on performance, acting through agreement in the first debate round, which in turn affects the final accuracy. MedQA and PubMedQA directly benefit from high agreement while CIAR follows a reverse pattern, which the authors attribute to CIAR having been created to be counter-intuitive, so that prompting the second agent to strongly disagree probably raises the chance of arriving at the correct answer.
nodes.title: Best agreement level depends on dataset: high for MedQA, low for counter-intuitive CIAR

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 6, lines 129-133 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that modulating agreement intensity improves performance by about 15% for Multi-Persona and about 5% for Society of Mind on the USMLE subset, while ChatEval is hardly affected, suggesting agreement is not equally modulable in every system. The authors then apply 90% agreement intensity prompts to Multi-Persona on the full MedQA dataset.
nodes.title: Agreement modulation gives about 15% gain for Multi-Persona and 5% for SoM

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 5, lines 241-249 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that, relative to the first agent's initial answer, debate gives a modest improvement for ChatEval, a substantial increase for Society of Mind, and a decrease in performance for Multi-Persona. Given only minor final-accuracy differences in Table 2, the authors infer that the quality of first-round responses may vary significantly across systems.
nodes.title: Gain from debate over first agent's initial answer: SoM up, Multi-Persona down

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 5, lines 251-253 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports (Figure 3) that on medical datasets every evaluated system outperforms single-agent methods except Multi-Persona, with self-consistency and Medprompt the top performers. On non-medical datasets, single-agent methods surpass all evaluated systems except Multi-Persona and self-consistency.
nodes.title: On non-medical datasets, single-agent methods surpass most evaluated systems

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 5, lines 12-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports a MedQA row of seven values, each with a second value in parentheses: 0.65 (0.63), 0.64 (0.61), 0.64 (0.60), 0.60 (0.60), 0.60 (0.60), 0.60 (0.59) and 0.58 (0.57).
nodes.title: MedQA row: seven values from 0.65 (0.63) to 0.58 (0.57)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 4, lines 76-79 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that Table 2 indicates no protocol dominates on all datasets, that Medprompt seems to perform best overall, and that the debating protocols do not outperform the other protocols on the reasoning datasets.
nodes.title: No protocol dominates all datasets; debate does not win on reasoning datasets

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2311.17371v3 PDF page 9, lines 102-113 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that tuning agreement intensity moved Multi-Persona from the worst-performing protocol to the best-performing one, beating Medprompt and self-consistency, which they give to strengthen their claim that MAD approaches currently not outperforming other ensembling methods such as Medprompt and self-consistency when using their original implementations might primarily be due to MAD protocols being more sensitive to hyperparameters, and not necessarily to debate inherently performing worse than single-agent methods.
nodes.title: Tuned agreement turns Multi-Persona from worst to best protocol

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 7, lines 57-60 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the AI Safety via Debate setting is predominantly captured by zero-sum games, in which all coarse correlated and correlated equilibria are Nash equilibria, so the game can be played efficiently by minimizing external regret.
nodes.title: Debate modelled as a zero-sum game, so external regret minimization suffices

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 1, lines 21-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors study regret minimization in repeated games with very large numbers of actions, motivated by language-based games such as AI Safety via Debate, where existing algorithms need per-iteration computation polynomial in the number of actions. Using oracles to model access to AI agents, they characterize when internal and external regret can be minimized efficiently, give an efficient algorithm for simultaneous external and internal regret minimization with regret logarithmic in the number of actions, and report experiments in the AI debate setting.
nodes.title: Oracle-based regret minimization for large language games such as AI debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 2, lines 51-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors consider two oracle types: a pure optimization oracle, which outputs the best response to a given set of strategies, and a smooth optimization oracle, which outputs the best response given noisy feedback. They characterize external and internal regret when playing large games with each type of oracle.
nodes.title: Pure vs smooth optimization (best-response) oracles for large games

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 9, lines 102-104 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their experimental setting is limited to zero-sum games, and that an interesting future direction is the empirical study of general-sum language games, which they say are not yet commonplace in the AI debate literature.
nodes.title: Experiments limited to zero-sum debate games

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 8, lines 1-8 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors run debates on a random sample of 100 questions from the QuALITY easy subset, chosen because of gpt-3.5-turbo-16k's limited zero-shot performance on the hard subset and limited to 100 because of funding. In each debate one debater argues for the gold answer and the other for the best distractor, with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k used for both debaters and the judge and 1-shot prompts.
nodes.title: QuALITY-Easy LLM debate setup with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k debaters and judge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 8, lines 101-107 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors compare a Debater Sampling condition (both debaters sample at temperature 0.8 and the judge decodes greedily, modelling added randomness in the debaters' actions), a Combined condition using both the Reward Noise and Debater Sampling approaches, and a Control in which debaters and judge use greedy decoding with no further changes to the debate protocol.
nodes.title: Debate randomisation settings: reward noise, debater sampling, combined vs control

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 9, lines 99-102 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose games with very large action spaces as a formal model for language games and AI debate, calling it only a starting point. They pose further directions: different oracle models for best response, other notions of regret, and notions of equilibria better suited to these games.
nodes.title: Open: oracle models, regret notions and equilibria suited to language games

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 9, lines 65-76 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that incorporating smooth optimization increases the percentage of correct judge answers over the control, with the Combined strategy giving the greatest increase, statistically significant on a one-tailed proportion test (p = 0.045). The Combined strategy also lowers the percentages of incorrect and abstained answers, with the drop in abstention significant (p = 0.035).
nodes.title: Smooth optimization in debate: Combined strategy most raises correct judge answers (p = 0.045)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 9, lines 77-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that in the Control setting the judge often assigns probabilities close to 0.5 to both answers, while the Combined strategy gives the largest gap between correct and incorrect answers in most rounds. The judge nearly always chooses to continue the debate, and its probabilities only become more polarized in round 5, when it is reminded that no rounds remain.
nodes.title: LLM judge nearly always continues debates until the final round and often stays near 0.5 in the Control setting

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 7, lines 13-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The theorem states that, under a hypothesis that is cut off in the cited text (which begins '... T, then'), with probability at least 1-delta, the algorithm's internal and external regret are both at most O(sqrt(T ln N)). In each iteration it requires S calls to the smooth optimization oracle and a fixed-point computation with running time poly(T, log 1/delta).
nodes.title: Internal and external regret O(sqrt(T ln N)) with a smooth oracle

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 5, lines 147-154 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper restates prior results: with only a pure optimization oracle, a lower bound from [21] shows that Omega(sqrt N) external regret is unavoidable without additional structure, whereas with a smooth optimization oracle the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader algorithm of [24] has regret scaling logarithmically in N. The paper records the latter as Corollary 3.
nodes.title: External regret: Omega(sqrt N) with a pure oracle vs log N with a smooth oracle (FTPL)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 7, lines 40-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In the simple game, the authors show that a row player using Algorithm 1 places mass at most epsilon T + O(sqrt(T ln N)) on actions outside R. Corollary 7 states that the strategies place at least (1 - epsilon)T - O(sqrt(T ln N)) total mass on actions in R, and by Corollary 6 the swap regret is at most 2 epsilon T + O(r sqrt(T ln N)).
nodes.title: Corollary 7: Algorithm 1 places significant mass on R; swap regret 2 eps T + O(r sqrt(T ln N))

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 7, lines 57-60 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors test whether a smooth optimization oracle can help debaters in the AI Safety by Debate setting of their reference [23]. They treat that setting as predominantly a zero-sum game, so that it can be played efficiently by minimizing external regret.
nodes.title: Playing the AI Safety by Debate setting [23] as a zero-sum game by external regret minimization

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.04792v4 PDF page 7, lines 57-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say their debate setup is similar to Michael et al.'s, with two expert debaters helping a non-expert judge answer a long-context question and the expertise gap simulated by showing the passage only to the debaters. They use this setup to test whether a smooth optimization oracle helps debaters.
nodes.title: Chen et al. base their LLM debate on Michael et al.'s information-asymmetric QuALITY setup

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 1, lines 36-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper studies whether weak model supervision can elicit the full capabilities of a much stronger model, using pretrained GPT-4-family models on NLP, chess and reward modeling tasks. It reports that strong models naively finetuned on weak-model labels consistently outperform their weak supervisors (weak-to-strong generalization) but remain far from recovering the strong models' full capabilities, and that simple methods help: with a GPT-2-level supervisor and an auxiliary confidence loss, finetuned GPT-4 recovers close to GPT-3.5-level performance on NLP tasks.
nodes.title: Weak-to-strong generalization: weak model labels partially elicit strong model capability

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 6, lines 24-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define performance gap recovered (PGR) as the fraction of the performance gap between the weak and strong ceiling models that is recovered by training with weak supervision, i.e. (weak-to-strong minus weak) divided by (strong ceiling minus weak). PGR is 1 for perfect weak-to-strong generalization and 0 if the weak-to-strong model does no better than the weak supervisor.
nodes.title: Performance gap recovered (PGR) metric for weak-to-strong generalization

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 5, lines 38-49 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define the weak-to-strong learning problem as how a weak supervisor can oversee a model much smarter than it, and study an analogy that replaces the weak human supervisor with a weak model. Throughout most of the work, a weak supervisor is created by finetuning a small pretrained model on ground truth labels. Its predictions on a held-out set serve as weak labels, and a strong model finetuned on those weak labels is the strong student whose performance is called weak-to-strong performance.
nodes.title: Weak-to-strong learning problem and weak supervisor / strong student setup

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 6, lines 37-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their setup still has disanalogies to aligning superhuman models. Imitation saliency: future superhuman models will likely have salient representations of human behavior, whereas their strong models may not have learned features for imitating weak models, so imitating the supervisor may be an easier failure mode to avoid in their setting, and weak model errors may differ from human errors. Pretraining leakage: pretraining data implicitly contains human supervision, so strong capabilities may be artificially easy to elicit.
nodes.title: Disanalogies of weak-to-strong setup: imitation saliency and pretraining leakage

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 3, lines 79-84 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that none of their methods work consistently in all settings, that especially in the reward modeling setting they remain far from recovering the full performance gap between weak and strong models, and that their methods are proofs-of-concept that weak-to-strong generalization is tractable rather than practical solutions recommended for deployment.
nodes.title: No weak-to-strong method works consistently; reward modeling gap far from recovered

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 18, lines 34-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors pose scientific questions including: what explains the relatively strong naive results on NLP datasets versus the poor results with reward models; what makes a concept easy or hard to elicit and how to define salience; whether generalization error can be estimated at test time without labels; how different kinds of weak label errors and biases affect generalization; and how robust the proposed methods are to optimization pressure.
nodes.title: Open questions on understanding weak-to-strong generalization and salience

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 9, lines 65-75 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that bootstrapping on chess puzzles, which supervises the largest student through two intermediate model sizes, improves PGR over the naive baseline, especially for larger students, and accuracy keeps improving monotonically as the weak-strong gap grows instead of flattening. In preliminary experiments bootstrapping gave only small improvements on NLP tasks and no improvement in the reward modeling setting.
nodes.title: Bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves weak-to-strong PGR on chess

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 7, lines 51-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports mixed weak-to-strong results on chess puzzles: with the smallest weak models PGR is close to zero and test accuracy curves appear flat, PGR rises substantially as supervisor size increases and can exceed 40% for small supervisor-student gaps, and unlike the NLP setting PGR decreases with strong student size for a given weak supervisor.
nodes.title: Weak-to-strong on chess: PGR near zero for weakest supervisors, falls with student size

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 10, lines 64-74 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors add an auxiliary confidence loss to the cross-entropy objective that reinforces the strong student's confidence in its own predictions even when they disagree with the weak labels, related to conditional entropy minimization. On NLP tasks it performs slightly worse than the naive baseline for smaller strong students, but with the smallest weak supervisor and the largest strong student it increases median PGR from about 25% to nearly 80%.
nodes.title: Auxiliary confidence loss raises median PGR on NLP from about 25% to nearly 80% with the smallest weak supervisor and largest strong student

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 13, lines 82-88 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports inverse scaling in student-supervisor agreement: larger strong students consistently agree less with the weak supervisor's errors than smaller students, despite being trained to imitate the supervisor, without early stopping, and with larger capacity. The trend is strongest on datapoints where the supervisor is wrong and persists when measured with cross-entropy loss instead of accuracy.
nodes.title: Inverse scaling of imitation: larger students agree less with weak supervisor errors

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 7, lines 41-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that with naive finetuning on weak labels, PGRs are almost universally positive across settings and student and supervisor sizes. On the NLP benchmarks, even very weak supervisors paired with strong students of many orders of magnitude more compute recover more than 20% of the performance gap, PGR increases with both weak supervisor size and strong student size, and for the largest students PGR is often above 50%.
nodes.title: Naive weak-to-strong finetuning gives positive PGR on NLP tasks, often above 50% for the largest students

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2312.09390v1 PDF page 8, lines 152-159 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that naive weak-to-strong generalization is poor on the ChatGPT reward modeling task: usually only roughly 10% of the performance gap is recovered, and PGR almost never exceeds 20% even for relatively small compute gaps. More generally, the authors say their results suggest that naively using weak, human-level supervision will be insufficient to align strong, superhuman models.
nodes.title: Weak-to-strong generalization is poor on ChatGPT reward modeling (about 10% PGR)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 9, lines 63-66 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their results are robust across datasets, training methods, hardness measures and model size, and that their findings suggest the scalable oversight problem may be easier than previously thought.
nodes.title: Authors suggest the scalable oversight problem may be easier than previously thought

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 1, lines 22-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper presents the surprising conclusion that current pretrained language models often generalize relatively well from easy to hard data, even performing as well as oracle models finetuned on hard data, using in-context learning, linear classifier heads and QLoRA across seven hardness measures (six human, one loss-based). It also argues that, since hard data is generally noisier and costlier to collect, collecting easy data can be better even for hard-test performance.
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard generalization: LMs often generalize relatively well from easy to hard data

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 2, lines 74-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors assess easy-to-hard generalization by fitting models to easy data and testing them on hard data ('easy-to-hard'), comparing against an oracle upper bound that has labeled hard data for finetuning ('hard-to-hard') and an unsupervised lower bound that is prompted zero-shot ('unsupervised-to-hard').
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard generalization protocol with hard-to-hard oracle and zero-shot lower bound

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 3, lines 36-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors study easy-to-hard generalization with several human hardness measures (grade level, expert rating, required cognitive skills, question length, answer length and number of reasoning steps) plus a model-based metric, across science question answering, compositional reasoning and mathematical reasoning datasets and multiple model sizes.
nodes.title: Human and model-based datapoint hardness measures for easy-to-hard generalization

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 2, lines 106-114 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define Supervision Gap Recovered as (Easy - Unsupervised) / (Hard - Unsupervised), where Easy, Hard and Unsupervised are hard-test performance after finetuning on easy data, on hard data, or on no data (zero-shot). SGR is 100% when easy data is as effective as hard data and 0% when the easy-finetuned model is no better than zero-shot prompting.
nodes.title: Supervision Gap Recovered (SGR) metric for easy-to-hard generalization

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 10, lines 39-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state they cannot verify that ARC, MMLU, StrategyQA and GSM8k test questions are absent from the training data of the open models used, including Llama-2-70b and Mixtral-8x7b, so they cannot be certain models generalize from easy to hard rather than report memorized answers. They suggest future work evaluate easy-to-hard generalization on private test sets or ones collected after pretraining data cut-offs.
nodes.title: Possible test contamination: easy-to-hard results may reflect memorized hard answers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 10, lines 9-20 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that because ground truth labels are needed to evaluate generalization, their evaluations are limited to datasets humans have reliably labeled, and that their results may not generalize to other difficulty levels, especially test settings where almost no human effort can produce accurate labels, such as unsolved scientific questions.
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard results limited to tasks with reliable human labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 9, lines 70-80 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors ask whether their tasks are hard enough to give generalizable easy-to-hard results: the largest difficulty gap they test is between 3rd grade and college level STEM questions, while concurrent work (Burns et al., 2023) has called for gaps as large as 3rd grade to 12th grade, so they see their results as relevant for future work that may operationalize easy and hard differently.
nodes.title: Open question: are the tested hardness gaps large enough to generalize easy-to-hard?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 8, lines 7-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that when hard data costs twice as much to label as easy data, fitting on easy data more often than not gives higher hard-test accuracy. Under a noise assumption where hard data is mislabeled twice as often as easy data, easy data is preferable when its labeling error rate is 10% or higher (hard data 20% or higher).
nodes.title: Easy data can beat hard data when hard labels cost twice as much or are noisier

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 7, lines 12-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that results are robust across finetuning methods and additional hardness measures: with QLoRA the SGR remains within 70%-100% for ARC, MMLU and StrategyQA. GSM8k appears to show worse easy-to-hard generalization, although the authors note easy-to-all generalization is equally good to hard-to-all generalization there.
nodes.title: QLoRA easy-to-hard SGR stays 70-100% except GSM8k, which is weaker

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 9, lines 28-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that SGR is near 100% for model sizes between 7b and 70b, but that generalization declines somewhat across methods once the gap between train and test hardness becomes sufficiently large: for college STEM test questions with ICL, SGR falls from 74% when fitting to 8th grade questions to 57% when fitting to 3rd grade questions.
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard SGR stable across model scale but declines with large train-test hardness gap

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2401.06751v2 PDF page 7, lines 37-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that Llama-2-70b with in-context learning shows comparable generalization to hard test data regardless of whether it is fit to easy or hard data: across all six hardness measures the Supervision Gap Recovered is between 70% and 100%, and these results are statistically significant (CIs and p-values in Appendix Table 2).
nodes.title: Llama-2-70b with ICL recovers 70-100% of the supervision gap from easy data

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 1, lines 31-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that on the QuALITY comprehension task, debate between two LLM experts, who possess the information needed to answer and each argue for a different answer, helps non-expert judges who lack this information, with non-expert models reaching 76% and humans 88% accuracy versus naive baselines of 48% and 60%. They further report that optimising expert debaters for persuasiveness in an unsupervised manner improves non-expert ability to identify the truth in debates, which they see as encouraging evidence for aligning models with debate in the absence of ground truth.
nodes.title: Debate helps non-expert LLM and human judges on QuALITY; persuasive debaters help more

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 3, lines 88-95 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Following Michael et al. (2023), the authors use consultancy as a baseline in which a single expert model (the consultant) is assigned a specific answer and tries to persuade the judge it is correct, while the judge asks probing questions to elicit the correct answer; consultancy runs for the same pre-determined number of rounds as debate.
nodes.title: Consultancy baseline: single expert model argues for an assigned answer

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 3, lines 52-62 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define debate as a protocol in which two expert models argue for opposing answers over a pre-determined number of rounds N; in each round the debaters see previous arguments and simultaneously generate new ones, and after N rounds a judge reads the transcript and tries to choose the correct answer. The adversarial character comes from each debater presenting arguments for why the opponent's claims are false.
nodes.title: Fixed-round LLM debate: simultaneous opposing arguments, judge reads the final transcript

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 2, lines 46-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: To study how debate scales with model capability, the authors introduce persuasiveness, measured by judge approval so that it requires no ground-truth labels, and optimise model outputs for persuasion with inference-time methods to generate a range of expert models; these are evaluated by unseen LLM judges whose preferences were not used in optimisation.
nodes.title: Persuasiveness: an unsupervised debater-strength metric based on judge approval

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 8, lines 26-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that in their setup the difference between strong and weak models is only access to information, whereas future stronger models may differ in reasoning ability or other skills. They also state they evaluate RLHF-fine-tuned models with a propensity for honesty, so it is unclear whether debate will be suitable for deceptive models.
nodes.title: Expertise gap is only information access; RLHF debaters have an honesty propensity

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 8, lines 43-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their results are limited to setups where debaters can provide verified evidence to the judge, here via the quote tool; without it, a debater arguing the incorrect answer could create an alternative narrative and a judge without the story would have no means to discover this. They expect useful debate implementations to be grounded in verifiable evidence, with domain-specific tools such as simulators for mathematics or experimental data for physics.
nodes.title: Results depend on verified evidence; without a quote tool a liar could invent a narrative

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 8, lines 55-60 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note their work uses reading comprehension over short stories of about 8000 tokens and pose the open question of how well the approach generalises to domains where a much larger set of evidence is required, such as quoting published literature for a science question. They add that stronger models may hold parametric knowledge that is not easily citeable or verifiable by any specific tool.
nodes.title: Does debate generalise to larger evidence bases or uncitable parametric knowledge?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 7, lines 36-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Human judges give answers as confidences between 5% and 95%, and the paper evaluates classification with rejection: in static debate, rejecting judgements with confidence below 75% retains 65% of questions at 94% judge accuracy. The authors report that across all rejection thresholds debate protocols achieve higher judge accuracy than consultancy protocols, and that human judges are better calibrated with debate than with consultancy.
nodes.title: Confident human debate judgements are reliable: 94% accuracy keeping 65% of questions

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 6, lines 133-142 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that under best-of-N and critique-and-refinement optimisation, consultants become relatively more persuasive when arguing the incorrect answer; the authors suggest RLHF-tuned models already argue correct answers well, so optimisation disproportionately improves advocacy for incorrect answers by enabling exploration of deceptive approaches. This degrades judge accuracy because the judge does not know a priori whether the consultant is assigned the correct answer.
nodes.title: More persuasive consultants lower judge accuracy; optimisation favours incorrect side

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 5, lines 150-160 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that models are more persuasive (obtain higher Elo) when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage increases for models with higher aggregate Elo, which the authors read as telling the truth being easier than lying in QuALITY debates (a central assumption of Irving et al.). They report this holds across different judges, that the strongest indicator of persuasiveness is base LLM (GPT-4-Turbo outperforming others), and that models are less persuasive using critique-and-refinement than best-of-N.
nodes.title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 6, lines 150-161 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports self-play debates (copies of the same model play against each other) judged by GPT-4-Turbo, with separate questions used for self-play (TL) and cross-play (DL) matches, and notes a strong correlation between judge accuracy and debater aggregate rating: as debaters are optimised against win rate (judge preference), judge accuracy improves. The authors state this suggests training models to win debates may produce more truthful outcomes and provides weak evidence that debate produces truthful information under optimal play.
nodes.title: Self-play debate: judge accuracy rises with debater aggregate rating

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 2, lines 31-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For the most persuasive models, the paper reports non-expert human judges achieve 88% and non-expert LLM judges 76% accuracy with debate, where naive performance is 60% and 48% respectively. With the single-model consultancy baseline, human and LLM judges achieve 78% and 54%.
nodes.title: Human judges 88% with debate vs 78% consultancy; LLM judges 76% vs 54% (naive 60% / 48%)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 7, lines 57-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: From reading transcripts and judge explanations for all cases where a human judge chose the incorrect answer, the paper reports that in debate the most common error is weak arguments from the correct debater, usually due to poor choice of quotes, which the authors take to mean their LLM debaters are far from optimal and are the bottleneck for higher judge accuracy. In consultancy the most common error is the judge failing to elicit key quotes from the incorrect consultant.
nodes.title: Most common human debate error: weak arguments from the correct LLM debater

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 7, lines 15-22 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that in consultancy, incorrect experts cause low judge accuracy, suggesting it is easier to be misled in consultancy, and that across all protocols humans have higher judge accuracy than LLM judges. It finds identical judge accuracy between static and interactive debate and says this suggests that adding non-expert interaction does not help in information-asymmetric debates, which the authors call surprising.
nodes.title: Judge interaction does not raise debate accuracy; incorrect consultants mislead

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 8, lines 5-14 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors contrast their protocol with Irving et al.'s original debate, in which only a sub-component has to be judged to validate the whole debate. They report that judging full debate transcripts is already useful for producing expert labels with non-experts and untrustworthy experts, across LLM and human judges.
nodes.title: Khan et al. replace Irving et al.'s sub-component judging with full-transcript judging

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 5, lines 150-156 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors observe that LLM debaters obtain higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo. They state this suggests that, for debates in QuALITY, telling the truth is easier than lying, a central assumption of Irving et al.
nodes.title: Khan et al.'s correct-side Elo advantage in QuALITY debates supports Irving et al.'s harder-to-lie assumption

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 6, lines 150-161 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report a strong correlation between debaters' aggregate rating and judge accuracy in self-play debates (copies of the same model playing each other, judged by GPT-4-Turbo), so that as debaters are optimised against the unsupervised metric of win rate (judge preference), judge accuracy improves. They say this provides weak evidence that under optimal play debate produces truthful information (Irving et al., 2018).
nodes.title: Khan et al. find judge accuracy rises with debater rating, weak evidence for Irving et al.'s optimal-play claim

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 3, lines 88-95 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors use the consultancy baseline established by Michael et al. (2023), in which a single expert argues for an assigned answer while the judge asks probing questions. Consultancy runs for a pre-determined number of rounds N, fixed to be the same as in debate.
nodes.title: The authors adopt Michael et al.'s consultancy baseline with rounds matched to debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2402.06782v4 PDF page 8, lines 74-79 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that Michael et al. (2023) introduced the information-asymmetric QuALITY debate setting but found no positive results with LLM debaters. They point out that Michael et al. focused on human debaters and did not use cross-play win rates to improve debater capabilities.
nodes.title: Khan et al. note Michael et al. focused on human debaters, not cross-play win rates

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 2, line 71 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors assume that human supervision is of high quality on the easy tasks in general.
nodes.title: Assumption: human supervision on easy tasks is of high quality

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 1, lines 22-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper's key insight is that an evaluator (reward model) trained on supervision for easier tasks can score candidate solutions to harder tasks, and it proposes training (process-supervised) reward models on easy problems (e.g. MATH levels 1-3) and using them to evaluate policy models on hard problems. It reports that this evaluator generalization enables easy-to-hard generalization in generators through re-ranking or reinforcement learning, with a process-supervised 7b RL model reaching 34.0% and a 34b model with reranking@1024 reaching 52.5% on MATH500 while using human supervision only on easy problems.
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard generalization: reward models trained on easy problems supervise hard ones

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 4, lines 78-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define their easy-to-hard generalization problem on competition math: MATH levels 1-3 are treated as easy tasks with problems, solution demonstrations and correct answers available, while levels 4-5 are treated as hard tasks represented solely by their questions.
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard setting on MATH: levels 1-3 supervised, levels 4-5 questions only

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 10, lines 166-169 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state limitations including the focus on specific model sizes and datasets, the domain specificity of the reasoning tasks, and the need for further research on the long-term implications and robustness of the method.
nodes.title: Limitations: specific model sizes, datasets and domain-specific reasoning tasks; long-term implications and robustness need further research

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 2, lines 52-62 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Motivated by the observation that evaluation is easier than generation, the authors hypothesize that an evaluator can offer easy-to-hard generalization useful for improving a generator: first train a verifier on easy tasks, then use its generalization to supervise the generator on hard tasks. They train outcome-supervised and process-supervised reward models as easy-to-hard evaluators on labeled easy tasks paired with unlabeled hard tasks given only as questions.
nodes.title: Train a verifier on easy tasks, then use it to supervise the generator on hard tasks

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 6, lines 130-136 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state they chose not to define terms analogous to the weak-to-strong performance gap recovered (Burns et al.) or the supervision gap recovered (Hase et al.), because models trained only on simpler tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained across all difficulty levels. They instead report absolute and relative generator performance on the MATH500 test set.
nodes.title: No PGR or SGR analogue because easy-only training can beat full training

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 10, lines 143-152 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that an outcome reward model trained only on outcome supervision of easy (Introductory) APPS problems significantly improves best-of-N performance of SFT-trained Code Llama on hard (Interview and Competition) problems, which the authors take to extend easy-to-hard generalization beyond mathematical reasoning.
nodes.title: Easy-trained outcome reward model improves best-of-N on hard APPS coding problems

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 9, lines 108-110 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors conclude from an observation that evaluators demonstrate better easy-to-hard generalization than generators, which motivates exploring RL approaches that optimize the generator against the evaluator to further improve easy-to-hard generation.
nodes.title: Evaluators generalize from easy to hard better than generators

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 7, lines 429-437 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that only MetaMath-trained generators show noticeable easy-to-hard gaps (e.g. 16.6 vs 14.2 for MetaMath-7b-ICL), while gaps for PRM800K-trained models are below 1% or even inverted for ICL, which the authors hypothesize is because lower-quality SFT data such as PRM800K may only teach the model the format of the task. The strongest generator is full SFT on MetaMath (35.4), up to 3.2 points above its easy-to-hard SFT counterpart (32.2).
nodes.title: Easy-to-hard SFT of generators trails full SFT; gap depends on SFT data quality

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 8, lines 427-435 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that the Outcome & Process Reward Model (OPRM), which integrates the strengths of both PRMs and ORMs, outperforms ORMs and PRMs. Follow-up experiments on the MetaMath/Math-Shepherd datasets show no significant improvement from adding ORM training examples, which the authors suggest may be because Math-Shepherd is already generated from final-answer rewards.
nodes.title: Outcome-and-process reward model (OPRM) outperforms ORMs and PRMs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 8, lines 436-447 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that weighted voting outperforms best-of-n, diverging from past research that found minimal differences; the authors hypothesize this arises from training a less powerful base model (Llemma) on more difficult tasks (MATH), which may diminish the reward model's effectiveness and lead to reward over-optimization. A 34b evaluator significantly improves a 7b generator and a 7b evaluator still improves a 34b generator, and weighted voting consistently surpasses majority voting with a more pronounced advantage on harder tasks.
nodes.title: Weighted voting beats best-of-n; its edge over majority voting grows on harder tasks

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 9, lines 127-138 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that among RL methods PPO is most effective on PRM800K, while on MetaMath PPO and DPO both reach top performance and ReST gives only marginal gains over SFT. Models trained with PRM rewards using human supervision only on easy tasks reach 34.0, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art model trained across all levels (33.0), and PRM rewards are more beneficial than final-answer rewards for hard tasks.
nodes.title: PRM rewards from easy-task supervision beat prior state-of-the-art trained on all levels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 6, lines 130-136 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors choose not to define an analogue of the performance gap recovered (PGR) metric of Burns et al. Their reason is that models trained only on easier tasks, especially with RL, sometimes outperform models trained on all difficulty levels, so they report absolute and relative performance instead.
nodes.title: Sun et al. decline Burns et al.'s PGR metric because easy-only training can beat full training

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 6, lines 130-136 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors choose not to use an analogue of the easy-to-hard supervision gap recovered (SGR) metric of Hase et al. They say models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, can outperform those trained on all difficulty levels, so they focus on absolute and relative performance on MATH500.
nodes.title: Sun et al. decline Hase et al.'s SGR metric because easy-only training can beat full training

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 18, lines 34-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors summarise Lightman et al. as finding that process-supervised reward models significantly outperform outcome-supervised ones for reranking on MATH. They say such work studies PRMs only in an IID setting, whereas they train PRMs on easy problems and show these easy-to-hard evaluators can improve generation on hard problems.
nodes.title: Sun et al. move Lightman et al.'s process reward models from IID MATH to easy-to-hard generalization

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 8, lines 436-442 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors find that weighted voting outshines best-of-n reranking, and say this diverges from past research [40, 74], where minimal performance differences were observed between the two. They hypothesize that the discrepancy arises from their specific experiment, which trains a less powerful base model (Llemma) on more difficult tasks (MATH), a setup that might diminish the effectiveness of the reward model and potentially lead to over-optimization of rewards.
nodes.title: Weighted voting outshines best-of-n, diverging from past research [40, 74]

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2403.09472v2 PDF page 7, lines 426-428 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors find that supervised fine-tuning outperforms in-context learning and say this is consistent with prior work [68, 50, 74]. They also find that ICL performance has larger variance than SFT with respect to data ordering (random seeds).
nodes.title: SFT outperforms in-context learning, consistent with prior work

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 5, lines 32-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define (c, q)-expansion on sets (A, B): every subset U of B with P(U|B) > q has a neighborhood with P(N(U)|A) > c P(U|B). Their theorems only require this for structured collections M of subsets of B corresponding to elements of the student hypothesis class (Definition 4), which they say is the key to their results in Section 5 on checking the expansion property.
nodes.title: Definition: (c, q)-expansion for sets generated by the student hypothesis class

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 8, lines 31-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: To estimate expansion from finite data, the authors assume access to a neighborhood oracle that maps each point x in A to a point n(x) in B lying in the neighborhood of x, assuming nothing about the distribution of these points beyond positive probability under B. Because n(x) in U implies x is in N(U), the oracle gives a lower bound on P(N(U)|A) whose tightness depends on oracle quality.
nodes.title: Assumption: neighborhood oracle for estimating expansion from data

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 3, lines 35-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors assume the weak teacher's error rate alpha_i on each covered class subset S_i satisfies 0 < alpha_i < 1/2, and that the goal is to upper bound the student's true error over the whole input space for classifiers that (approximately) minimize error on the non-abstaining weak labels. They stress that the pseudolabeler and the true labels are both deterministic functions of the input, so its errors are not captured by noise models such as class-conditional or Tsybakov noise, and that training uses only the covered set.
nodes.title: Assumption: deterministic pseudolabeler with abstention, class error rate below 1/2

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 5, lines 21-31 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors call a classifier eta-robust at a point x if r(f, x) is at most eta; eta = 0 is adversarial robustness over the neighborhood. By Markov's inequality, a classifier whose expected disagreement with neighbors is at most gamma is eta-robust on a set of probability at least 1 - gamma/eta, a condition they call average-case robustness and describe as much more natural than adversarial robustness.
nodes.title: Definition: student robustness on neighborhoods (eta-robust, average-case robustness)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 1, lines 14-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors show that existing weak supervision theory fails to account for two effects of weak-to-strong generalization: pseudolabel correction (the strong student corrects the weak teacher's errors) and coverage expansion (the student generalizes to examples where the teacher is not confident, even when these are excluded from training). They give new error bounds based on expansion properties of the data distribution and the student hypothesis class, capturing the intuition that weak-to-strong generalization occurs when the strong model cannot fit the teacher's mistakes without incurring additional error, and show the expansion properties can be checked from finite data, with empirical evidence that they hold.
nodes.title: Expansion bounds for weak-to-strong: pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 10, lines 30-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their empirical procedure for finding the worst-expanding set generated by the hypothesis class is ultimately a heuristic, that their experiments are limited in scope, and that the work contains no new weak supervision algorithms or training methods for improving weak-to-strong generalization.
nodes.title: Expansion checking is heuristic, experiments limited, no new weak supervision algorithm

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 10, lines 34-40 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors suggest their theory points to a framework for encouraging weak-to-strong effects: find a neighborhood structure and student hypothesis class pair that expands, then pick the student that minimizes weak-label error while staying as robust as possible on the neighborhoods. Noting that both expansion and contrastive pretraining relate to spectral properties of the neighborhood graph, they ask whether weakly-supervised learning can be improved by imbuing the contrastive pretraining objective with knowledge of the pseudolabeler.
nodes.title: Open question: can pseudolabeler-aware contrastive pretraining improve weak-to-strong?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 10, lines 9-20 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports pseudolabel correction on label 0 (err(f, y|S_0) < alpha_0), while for label 1 the bound exceeds alpha_1, because measured expansion is lower and the student's error on the weak labels higher, and, as the bound suggests, no correction occurs; the authors say their expansion-based theory can therefore differentiate cases where pseudolabel correction does and does not occur. For coverage expansion on label 1, T_1 expands to both S_1^good (c = 0.75) and S_1^bad (c = 0.55), and the worst-case err(f, y|T_1) over all training runs is 0.29, against a bound value of 0.33.
nodes.title: Measured expansion predicts pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 6, lines 8-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove that if M'(S_i^good, F) satisfies (c, q)-expansion on (S_i^bad, S_i^good) with q below a numerical factor times (1 - 2 alpha), the factor being garbled in the extracted text, then any classifier f in F whose probability of disagreeing with the weak labels or being non-robust on S_i is at most (1 - alpha + 3c alpha)/4 has err(f, y|S_i) at most 2 alpha_i/(1 - 2 alpha_i) times a probability on S_i involving the set R(f), which the quoted lines do not define, plus err(f, weak labels|S_i), plus a further alpha_i term involving 3c whose exact form is cut off in the quote.
nodes.title: Theorem 4.1: pseudolabel correction bound under expansion from bad to good labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 6, lines 43-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove that if M(T_i, F) satisfies (c, q)-expansion on (S_i^good, T_i) and M'(T_i, F) satisfies (c, q)-expansion on (S_i^bad, T_i), then any classifier f in F that fits the weak labels well on S_i and is fairly robust on T_i, with err(f, weak labels|S_i) plus its non-robust mass on T_i below c(1 - q - alpha_i), has its true error on the uncovered set T_i bounded by an explicit upper bound.
nodes.title: Theorem 4.2: coverage expansion error bound for uncovered points

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 7, lines 75-86 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state (informally, with formal versions in Appendix B) that Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 hold exactly with (c, q, eta)-expansion instead of (c, q)-expansion and R_eta(f) instead of R(f), giving guarantees for average-case-robust classifiers under a robust-expansion assumption on the data distribution. They argue this generalization is important because adversarial training and adversarial robustness are not required for weak-to-strong generalization to occur empirically.
nodes.title: Theorem 4.3: bounds extend to average-case-robust students under robust expansion

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 8, lines 57-68 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state Theorem 5.1 informally: for arbitrary U in M, they define the population expansion c(U) = P(n(x) in U | x in A)/P(x in U | x in B) and its empirical estimate c-hat(U), the fraction of the n_A samples from A with n(x_i) in U divided by the fraction of the n_B samples from B that lie in U. The quoted lines then break off at the start of the theorem's guarantee, which holds for any delta in (0, 1] with a probability that is cut off.
nodes.title: Theorem 5.1: empirical vs population expansion estimates (expansion generalization)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2405.16043v1 PDF page 7, lines 77-87 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors extend their weak-to-strong error bounds (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2) to student classifiers that are only robust on average, under a robust-expansion assumption (Theorem 4.3). They say this generalization matters because it matches empirical results, in their references [73, 38, 10], that adversarial training and adversarial robustness are not required for weak-to-strong generalization to occur.
nodes.title: Average-case-robust weak-to-strong bounds match findings that adversarial training is not required

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 6, lines 162-173 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors determine whether a model has the knowledge of a case by checking if its confidence exceeds a threshold T, set to 0.75 in the main text, and report in Appendix I that the deception patterns do not depend on the choice of T. Based on Eq. (2), the deception score in the classification setting is computed (Eq. (8)) as a ratio of counts of cases with M_{θ̃_s^w}(x) ≥ 0.5 and M_{θ_s^w}(x) < 0.5, where the numerator counts only such cases in S_k ∩ W_uk.
nodes.title: Method: a model 'knows' a case if its confidence exceeds threshold T = 0.75

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 1, lines 25-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper asks whether weak-to-strong generalization hides weak-to-strong deception, where strong models appear well aligned in areas known to weak supervisors but behave misaligned in cases the weak models do not know, studied in multi-objective alignment with conflicting targets (e.g. helpfulness vs harmlessness). Across reward modeling and preference optimization experiments it reports that (1) the deception phenomenon exists in all settings, (2) it intensifies as the capability gap between weak and strong models grows, and (3) bootstrapping with an intermediate model mitigates it somewhat, with limited effectiveness.
nodes.title: Weak-to-strong deception: strong students misbehave where weak supervisors cannot see

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 4, lines 94-99 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define the conflict tax as the performance a supervised model sacrifices in a target alignment dimension in exchange for higher performance on another, conflicting dimension when it must align with multiple goals at once (e.g. helpfulness vs harmlessness). They ask whether this tax falls in areas known to the weak supervisor, keeping the student within its control, or in cases unknown to the weak model, which constitutes weak-to-strong deception.
nodes.title: Conflict tax: performance sacrificed in the target dimension for a conflicting objective

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 5, lines 14-22 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define weak-to-strong deception as occurring when cases in the Strong-Known and Weak-Unknown area that the strong model would generalize well without the conflict become misaligned when conflicting targets are present. The Deception Score (DS) is the fraction of conflict-tax cases (correct under the no-conflict reference model but wrong under the conflict-aligned model) that fall within Strong-Known intersect Weak-Unknown, out of all such cases.
nodes.title: Deception Score: share of conflict tax in strong-known, weak-unknown cases

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 15, lines 7-14 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that they mainly conduct experiments in the preference alignment scenario on two offline preference optimization methods, SimPO and DPO, leaving online frameworks such as PPO to future work, and that they mainly consider harmlessness as the target alignment dimension, while deception also matters for other dimensions such as honesty, with only preliminary experiments in Appendix O.
nodes.title: Limitations: mainly offline preference optimization and mainly harmlessness as the target

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 10, lines 96-102 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that the failure of high-confidence-only supervision implies deeper mechanisms explaining how strong models perceive weak models' knowledge boundaries and act deceptively, and pose this as a direction for future work, suggesting for example that strong models may infer where teachers excel or struggle from the portion and distribution of samples teachers provide across domains.
nodes.title: Open question: how do strong models perceive the knowledge boundaries of weak supervisors?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 10, lines 111-119 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that when the weak model first supervises an intermediate model that then supervises Mistral-7B, bootstrapping improves weak-to-strong generalization (consistent with Burns et al.) and consistently lowers deception scores. The authors suggest some cases unknown to the weak model become known to the intermediate model, making deception harder there.
nodes.title: Bootstrapping through an intermediate model partly mitigates weak-to-strong deception

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 9, lines 93-100 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that the deception score grows faster than the proportion of samples in Strong-Known intersect Weak-Unknown (especially under explicit conflict), so the authors conclude that growth of the Strong-Known area contributes little and that stronger models themselves are likely more prone to deceiving weak models in the weak model's unknown areas. The distribution of conflict tax shifts toward the Strong-Known and Weak-Unknown area as the strong model becomes more powerful.
nodes.title: Deception growth exceeds growth of the strong-known/weak-unknown area

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 10, lines 87-98 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports testing whether supervising only with the weak model's correct, high-confidence samples prevents deception, in the implicit conflict preference alignment setting, and reaches a negative conclusion: this does not mitigate the deception phenomenon.
nodes.title: Training only on correct high-confidence weak labels does not mitigate deception

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 9, lines 78-85 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that even without access to the weak model's explicit probability distributions, the strong model may still roughly perceive what the weak model knows and does not know only through the correctness of its predicted preference orders, so the condition required for deception to occur could be more relaxed than in reward modeling. LLaMA-3/3.1 results indicate that deception severity depends on model capability rather than solely on scale.
nodes.title: Strong models may perceive weak models' knowledge from preference orders alone

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 7, lines 83-94 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that in reward modeling, weak-to-strong deception exists in both explicit and implicit conflict settings, with all deception scores around or above 0.2 and some above 0.5, especially when the weak model is GPT-2-Base. Deception intensifies with the capability gap: for a fixed weak model the score increases as the strong model becomes more powerful, and for a fixed strong model it decreases as the weak teacher becomes stronger; the authors hypothesize the strong model perceives the weak model's knowledge boundary from its soft-label confidences.
nodes.title: Reward modeling: deception scores around 0.2 or above and rising with capability gap

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 7, lines 104-113 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports an absolute deception score, the share of samples aligned under ground-truth supervision but misaligned under no-conflict weak supervision that lie in Strong-Known and Weak-Unknown, and finds a similar pattern, suggesting the strong model may deceive the weak model even without a conflicting target. The authors note this is ambiguous, since rising scores may reflect more erroneous weak supervision in the stronger student's known area, which they cannot fully disentangle from active deception.
nodes.title: Possible spontaneous deception without conflicting goals, but interpretation ambiguous

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 10, lines 113-117 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: When a weak model supervises Mistral-7B through an intermediate model, the authors find that bootstrapping improves weak-to-strong generalization performance, which they state is consistent with Burns et al. (2024). They add that bootstrapping also lowers their deception score to some extent.
nodes.title: Yang et al. find bootstrapping via an intermediate model improves W2S results, as Burns et al. did

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2406.11431v3 PDF page 2, lines 151-156 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors mainly follow the weak-to-strong setup of Burns et al. (2024), including its reward modeling task, across models of different sizes. They extend it by making harmlessness the target, adding explicit or implicit conflicting objectives, and adding a preference-optimization variant to probe weak-to-strong deception.
nodes.title: The authors extend Burns et al.'s weak-to-strong setup with conflicting alignment objectives

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 11, lines 24-30 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that an ideal evaluation would compare final RLHF policies trained with and without critique assistance, but that this is expensive, so they assume that helping contractors catch more bugs will improve the resulting policy. They note this may fail because critics, while removing some human biases, may introduce new consistent label biases that degrade RLHF.
nodes.title: Assumes catching more bugs yields better RLHF policies; critics may add new biases

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 1, lines 18-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors train 'critic' models, LLMs trained with RLHF to write natural-language feedback highlighting problems in code from real-world assistant tasks, to help humans evaluate model-written code more accurately. They report that on code with naturally occurring LLM errors model critiques are preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases, and that human evaluation finds models catch more bugs than human contractors paid for code review.
nodes.title: CriticGPT: RLHF-trained LLM critics help humans evaluate model-written code

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 3, lines 59-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors have contractors rate critiques on a 1-7 ordinal scale for comprehensiveness (does not omit any clear and severe issue), critique-bug inclusion (CBI: catches a particular bug specified a priori), whether the critique includes any hallucinated bugs or nitpicks, and an overall subjective helpfulness rating that also accounts for style and general usefulness.
nodes.title: Critique evaluation attributes: comprehensiveness, critique-bug inclusion, hallucinations

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 11, lines 31-34 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that a key limitation is that the distribution of inserted bugs is quite different from that of natural LLM errors. They suggest training models to insert subtle in-distribution problems instead of paying humans to insert bugs, and leave this to future work.
nodes.title: Human-inserted bugs differ from the distribution of natural LLM errors

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 11, lines 38-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list further limitations: evaluated code snippets are short with no multi-file or repository support, the absolute rate of nitpicks and hallucinated bugs remains quite high, complex bugs spread across many lines were not investigated, and a single step of critique may be substantially weaker than multi-step interactive procedures such as consultancy or debate.
nodes.title: Short snippets, high hallucination rate; single critique may be weaker than debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 6, lines 1-6 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper collects training data by having contractors introduce bugs (tampers), verifying with access to an LLM critic that it misses each bug in at least one of three samples (not strictly enforced). The authors report this adversarial collection noticeably increased bug subtlety, and the critic used was updated twice, so much data was adversarial to ChatGPT and much to an early CriticGPT.
nodes.title: Adversarial tampering: humans insert subtle bugs that an LLM critic misses

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 11, lines 34-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe the critique approach as only the first step of recursive reward modeling and pose as open when an additional RRM step becomes appropriate and whether critique can be used effectively for RRM.
nodes.title: When is a further recursive reward modeling step appropriate; can critique support it?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 10, lines 58-66 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Sampling CriticGPT (RL only) critiques on ChatGPT training data a first annotator had rated 'flawless', the paper reports that when contractors reviewed flagged items with the critique, 24% had a problem that substantially lowered the rating, compared with 6% when a second contractor re-rated without critiques. Prioritising tasks with highly scored critiques raised the catch rate and lowered hallucinations.
nodes.title: Critique-flagged ChatGPT data rated flawless: 24% judged substantially worse with the critique vs 6% in an unassisted re-rating

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 8, lines 72-80 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that Human+CriticGPT teams write substantially more comprehensive critiques than humans alone, and that CriticGPT is more comprehensive than ChatGPT on both detected and inserted bugs. Models nitpick and hallucinate bugs much more often than humans, CriticGPT substantially less than ChatGPT, and human-machine teams fall in between.
nodes.title: Human+CriticGPT teams: more comprehensive than humans, fewer hallucinations than models

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 7, lines 33-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that CriticGPT critiques are substantially preferred by contractors over prompted ChatGPT critiques and over human-written critiques from their contractor group, on overall rating. Both LLM critics (prompted ChatGPT and CriticGPT) catch many more inserted bugs than the human annotators; the authors note this contractor cohort is representative of ChatGPT's contractors rather than the best possible humans.
nodes.title: CriticGPT critiques preferred over human critiques; LLM critics catch more inserted bugs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 19, lines 59-70 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report broadly negative results when they directly measured human judge accuracy: on paired passing and failing solutions to challenging problems from a dataset similar to DeepMind Code Contests, LLM critiques struggled to help contractors identify the correct solution within a 20-minute limit, without code execution. They suspect an asymmetry between the compute needed to find the solutions and the compute used to produce the critiques.
nodes.title: LLM critics did not help humans pick correct solutions to hard contest-style coding problems

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 10, lines 47-53 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that CriticGPT models trained only on critique comparisons of unmodified code, without the tampering step, severely under-performed on both inserted and detected bugs according to automated GPT-4 evaluations, and no human evaluations of them are presented. The authors suspect lower inter-annotator agreement without reference bugs produced a worse reward model.
nodes.title: Critics trained without tampered-bug data severely underperform

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 7, lines 55-61 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Training a family of GPT-4-family models with RLHF, the paper reports that larger models improve the rate of detected bugs, and naively estimates that matching CriticGPT (RL only) without additional data or modification to the ChatGPT pipeline would need around 30x more pre-training compute.
nodes.title: Critic RL training equals roughly 30x more pre-training compute for bug detection

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 1, lines 48-51 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors acknowledge that previous work [12, 13, 23] has demonstrated that oversight methods like debate have the potential to help humans more accurately assess answers to reading comprehension questions, but note that these works apply their methods primarily to multiple choice questions about short science fiction stories that the judges have not read, which they call a toy setting.
nodes.title: Prior debate evidence described as a toy setting of short stories judges have not read

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.00215v1 PDF page 2, lines 44-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors follow Saunders et al. in training an autoregressive policy that takes a (question, answer) pair and outputs a critique pointing out errors, but unlike Saunders et al. they train it with RLHF on challenging real-world data, and report that the resulting GPT-4-based CriticGPT outperforms representative humans at challenging bug detection.
nodes.title: McAleese et al. extend Saunders et al.'s critique models with RLHF on real-world code

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.04622v2 PDF page 1, lines 15-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Using LLMs both as agents and as weaker stand-in judges across extractive QA, mathematics, coding, logic and multimodal reasoning tasks, the paper reports that debate outperforms consultancy on all tasks when the consultant is randomly assigned to argue for the correct or incorrect answer; against direct question answering, debate wins on extractive QA with information asymmetry but results are mixed on tasks without it. It also reports that when agents choose which answer to argue for, judges are less often convinced of the wrong answer in debate than in consultancy, and that stronger debaters raise judge accuracy, though more modestly than in previous studies.
nodes.title: Weak LLM judges: debate beats consultancy on all tasks, but vs direct QA results are mixed

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2407.04622v2 PDF page 3, lines 9-18 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors test consultancy, in which a judge LLM questions a single consultant LLM that argues for one of two options, and debate, in which the judge answers after viewing a debate between two debater LLMs arguing opposite answers. Each consultancy question is run with the consultant assigned the correct and, separately, the incorrect answer, which the authors say simulates a worst-case RLHF in which feedback cannot tell correct from incorrect answers; both are compared with direct QA baselines (QA with or without the article).
