nodes.text: The paper argues that recent empirical studies of scalable oversight protocols, especially Debate, use experiments that do not generalize to other protocols, and introduces a scalable oversight benchmark built on the agent score difference (ASD) metric, which measures how much a mechanism advantages truth-telling over deception. It supplies a Python package for evaluating protocols on the benchmark and runs a demonstrative experiment benchmarking Debate.
nodes.title: Scalable oversight benchmark based on agent score difference (ASD), with a Debate demo

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 2, lines 8-16 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue judge accuracy relative to a Consultancy baseline is the wrong metric for evaluating scalable oversight protocols from an alignment perspective, and define ASD as the difference between the score an agent earns arguing for the true answer and for the false answer (e.g. judge belief 0.8 for a truthful agent and 0.6 for a lying one gives log 0.8 minus log 0.6, about 0.29). They state ASD is equivalent to judge accuracy for simultaneous debate but not for Consultancy, so the baseline comparison in previous debate experiments is incorrect.
nodes.title: Agent score difference (ASD) replaces judge accuracy as the protocol metric

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 4, lines 40-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that ASD measured on current models estimates a protocol's present training signal, and to ask whether it will hold as capabilities grow they generalize the debater Elo used in earlier debate experiments to any protocol by defining Expected Agent Score, EAS = (log p_true, log p_false) dotted with q, as a pure measure of the agent's capabilities.
nodes.title: Expected Agent Score (EAS) as a capability measure generalizing debater Elo

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 1, lines 35-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe scalable oversight (citing Bowman et al. 2022) as the problem of developing a human feedback mechanism that scales to superhuman intelligences, and give two framings: a training method that makes honesty (or alignment) the best policy for the model, extending RLHF to the superhuman realm, or an inference-time mechanism that catches a model when it says something false or does something bad, framed as mechanism design.
nodes.title: Scalable oversight as a training method or as an inference-time oversight mechanism

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 6, lines 16-27 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that an empirical benchmark is no substitute for formal guarantees and that it, like previous debate experiments, only compares reward for simulated aligned versus misaligned behaviour, so results assume current language models can simulate both reasonably well when instructed. They add that only current models can be tested, extrapolating ASD versus EAS trends is not a formal guarantee, and protocols that do well may only work where ground truth is available.
nodes.title: Benchmark relies on prompted LLMs simulating aligned and misaligned behaviour

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 7, lines 28-35 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state the main contribution is the benchmark and the experiments are small and demonstrative, with 100 questions, one judge model (gpt-4o-mini) and five agent configurations, and that future work should cover more agent and judge models and more questions for statistical significance, with reasoning models such as deepseek-r1 and o3 as agents.
nodes.title: Demonstration uses 100 questions, one judge (gpt-4o-mini), five agent configurations

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 6, lines 35-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors benchmark Propaganda, which simulates RLHF (the judge's probability for the answer an agent argues for is the preference signal); NaiveJudge, which simulates supervised learning (the judge answers without the agent and the agent is scored by agreement); Consultancy, like Propaganda but with judge-consultant interaction, in four versions (2 or 4 turns, consultant or judge starts); and Debate in four versions (2 or 4 turns, simultaneous or sequential).
nodes.title: Protocols benchmarked: Propaganda (RLHF), NaiveJudge, Consultancy and Debate variants

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 9, lines 62-67 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors name as an important direction measuring worst-case rather than average-case ASD, since superhuman AI oversight must prevent rare catastrophic actions (e.g. one piece of vulnerable code enabling weight exfiltration), and suggest protocols that raise worst-case ASD should be more robust to such failures.
nodes.title: Do protocols that raise worst-case ASD resist rare catastrophic failures?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 7, lines 14-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that Consultancy significantly underperforms both NaiveJudge and Propaganda on ASD and shows no significant EAS-ASD trend, with consistently high EAS that the authors read as judge-consultant interaction making a gpt-4o-mini judge more vulnerable to manipulation; Propaganda (RLHF) does not beat NaiveJudge (supervised learning) on inducing alignment but does show the same positive association between EAS and ASD.
nodes.title: Consultancy underperforms NaiveJudge and Propaganda; Propaganda does not beat NaiveJudge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 6, lines 52-55 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that Debate outperforms all other tested protocols both on inducing alignment (Figure 1) and on the combined capability-and-alignment measure Expected Judge Score (Figure 3).
nodes.title: Debate outperforms all other tested protocols on inducing alignment and Expected Judge Score

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 7, lines 10-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports reproducing Khan et al. (2024) with its new metrics: in Debate, higher Expected Agent Score is associated with higher ASD, which the authors take to suggest Debate will keep incentivizing alignment as capabilities scale, while noting this is not a formal guarantee for the superhuman regime.
nodes.title: In Debate, more capable (higher-EAS) agents give higher ASD

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 6, lines 56-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports no significant effect of changing the number of turns or of switching between simultaneous and sequential debate.
nodes.title: No significant effect of debate turns or simultaneous vs sequential debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 4, lines 24-30 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue that evaluating Consultancy by judge score requires assumptions about consultant behaviour, such as Random Consultancy or Open Consultancy (Kenton et al., 2024). They say Random Consultancy is a weak baseline and that experiments with Open Consultancy are heavily biased by the behaviour of current language models, which may not generalize to superhuman AI; their ASD metric needs no such assumption.
nodes.title: Sudhir et al. argue Kenton et al.'s open consultancy is biased by current models' behaviour

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 4, lines 3-10 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say previous debate experiments used Random Consultancy as a baseline and, as Kenton et al. (2024) note, this is still a weak baseline: debate beating it amounts to hearing both sides being better than hearing only the wrong side half the time. They conclude it is only a sufficing result that does not help compare protocols.
nodes.title: Sudhir et al. agree with Kenton et al. that random consultancy is a weak baseline for debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 4, lines 43-46 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that previous debate experiments used debaters' Elo ratings as a capability measure, called persuasiveness in Khan et al. (2024), and correlated them with judge accuracy. They generalize this to other scalable oversight protocols by defining Expected Agent Score as a pure measure of agent capability.
nodes.title: The authors generalize Khan et al.'s Elo persuasiveness measure into Expected Agent Score

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.03731v1 PDF page 7, lines 10-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say they reproduce the finding of Khan et al. (2024) with their new, more general metrics: in Debate, higher EAS is associated with higher ASD. They suggest Debate will continue to incentivize alignment as capabilities scale, though this is not a formal guarantee for the superhuman regime.
nodes.title: Sudhir et al. find higher EAS is associated with higher ASD in Debate, reproducing Khan et al.

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 3, lines 54-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors model domain-specific Elo as a function of general-intelligence Elo with three phases: a plateau below a minimum general intelligence g1 (task incompetence), a linear increase between g1 and g2 (intelligence payoff), and a plateau above g2 (task saturation), written as a difference of two ReLUs with slope alpha.
nodes.title: Double ReLU model: domain Elo vs general Elo with incompetence and saturation plateaus

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 8, lines 34-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that NSO is better than a single step of oversight: multiple oversight steps let Guards oversee much smarter Houdinis, in some regions moving Guard log odds from -3 to 3; that the optimal number of steps grows with Delta_general at fixed Delta_domain; that larger Delta_general at fixed Delta_domain makes oversight easier; and that in Houdini-favoured games (Delta_general < Delta_domain) one step appears optimal.
nodes.title: NSO findings: multi-step oversight beats one step as the capability gap grows

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 1, lines 25-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper proposes a framework that models oversight as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence, with two plateaus for task incompetence and task saturation, validates it on a modified version of Nim, fits scaling laws for four oversight games (Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, Wargames), and then theoretically studies Nested Scalable Oversight, identifying conditions under which it succeeds and deriving the optimal number of oversight levels.
nodes.title: Scaling laws for scalable oversight: Elo oversight games and nested scalable oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 1, lines 49-56 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe recursive reward modeling, iterated amplification, scalable oversight, weak-to-strong generalization and related methods as sharing the goal of weaker systems overseeing stronger ones, and define Nested Scalable Oversight as the iterated process in which weaker systems oversee stronger ones, which then oversee even stronger models at the next stage.
nodes.title: Nested Scalable Oversight (NSO): bootstrapped weak-to-strong oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 40-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their simple debate assumes both debaters faithfully engage adversarially, whereas advanced agents might collaborate to deceive the judge, and that agents may argue some perspectives more effectively regardless of truth; they treat these incentive and systematic problems as out of scope.
nodes.title: Debate game assumes debaters faithfully compete; collusion and side bias out of scope

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 10, lines 10-16 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their oversight settings remain simplified: they simulate only single-step oversight, which may not capture dependencies between steps that compound or attenuate errors; deception is induced by prompting rather than adversarial fine-tuning, since many tested models are proprietary; and Chatbot Arena Elo is a reasonably reliable but imperfect proxy for general intelligence.
nodes.title: Single-step games, prompted deception, and Chatbot Arena Elo as intelligence proxy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 7, lines 95-100 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For a parameterized game, the authors pick a number of oversight steps n and play a chain of games in which each Guard faces a Houdini whose general Elo is Delta_general/n higher, the previous Houdini becoming the next Guard, and seek the n* that maximizes the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities.
nodes.title: NSO model: n oversight games with Elo steps of Delta_general/n, success = product of wins

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 10, lines 17-23 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose applying the framework to more realistic settings such as RLHF, supervised fine-tuning and AI control environments, where the framework's win probability from Eq. (5) would estimate p, the probability that artificial superintelligence escapes human control, which they call the Compton constant for ASI; they also propose generalizing the work to estimate risk over time.
nodes.title: What is the probability that ASI escapes control (Compton constant) in realistic settings?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 31-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that on TruthfulQA, debater (Houdini) performance stays constant with general intelligence rating while the judge's (Guard's) performance scales with it, with similar behaviour on QuALITY and PrOntoQA and mostly flat performance for both roles on BoolQ; the authors read this as promising because an oversight-specialised judge may stay effective against very persuasive debaters.
nodes.title: Debate on TruthfulQA: judge (Guard) performance scales with general intelligence while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 9, lines 72-83 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Assuming all Guards and Houdinis lie on the fitted Elo lines with no saturation, the paper predicts oversight success at a 400-point general Elo gap ranging from 9.4% for Wargames to 51.7% for Debate, noting that a random judge already gets 50% in Debate so its curve converges to about 50%. Win probability generally falls as Delta_general grows, n* increases with Delta_general where mG > mH (Mafia, Debate, Wargames), and Backdoor Code has a zone where two steps are optimal.
nodes.title: Predicted NSO success at a 400-point general Elo gap: 51.7% Debate, 9.4% Wargames

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 7, lines 71-79 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that fitted Elo slopes and intercepts vary widely across games: in Backdoor Code the Guard slope is nearly flat and the Houdini slope steep, while Debate shows a positive Guard slope and a near-zero Houdini slope. The authors conclude effective oversight games should give Guards a higher intercept than Houdinis and a steeper slope.
nodes.title: Guard vs Houdini Elo slopes by game: Debate favours overseers, Backdoor Code attackers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 9, lines 55-66 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors derive that as Delta_domain goes to minus infinity (very hard games for Houdini) n* tends to Delta_general times log(10)/400, explaining the equally spaced vertical lines in Fig. 7; as Delta_domain goes to infinity (very hard games for the Guard) n* tends to 1; and on the line Delta_general = Delta_domain, n* = 1.
nodes.title: Asymptotics of the optimal number of NSO steps n*

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 28-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say they systematically study the scaling behavior of debate as a scalable oversight protocol, modeling their setup on Kenton et al. (2024), with the debaters as Houdinis and the judge as the Guard. On TruthfulQA, Houdini performance stays constant while the Guard's performance scales with general intelligence rating, which they call consistent with prior work including Kenton et al., though that work tested only a few models and did not explicitly compare different judges.
nodes.title: Engels et al. model their debate game on Kenton et al.'s debate setup to study scaling

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 31-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors find that on TruthfulQA their debate judge's (Guard's) performance scales with general intelligence rating, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA but mostly flat performance for both Guards and Houdinis on BoolQ. They state that their observations are consistent with Kenton et al. (2024), who find that judge accuracy may improve with better models, and add that the explicit comparison between different judges had not been undertaken in prior work.
nodes.title: Debate judge (Guard) scaling on TruthfulQA is consistent with Kenton et al.'s finding that better models may improve judge accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 31-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors find that on TruthfulQA the judge's (Guard's) performance in their debate game scales with general intelligence rating while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA but mostly flat performance for both Guards and Houdinis on BoolQ. They state that their observations are consistent with Khan et al. (2024), who find that judge accuracy may improve with better models, and add that prior work tested only a few models and did not explicitly compare different judges.
nodes.title: Debate judge (Guard) performance scales with general intelligence on TruthfulQA, consistent with Khan et al.

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2504.18530v3 PDF page 5, lines 31-39 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors report that on TruthfulQA the Guard's (judge's) performance in their LLM debate game scales with general intelligence rating, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA but mostly flat performance for both Guards and Houdinis on BoolQ, and state that this is consistent with Michael et al. (2023), among prior work finding that judge accuracy may improve with better models. They note prior work tested only a few models.
nodes.title: Judge (Guard) performance scaling in LLM debate is consistent with Michael et al.

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 2, lines 14-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors require a solution to exploration hacking, in which debaters avoid exploring highly rewarded strategies so that these are not reinforced, suggesting for example that eliciting 'bad' contexts could detect it. They argue that with a mostly trusted reward signal one need not look for 'scheming' explicitly, only for an exploration guarantee showing that the model is not foregoing substantial reward.
nodes.title: Exploration guarantees assumption against exploration hacking

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 14, lines 24-27 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors require that simulated human judges are competent at assessing debate outcomes; random errors should wash out over training, so the concern is systematic error, for example from claims playing on human biases or emotions. This needs two claims: the human input being simulated has bounded systematic error with respect to reality, and the simulation has bounded systematic error with respect to the human input.
nodes.title: Good human input: bounded systematic error of human judges and their simulation

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 5, lines 5-13 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The strategy requires a low-stakes deployment context so that online training can minimise the effect of distribution shifts; following Christiano (2021), low-stakes means a few decisions can only cause a small amount of damage, formally that rho times k is small relative to the total value at stake, where rho bounds the utility difference from any single decision and k is the latency before retraining. The authors state that with a perfect training objective total utility could then be kept within a regret bound in rho, k and the number of timesteps T of an aligned system.
nodes.title: Low-stakes deployment assumption enabling online training against distribution shift

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 2, lines 22-30 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors require a debate protocol that avoids the obfuscated arguments problem, in which debaters can win with a false argument whose flaw is computationally intractable for both debaters to identify. The sketch relies on a forthcoming protocol they believe evades the problem, but which requires a stability assumption: that the computation accelerated by debate is not sensitive to small variations in input probabilities.
nodes.title: No-obfuscated-arguments assumption and the stability requirement it brings

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 1, lines 33-43 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors sketch an alignment safety case, an argument that an AI system will not autonomously take actions that could lead to egregious harm, for an AI R&D agent inside an AI company that might sabotage research, e.g. by producing false results. The agent is trained via debate subject to exploration guarantees and kept honest in deployment by online training, and the case rests on four claims: the agent is good at the debate game, good debate performance implies it is mostly honest, it will not become significantly less honest during deployment, and the deployment context tolerates some errors.
nodes.title: Alignment safety case sketch based on debate for an AI R&D agent

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 17, lines 52-54 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state the sketch only works in low-stakes contexts where many bad actions are needed to cause unacceptable outcomes. In high-stakes contexts key claim 4 (that we are in a low-stakes context) breaks by definition, and key claim 3 (that the error rate will stay consistent throughout deployment) breaks because online training can no longer be relied on, opening up alignment faking and other distribution-shift problems.
nodes.title: Safety case covers only low-stakes contexts; claims 3 and 4 break in high stakes

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 36-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors conclude that the argument in the sketch is not strong with current techniques and that much better techniques are needed before developers can rely on alignment arguments, while stating there are useful directions for future research.
nodes.title: The debate safety case argument is not strong with current techniques

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 2, lines 33-40 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list four key claims a developer must defend: (1) training has reached an approximate global equilibrium of the debate game; (2) in approximate global equilibria the system makes mistakes in at most an eps'-fraction of cases; (3) during deployment, with online training, the error rate will not drift past eps; and (4) the system cannot cause unacceptable outcomes given an error rate of eps.
nodes.title: Four key claims of the debate safety case: equilibrium, error bound, no drift, low stakes

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 4-14 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors say there is only limited data on debate's practical effectiveness, with most experiments using the QuALITY dataset and simple low-depth protocols. They list as key questions whether debate measurably improves performance, whether training reliably reaches equilibrium, whether stability is a real problem, whether obfuscated arguments emerge as predicted, how good humans are and what systematic errors they make, and deployment questions such as what counts as an action and whether domain questions are hard to answer with deductive arguments.
nodes.title: Open empirical questions: does debate help, reach equilibrium, show obfuscation?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 15-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors call the requirement for exploration guarantees a major gap: little is known about how serious exploration hacking is or how to prevent it, yet the sketch depends on avoiding it. They call for developing and testing interpretability, singular learning theory and more prosaic approaches, building model organisms of exploration hacking, and possibly addressing gradient hacking for very superhuman systems.
nodes.title: Open: how serious is exploration hacking and how can it be prevented?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 22-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For high-stakes contexts the authors note that online training is lost, so distribution shifts, alignment faking and coordinated errors not captured by the reward signal must be handled another way. They also ask how much honesty plus absence of alignment faking translates into aligned actions during alignment research, and how deployment environments can be designed to minimise risk while keeping the system useful.
nodes.title: Open: extending to high stakes, and how much honesty buys alignment

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 18, lines 35-41 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Among desired properties of improved debate protocols, the authors list as an open question whether prover-estimator debate avoids obfuscated arguments. They also note that lower complexity of reaching equilibrium makes equilibrium models more likely to be findable by stochastic gradient descent, and that for prover-estimator debate it is unclear whether the debaters can be constructed with polynomial-time algorithms.
nodes.title: Open: does prover-estimator debate avoid obfuscation, and are its debaters poly-time?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 18, lines 42-48 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors ask for protocols that do not require stability, since it might not hold for relevant queries, for example by targeting honesty instead of correctness or by transforming an unstable computation into a stable one. They also note that cross-examination punishes debaters for inconsistency across claims at the same recursive level while prover-estimator debate does not, and suggest combining these protocols or finding other solutions.
nodes.title: Open: relax the stability assumption and avoid gerrymandering across subclaims

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 4-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list Arnesen et al. (2024) among the studies of debate's practical effectiveness and say there is only limited data, with most previous experiments using the QuALITY dataset and simple debate protocols with low recursive depth. They list whether training reliably reaches equilibrium among the key questions.
nodes.title: Buhl et al. cite Arnesen et al. among limited data on debate's practical effectiveness

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 13, lines 80-85 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors reproduce Irving et al.'s figure (Figure 8) as an analogy between debate and Go: in both cases a single game with strong players is evidence as to which moves were best. They say their M is equivalent to expanding the whole tree, a computation that produces every possible argument and counterargument at every stage and calls (simulated) human judges to adjudicate every path through the tree; they hypothesize it would produce correct outputs within the question domain, and the goal of their debate protocol is to produce the same outputs more efficiently.
nodes.title: Buhl et al. reproduce Irving et al.'s debate-Go analogy; their M expands the whole tree

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 10, lines 16-27 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In discussing the subclaim that there exists an efficient pair of models achieving an approximate global equilibrium of the game, the authors note that with computationally unbounded debaters, debate with optimal play (and cross-examination) can answer any question in NEXP given polynomial-time judges (Irving et al., 2018). They call the unbounded-debater assumption unrealistic and say a different, realistic efficiency notion is needed.
nodes.title: Unbounded-debater assumption behind Irving et al.'s complexity results called unrealistic

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 4-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors cite Khan et al. (2024) among the studies of debate's practical effectiveness and say there is only limited data: most previous experiments use the QuALITY dataset and simple debate protocols with low recursive depth. They list key questions such as whether training reliably reaches equilibrium and whether obfuscated arguments actually emerge as predicted.
nodes.title: Buhl et al. cite Khan et al. among limited data on debate's practical effectiveness

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2505.03989v3 PDF page 19, lines 4-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors list Michael et al. (2023) among the studies of debate's practical effectiveness and say there is only limited data, with most previous experiments using the QuALITY dataset and simple debate protocols with low recursive depth.
nodes.title: Buhl et al. cite Michael et al. among limited data on debate's practical effectiveness

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 1, lines 27-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper has two AI systems debate opposing sides of controversial factuality claims on COVID-19 and climate change, where people hold strong prior beliefs, comparing debate with single-advisor consultancy for human judges with mainstream or skeptical beliefs (Study I) and for AI judges with and without personas (Study II). It reports that in Study I debate improves human accuracy and confidence calibration, outperforming consultancy by 4-10% across the two domains, most for mainstream-belief judges (up to +15.2% accuracy on COVID-19), while also helping skeptical judges who initially misjudge claims move toward accurate views (+4.7% accuracy).
nodes.title: AI debate helps human judges with strong prior beliefs assess controversial COVID-19 and climate claims

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 4, lines 12-23 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe debate as two GPT-4o debaters arguing opposite positions (true vs false) in strict turns (debater A, debater B, judge) for three rounds, with the judge able to question either debater, highlight issues or ask for clarification; consultancy is a single GPT-4o consultant arguing an assigned position over three structured rounds with judge questions. For COVID-19 the consultant's position is random (50% correct); for climate change consultants choose their preferred position to make a harder baseline.
nodes.title: Interactive debate vs single-sided consultancy with a questioning judge

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 10, lines 41-45 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their experiments are a controlled simulation of debate and consultancy and in-the-wild deployment may differ; that annotators are U.S.-based English speakers selected by belief and demographics; and that each high-stakes domain beyond COVID-19 and climate change needs its own empirical validation before deployment.
nodes.title: Controlled simulation, U.S. English-speaking annotators, two scientific domains

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 4, lines 29-40 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors recruited judges via Prolific with mainstream (scientific consensus) or skeptical views: for COVID-19, 68 qualified participants (34 per belief group) from 650 candidates, giving 448 consultancy and 448 debate sessions after quality filtering; for climate change, 146 participants (73 per group) from 1,000 candidates, giving 421 debate and 424 consultancy sessions.
nodes.title: Human judge recruitment by prior belief: 68 COVID-19 and 146 climate participants

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 16, lines 27-36 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors propose testing persona-aware debate and consultancy with human judges, as they did with persona-conditioned LLM judges, extending beyond binary verifiable claims to manipulated content, satire and propaganda, and running longitudinal studies on initially unresolved prediction-market claims to separate mainstream bias from truth-seeking.
nodes.title: Persona-aware debate with human judges; unresolved claims to separate bias from truth

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 4, lines 50-59 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that debate raises human judge accuracy from 63.2% to 70.1% while consultancy goes from 61.4% to 60.0%, a 10% advantage (p < 0.01); for mainstream-prior judges debate goes from 64.2% to 71.1% while consultancy drops from 63.4% to 55.9% (15.2% advantage, p < 0.01); for skeptical-prior judges debate (62.0% to 69.0%) beats consultancy (59.3% to 64.3%) by 4.7%, not significant (p = 0.2).
nodes.title: Debate 70.1% vs consultancy 60.0% final human judge accuracy

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 5, lines 202-208 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that debate and consultancy produce significantly different answer-transition patterns (chi2 = 19.81, p < 0.01); for mainstream-prior judges debate reduces correct-to-incorrect transitions (8.6% vs 22.9%, z = -4.21, p < 0.01) and preserves correct judgments more often (55.6% vs 40.5%, z = 3.23, p < 0.01), while skeptical-prior judges show similar patterns under both protocols (chi2 = 3.02, p = 0.39).
nodes.title: Debate reduces harmful correct-to-incorrect belief reversals for mainstream judges

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 7, lines 39-47 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that judges are overconfident in both conditions, most at confidence above 80%, but that debate gives significantly better calibrated judgments than consultancy, with a lower Brier score (0.231 vs 0.335).
nodes.title: Judges are overconfident under both protocols; debate Brier 0.231 vs 0.335

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 5, lines 94-96 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that on climate-change claims debate keeps its advantage over consultancy (72.1% vs 68.3%, p < 0.01) even though consultants argued for the correct answer 92.5% of the time, compared with 50% random assignment in the COVID-19 study.
nodes.title: Climate claims: debate 72.1% vs consultancy 68.3% even with 92.5%-correct consultants

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 9, lines 38-49 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that two persona-based LLM judge settings reach 78.5% and, for private-personalized judges, 77.3%, and that both outperform human judges (70.1%; p < 0.01 for both comparisons), suggesting that LLM judges with human-like personas better detect controversial factual arguments after debate. Default LLM judges without personas show comparable performance to human judges, with GPT-4o at 69.8% and Qwen2.5-7B at 70.7% in debate (not statistically significant).
nodes.title: Persona-conditioned LLM judges of debate reach 78.5% and 77.3% vs 70.1% for human judges

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 8, lines 1-8 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Using GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash to rate persuasion strategies, the paper reports that Conflicting Evidence is the most used strategy regardless of judge prior, used more by debaters than consultants (67-68% vs 43-56%), and that incorrect consultants and incorrect debaters use Critical Thinking more often than correct ones.
nodes.title: Persuasion strategies in debate and consultancy: conflicting evidence dominates

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 7, lines 75-86 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that under consultancy participants with mainstream prior beliefs about COVID-19 showed lower accuracy than those with skeptical prior beliefs (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI [0.42, 1.10], p = 0.11), while debate settings showed virtually identical accuracy regardless of belief orientation (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [0.71, 1.71], p = 0.66).
nodes.title: Prior-belief effects on accuracy: consultancy vs debate odds ratios

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 8, lines 56-65 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe standard LLM judges without persona conditioning as the conventional approach used in previous oversight studies [30, 31], and run them as an alternative evaluation. They report that persona-based LLM judges outperform both human judges and these default LLM judges in supervising unreliable experts.
nodes.title: Persona conditioning added to the plain LLM judges of previous oversight studies [30, 31]

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 2, lines 71-82 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors argue that existing debate work overlooks human rationality and judgment, and that judges' prior beliefs have not been considered when evaluating debate's effectiveness, citing [18, 31, 36]. They add that no systematic study has examined whether debate guides judges with divergent prior beliefs toward more accurate judgments than single-advisor consultancy.
nodes.title: Prior beliefs not considered in previous evaluations of debate [18, 31, 36]

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 4, lines 12-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe their debate protocol, two GPT-4o debaters arguing opposite positions over three fixed rounds with judges able to question either debater, and state that it builds on previous interactive debate designs [30, 31, 36]. They pair it with a single-consultant baseline arguing an assigned position.
nodes.title: Three-round GPT-4o debate protocol builds on previous interactive debate designs [30, 31, 36]

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.02175v2 PDF page 9, lines 63-73 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors cite their reference [36] among work showing debate's effectiveness with unreliable experts, and say prior work largely ignores judges who exhibit cognitive biases or hold strong prior beliefs. They state that their work addresses this by testing whether debate remains effective when judges have such biases about controversial topics, using human judges with varying prior beliefs and LLM judges with and without simulated personas.
nodes.title: Gap in prior debate work, including reference [36], on judges with strong prior beliefs

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 3, lines 91-95 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors assume they are given a logical consistency function c(x_i, y_i, x_j, y_j) in {0, 1} that checks whether labels on two data points are logically consistent, and use it to count inconsistencies in the label set so as to rule out degenerate solutions of maximizing mutual predictability alone.
nodes.title: Assumption: a logical consistency function between label pairs is given

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 1, lines 17-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors introduce Internal Coherence Maximization (ICM), an unsupervised algorithm that fine-tunes pretrained language models on their own generated labels without external supervision. They report that on GSM8k-verification, TruthfulQA and Alpaca reward modeling ICM matches training on golden labels and outperforms crowdsourced human supervision, that it elicits strongly superhuman capabilities better than human labels, and that an RL-trained Claude 4 Sonnet-based assistant using an ICM reward model matches its counterpart trained on production-grade human labels on average, with higher chat and safety scores and lower math and coding scores.
nodes.title: Internal Coherence Maximization (ICM): unsupervised elicitation matches golden labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 2, lines 8-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define ICM as searching for a set of labels that are logically consistent and mutually predictable according to the pretrained model, where mutual predictability measures how likely the model infers each label when conditioned on all other labels, which encourages the labels to reflect a single concept. Logical consistency blocks superficially predictable assignments such as giving every point the same label, and because exact maximization is computationally infeasible, ICM uses a search inspired by simulated annealing.
nodes.title: ICM objective: mutual predictability plus logical consistency, simulated-annealing search

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 9, lines 45-50 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that ICM cannot elicit any concepts or skills unless they are salient to the pretrained model, and that unsupervised elicitation might be related to data contamination from pretraining. They cannot verify this directly because the Llama pretraining corpus is not accessible, but cite evidence making it less worrying, such as the production assistant training data not being in Claude 4 Sonnet's pretraining corpus.
nodes.title: ICM limits: only salient concepts; possible pretraining data contamination

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 9, lines 36-44 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that using unsupervised elicitation for alignment would still need humans in the loop, for example applying ICM to constitutional AI by labeling which response follows a human-specified constitution, training an unsupervised reward model and running RL. They add that humans would still need to validate whether the model interprets the constitution as intended, for example using scalable oversight techniques.
nodes.title: Humans still needed to validate unsupervised elicitation, e.g. via scalable oversight

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 6, lines 25-33 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that ICM outperforms zero-shot prompting of commercial chat models that were heavily post-trained on human supervision by a large margin. On TruthfulQA, ICM moderately underperforms the golden label baseline with Llama 8B but performs comparably with Llama 70B.
nodes.title: ICM beats zero-shot post-trained chat models and improves with pretrained model scale

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 7, lines 46-56 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports building 5,000 pairwise preference examples with the description 'Output A is more helpful, harmless, and honest than Output B', labeling them with the authors' method using Claude 4 Sonnet pretrained models, and training a reward model, compared against one trained on production-grade human labels. After RL on 250,000 episodes and scoring on RewardBench by a production-grade Claude 4 Opus reward model, the unsupervised assistant matches its human-supervised counterpart on average, scoring higher on chat and safety and lower on math and code.
nodes.title: Assistant RL-trained on unsupervised-label reward model matches human-supervised counterpart on average on RewardBench

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 9, lines 15-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that removing logical consistency from ICM only moderately worsens TruthfulQA results, because the degenerate same-label solution rarely occurs, whereas logical consistency is crucial on Alpaca, where the degenerate solution almost always happens without it.
nodes.title: Logical consistency matters on Alpaca but only moderately on TruthfulQA

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 7, lines 24-35 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that on author gender prediction from pairs of blog posts, human labels from 5 annotators are perfectly consistent but inaccurate (60% on the test set, 53.8% on the training set), while ICM matches golden supervision at 80% accuracy. Prompting with weak human labels or commercial post-training fails to fully use the pretrained model's superhuman capability.
nodes.title: ICM elicits superhuman author-gender prediction: 80% vs 60% for human labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 6, lines 17-24 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that even with a highly optimized prompt, zero-shot accuracy is often no better than random on the three benchmarks, while ICM matches golden supervision on TruthfulQA and GSM8K without any external labels. On Alpaca, ICM substantially outperforms training with preference labels annotated by real humans.
nodes.title: ICM matches golden supervision on TruthfulQA and GSM8K and beats human labels on Alpaca

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 8, lines 185-191 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: To test whether pretrained models are simply robust to label noise, the authors construct randomly perturbed labels with the same accuracy as ICM's labels and report that ICM-generated labels always achieve substantially better performance with many-shot prompting. They suspect this is because ICM labels are more aligned with the model's own understanding of the task.
nodes.title: ICM labels beat equally accurate randomly perturbed labels

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 7, lines 9-17 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports a task designed to be impossible for unsupervised elicitation: comparison pairs where poems mentioning 'sun' are preferred while the model is only told to judge which poem is better. With Llama 70B, ICM performs no better than random guessing, which the authors attribute to the concept not being salient to the pretrained model.
nodes.title: Unsupervised elicitation fails when the target concept is not salient (sun-poem task)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.10139v2 PDF page 12, lines 53-57 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe CCS (Burns et al., 2022) as one of the most representative works for unsupervised elicitation, which works by solely using simple logical consistency to find latent knowledge, and say that while it moderately outperforms the zero-shot prompting baseline it still significantly underperforms supervised approaches. Citing Farquhar et al. (2023), they add that CCS and other unsupervised approaches often cannot find knowledge.
nodes.title: Wen et al. argue Burns et al.'s CCS, using logical consistency alone, lags supervised methods

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 7, lines 29-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define a recursive decomposition as A-provable with probability 1-gamma if a single strategy A in the set of functions A_n, with probability at least 1-gamma over inputs, answers every query in the decomposition correctly, satisfies A(x, j) = u_j for every j in S_i in the base case of the decomposition (where S_i is the subset given by y_i0), and answers the original question correctly. They describe this as capturing problems where an AI can solve any subproblem if asked and so in some sense 'knows' the answer.
nodes.title: A-provability: one strategy answers every subproblem in the decomposition

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 3, lines 15-21 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that prover-estimator debate makes Alice's task harder because Bob can defeat an argument by assigning low probabilities to many subclaims, which rules out delicate but correct arguments that are highly sensitive to subclaim probabilities. They formalise a rho-stability requirement that argument validity cannot hinge on arbitrarily small changes in subclaim probabilities, and require it only for usefulness, not safety: without stability an honest estimator can still win against any incorrect argument by a dishonest prover.
nodes.title: rho-stability assumption: needed for usefulness, not for safety

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 1, lines 38-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that existing recursive debate protocols suffer from the obfuscated arguments problem, where a dishonest debater can use a computationally efficient strategy that forces an honest opponent to solve a computationally intractable problem to win. They propose a new recursive debate protocol that, under certain stability assumptions, ensures an honest debater can win with a strategy requiring computational efficiency comparable to its opponent.
nodes.title: Prover-estimator debate mitigates the obfuscated arguments problem in recursive debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 2, lines 79-85 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe the obfuscated arguments problem (Barnes, 2020): in recursive debate a dishonest debater can decompose an easy problem into difficult or intractable subproblems, so the honest debater cannot find the flaw even when both debaters know one exists, and the debate fails to identify the correct answer. They state obfuscation emerged naturally in prior empirical work, suggesting it is a likely attractor state in some settings.
nodes.title: Obfuscated arguments problem in recursive debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 3, lines 8-15 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: In prover-estimator debate the prover (Alice) decomposes a problem into subclaims, the estimator (Bob) only assigns probabilities to those subclaims, and the prover uses the probabilities to choose which subclaim to recurse on, unlike earlier protocols where the opponent selects the subclaim to challenge. The authors show Bob can always produce probabilities Alice cannot distinguish from the truth while spending computation not much greater than Alice's, so Alice cannot on average pick a subproblem where Bob is non-trivially wrong.
nodes.title: Prover-estimator debate: prover decomposes, estimator assigns subclaim probabilities

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 13, lines 13-19 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state their results hold in an average-case rather than worst-case sense: they do not prove the judge can tell which debater is correct on every question, only that the payoffs incentivise debaters to converge to answering correctly, so the payoff is a random variable imperfectly correlated with correctness. They call formalising why such average-case analysis is necessary an open question, and ask whether there are lower bounds on B's circuit size for constant rho.
nodes.title: Limitation: average-case guarantees only; judge payoff imperfectly tracks correctness

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 13, lines 31-38 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors frame the broad question as whether some variant of debate works as a component of an overall alignment strategy, pointing to the Buhl et al. (2025) safety case sketch, and hope future protocols combine prover-estimator debate with advantages of other scalable oversight methods. They highlight protocols that mitigate systematic errors in human input and the potential for debaters to hide information in subclaims, noting the safety case sketch has many more holes to fill.
nodes.title: Open: protocols robust to systematic human error and information hidden in subclaims

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 13, lines 1-12 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note the protocol is safe to use without confidence in stability, but a prover that only knows unstable decompositions into solvable subproblems cannot get some problems judged accurately even when both debaters know the answer. They pose whether stability is necessary, suggest problems might split into those needing precise dependence on subclaims (e.g. mathematical proofs, perhaps checked as Lean proofs) and those that do not (e.g. noisy empirical evidence), and say progress requires characterising which problems admit stable decompositions.
nodes.title: Open: is stability necessary, and which problems admit stable decompositions?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 9, lines 46-52 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: With q constant and q^d = O(n^c), the authors state that a single prover-estimator debate costs O(q 2^(3q) n d^3 / eta^2) queries to debater functions, a polynomial improvement over the O(n^c) cost of checking the full human-judgeable transcript when a very stable decomposition exists (rho much smaller than q). They state doubly-efficient debate would need O(n^c) debater queries, while naive recursive debate would either fail soundness or require expanding the whole O(n^c)-size search tree.
nodes.title: Cost of prover-estimator debate vs doubly-efficient and naive recursive debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 9, lines 14-25 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Theorem 6.1 (completeness) states that, for any class of functions on {0,1}^n, a distribution mu on inputs x, a language L in Gamma^O(n^c) with a recursive decomposition M_D of depth d and width q, 0 < gamma < 1/2 and a stability parameter rho, the protocol of Figure 2 run on M_D satisfies the following: if M_D is A-provable with probability 1-gamma over x drawn from mu, achieved by a function A* in the class, and is also rho-stable at x with respect to A* with probability 1-gamma, then there exists A in the class such that for all B (of any size), with probability at least 1-2gamma, E[V^{A,B}(x)] is at least 1/rho^(d+1).
nodes.title: Theorem 6.1 completeness: some A guarantees expected payoff at least 1/rho^(d+1) against every B

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 9, lines 31-42 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: Theorem 6.1 (soundness) states that, with B the set of circuits of size O(q 2^(3q) n d^2 / eta^2) that may query a function A in the class at each gate, for every strategy A there exists B in that set such that the expected value of V^{A,B}(x) over inputs is at most P[A(x) = L(x)]/rho^(d+1) + eta. The authors note that L is required to admit an A-provable, rho-stable decomposition only in the completeness case, which means a dishonest debater A may produce an incorrect decomposition into queries for some input.
nodes.title: Theorem 6.1 soundness: efficient estimator caps a dishonest prover's payoff

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 10, lines 29-37 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that their two main theorems mean debaters can be trained in the prover-estimator debate protocol via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games: if claims are rho-stable and the AI debaters only make claims they actually know the answer to (A-provability), Theorem 6.2 implies A will produce the correct answer with probability at least 1-5 eps. If such decompositions are impossible, the soundness case of Theorem 6.1 implies A's payoff will fall below a known threshold, so training success can be read off A's expected payoff.
nodes.title: Theorem 6.2: correct answers at Stackelberg equilibria (prob. 1 - 5 eps)

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 4, lines 18-22 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that doubly-efficient debate (Brown-Cohen et al., 2024) relaxes the unbounded-debater assumption of the original debate proposal, but at the price of solving a more limited class of problems.
nodes.title: Prover-estimator debate paper: doubly-efficient debate (Brown-Cohen et al.) solves a narrower class

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2506.13609v2 PDF page 4, lines 18-22 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors describe Irving et al. (2018) as introducing AI debate and its complexity-theoretic formalization, and state that this original proposal makes the too-strong assumption that both debaters are computationally unbounded.
nodes.title: Irving et al.'s assumption of computationally unbounded debaters called too strong

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 6, lines 61-67 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define (Definition 2) that in each debate round an agent updates its Dirichlet parameters by adding the counts of answers chosen by its neighbours, and call this a Bayesian belief update from neighbour responses.
nodes.title: Debate modelled as Bayesian count update from neighbours' answers

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 5, lines 64-72 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: For the theory, the authors model each agent at round t by a belief vector over K answer options: it samples a probability vector from a Dirichlet with those parameters and then samples its response from the resulting categorical distribution.
nodes.title: Agents modelled as Dirichlet-Compound-Multinomial samplers over a finite answer set

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 1, lines 15-26 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors split multi-agent debate (MAD) into majority voting and inter-agent debate and, across seven NLP benchmarks, find that majority voting alone accounts for most of the gains usually attributed to MAD. They model debate as a stochastic process, prove it induces a martingale over agents' beliefs so that debate alone does not improve expected correctness, and show that interventions biasing belief updates toward correction improve debate.
nodes.title: Majority voting, not inter-agent debate, accounts for most multi-agent debate gains

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 3, lines 21-28 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors define majority voting as directly aggregating the N agents' initial responses with a voting function V, typically returning the most frequent answer, and multi-agent debate as T rounds of iterative communication on an undirected graph in which each agent, at each round t >= 1, observes the responses of its neighbouring agents at the previous round and updates its answer accordingly.
nodes.title: Formal setup: majority voting over initial answers vs. T rounds of debate on a graph

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 26, lines 56-66 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state that they mainly study the simultaneous-talk protocol, which does not cover alternatives such as one-by-one or simultaneous-talk-with-summarizer that may change rates of subversion and correction. They also state that their theory assumes agent homogeneity and may not directly generalize to heterogeneous agents, and name extending the martingale analysis to agents with differing priors or reasoning abilities as future work.
nodes.title: Limits: mainly the simultaneous-talk protocol studied; theory assumes homogeneous agents

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 23, lines 7-9 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that Proposition 1 provides several sufficient conditions under which equation (1) holds, that other debate graph topologies may also satisfy this condition, and that a complete characterization of such cases is left for future work.
nodes.title: Which debate graph topologies satisfy the condition in equation (1)?

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 7, lines 18-22 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that, estimating the belief in the correct answer as the mean accuracy of the five agents at each round, the trajectories across debate rounds are essentially flat on each benchmark, consistent with a martingale.
nodes.title: Mean agent accuracy stays flat across debate rounds, as the martingale predicts

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 8, lines 309-316 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper proposes MAD-Conformist (an agent keeps its answer if it matched the previous round's majority) and MAD-Follower (an agent adopts the previous majority answer with 30% probability, otherwise samples anew), and reports that both consistently outperform vanilla MAD but do not reach the oracle's upper bound.
nodes.title: MAD-Conformist and MAD-Follower, guided by the majority vote, beat vanilla debate

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 5, lines 1-6 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that MAD does not reliably surpass the simpler majority-voting strategy, which in most cases performs on par with MAD; with the larger Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, overall MAD performance improves but majority voting still accounts for most of the gains. The authors say these findings suggest that MAD's effectiveness is largely driven by ensembling rather than iterative debate.
nodes.title: Majority voting performs on par with multi-agent debate in most cases

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 8, lines 290-296 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The paper reports that MAD-oracle yields substantial improvements over standard MAD and always surpasses the majority-voting baseline by a large margin; for Decentralized MAD with T = 5, MMLU Formal Logic accuracy rises from 0.5000 to 0.6825. The authors note it is infeasible in practice because the true answer is unavailable, and treat it as an upper bound on the benefit of biasing belief updates toward correct signals.
nodes.title: MAD-oracle beats majority voting by a large margin

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 5, lines 83-94 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors state Theorem 1 (Majority Voting Success Probability): with theta-bar the mean of the Dirichlet distribution over K options and the margin Delta := theta-bar_1 - theta-bar_2, if N > K/Delta^2 then majority voting selects answer 1 with probability at least 1 - exp(-N (Delta/sqrt(K) - 1/sqrt(N))^2).
nodes.title: Majority voting success probability approaches 1 as the number of agents grows

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 6, lines 97-107 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors prove that for any agent i at round t > 0, if the average previous-round belief over its neighbours equals the agent's own previous belief (condition (1)), then the agent's belief sequence {p_i,t} forms a martingale: its expected belief at the next round equals its current belief.
nodes.title: Multi-agent debate as a martingale: under condition (1), an agent's expected belief is unchanged

source_refs.locator: arXiv 2508.17536v2 PDF page 25, lines 186-192 of the pdftotext reading-order text

nodes.text: The authors note that prior works [2, 3, 10] reported consistent gains from multi-agent debate over majority voting, and argue that these results may be partially driven by error-prone rule-based answer extraction that can mark correct responses as incorrect.
nodes.title: Authors argue prior reported MAD gains over majority voting may partly reflect answer parsing

Hatem did not report personally checking the probe files. The restricted-oracle, stage-order and Figure 1 probes were added to debate.json on 2026-10-06, after the 2026-10-05 decision; they were not before the reviewer and are listed here by Claude on 2026-10-13. On 2026-10-13 Claude added five Lean-checked examples for the Definition 6.1 readings; the review packet refused promotion for the one combination (𝒪 itself included, strict <) under which no oracle meets the definition.
counterexample_search.result: Literal self-inclusive strict comparison is impossible; Lean's weak predicate does not imply strict comparison at the same k; a restricted query-oracle bound does not imply universal Lean Lipschitzness; a bit-sensitive Bob is outside the checked handoff. None of these refutes the intended paper theorem, and none establishes the correctness-only correspondence. On 2026-10-13: the reviewer's readings avoid the one vacuous combination (𝒪 itself included with a strict <), the restated condition implies Oracle.lipschitz (at_most_without_self_transfers), and distinct zero-distance oracles cannot arise (zero_distance_means_same_oracle).
